The Garland of the Five Hymns:
1. The Laghustava and Carcastava, accompanied by the commentary of Harabhaṭṭa.
Edited by Paṇḍita Dīnānātha Śāstrī, known as Yakṣa,

Part I.
Oṃ, salutations to Tripurasundarī!
She whose body surges with an abundance of supreme bliss, who is immeasurable, and who is deeply immersed in the ocean of the nectar of Paraśiva, which is filled with the jewels of the universe.
May some supreme, indescribable wave of my good fortune manifest, which has arisen as if to wander outside due to its inclination toward grasping [the world]. || 1 ||
Śiva, though full and whose nature is the essence of delighting in his own self, does not remain for even a moment or an hour without her, whose body is the form of limitless innate bliss;
she is the supreme glory of good fortune and the ground of the playful happiness of Paraśiva.
May that Śiva bestow upon us within the auspiciousness of the expansion of the Fullness. || 2 ||
She who, within the mirror of her own self-consciousness, expands the multitudes of existents— arranged in sequence—
in three ways by means of the three powers known as Aparā and the others; she who, in the *Pañcastavī*, shines forth in ever-new forms, is the power called Prātibhā.
May that Śāradā reveal the expressed meanings to me as I desire to provide a commentary. || 3 ||

The marvelous manifestation of the Teacher of Dharma, which delights the minds of the wise, is radiant with the essence of the meaning of sublime speech and filled with the experience of the supreme Great Mantra;
it displays its skill in movement within the young child, in the sky, and even within a jar.
This effort of mine toward her exposition has arisen even from my sincere exhortation.
A Commentary on the *Laghustava* within the *Pañcastavī* (The Five Hymns)

Having first, by its own sovereignty, taken recourse to the ground of the initial vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇana*) which contains within it the flood of sounds of the six pathways of speech (*ṣaḍayana*),
[the Supreme Speech] gradually expands to the ground of the Great Resonance (*mahānāda*), the essence of the unsurpassed aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
I take refuge in that supreme ground of mantra, which is speech that makes the entire universe flavorful.

Oṃ, salutations to Tripurasundarī! Here, indeed, within the teachings of the Supreme Lord consisting of six parts (the Trika), [this work is composed] through a sequence that reveals the relationship between questioner and respondent, by one whose heart is moistened with the essence of the desire to grace those who are to be graced, following the traditional lineage.

By the venerable Lord Sādāśiva himself, having first assumed the roles of teacher and disciple— standing in the positions of both guru and disciple— the Lord Sadāśiva [revealed] the Tantra through statements consisting of preceding and subsequent words, according to the various supports.

According to the principle thus stated, as the sixfold sequence of relations beginning with the Supreme (parā) is introduced, there is but one single reality of supreme consciousness— a mass of light and bliss— which is the true essence of the repose of all cognitions; for it manifests as pervading the entire universe, since its manifestation would otherwise be impossible.

It is taught as being manifest. (That very [reality] is celebrated in the systems of the Anuttara [Trika] as being designated by terms such as *kula* and so forth. It is that which, in the emission whose nature is the expansion of the six paths—from Śiva down to the earth—is about to arise.
Because it cannot endure specific designations such as "the expanding power of Śiva" (*prasara-cchiva-śakti*), it is figuratively designated by names such as "the Unnameable" (*anākhyā*).
As it has been said: (p. 2)
"O Omniscient One! Know that family (kula) in which this variegated universe arises and in which it sets, to be devoid of Śiva and Śakti.
Thus, by its own sovereignty, that very [reality] always possesses the nature of performing the fivefold acts (pañcakṛtya).
For the Lord who is established within himself, there exists indeed the latent impression (*vāsana*) of the multitude of objective states;
without that, the reflective awareness of will (*icchāmarśa*) does not proceed.

According to the state thus described, for the purpose of manifesting the universe— which exists in a state of identity within Himself like the fluid within a peacock’s egg— the Light shines forth in various ways, appearing as a unity of both difference and non-difference like a reflection in a mirror; and even while shining, It withdraws the universe back into Its own self.

Because it is the locus of the emergence and dissolution of the universe, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), and "Brahman is one only, without a second" (Triśikhibrāhmaṇa-mahātāpanīya Upaniṣad 3.3), according to such scriptural passages as "from which indeed these beings are born. And such is that [Being].

Because it consists of the great mantra whose essence is the reflective awareness of that full state of "I-ness," its true nature is the awareness of all signified objects and signifying words made one with one's own self; it is the Supreme Brahman, a single mass of independent Light, or Parā Śakti, through the conceptualization of the division into the aspects of Light (prakāśa) and Reflective Awareness (vimarśa).
It manifests as a divine couple:

"The Lord, having created his own self— which is liberated through freedom— from that non-dual freedom by means of volitions such as 'I am Īśvara' and so forth, engages in worldly transaction" (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.5.47).
According to the principle stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*, although [reality] is of a single, unsurpassed nature, it appears as divided. Thus says the Śruti:
"In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, in the form of a person (*puruṣavidha*). He looked around and saw nothing other than Himself.
He first uttered, 'I am,' and from that the name 'I' arose; therefore even now..."
"Having first said, 'I am this one,' he then speaks another name," and so forth; likewise in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*:
"He did not find delight; therefore, one who is alone does not find delight. He desired a second; thus he became as large as..."
"The two, woman and man, were joined together; he caused this very Self to fall into two parts, and from that there arose the husband and the wife" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.3).
In reality, however, there is only one nature, that of the couple (*yāmala*). As it has been said:
"The Goddess is not without Śiva, nor is Śiva without the Goddess;
there is no difference whatsoever between the two, just as there is none between the moon and its moonlight."
Likewise: "Śiva is not devoid of Śakti, nor is Śakti separated from Śiva;
everything is an unfolding of the couple (yāmala)," and so forth.

With this intention, it has been stated that even when contemplating the entire nature [of the deity], "O Goddess, one should contemplate either the female form or the male form"; thus, it is taught that one should practice the contemplation of the Supreme Deity as non-different from oneself, according to one's desire and without conceptual differentiation. And the Śruti says:
"This is neither female, nor male, nor even neuter;
whatever body it assumes, by that it is protected" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.10).
Also, in the Śrī Bhāgavata:

"He is indeed neither god, nor asura, nor mortal, nor animal; neither female, nor neuter, nor male, nor a living being"—by this, the supreme reality, which is partless, is illuminated. Thus: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman alone; it knew only itself, thinking 'I am Brahman. 'A' is Brahman; therein has the 'I' come to rest" (Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad 6.17).
That very Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā), who consists of unartificial self-reflection (vimarśa) made of the vibration (spanda) of the unsurpassed bliss and other states internalized by the Śruti,
manifests the nature of all mantras and so forth consisting of the Mātṛkā from *A* to *Kṣa*;
and by that very [power] which consists of reflection (*manana*) and protection (*trāṇa*).

By the power of the mantra, having first bestowed the enjoyment of sovereignty over various worlds and so forth, it unites those who are to be favored— whether they have been favored or not— with liberation, making them the sole recipients of both worldly enjoyment and emancipation;
thus, at each respective occasion, it joins them with the supreme Brahman, whose nature is characterized by the reality of supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvitti*).

This will be demonstrated. As for the sequence of the vibration (*sphurattā*) of mantra: the Supreme Goddess Śakti, desiring to manifest the universe through her own sovereignty, first transforms into prior consciousness within the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Thus, by means of this statement, she takes recourse in the plane of animation (*prāṇana-bhūmikā*), which consists of the vibration of the vital breath and so forth.

The venerable Great Sound (Mahānāda-bhaṭṭāraka), which contains within it the manifold expansion of words and meanings consisting of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) in the nature of the signified and the signifier, [arises] through the causal sequence as Paśyantī and Madhyamā.

In the form of *vaikharī* speech, she unfolds as the wonder of her own self. Among these, in *paśyantī*, because the distinction between the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*) is indistinct, there is no manifestation of sequence at all, since its nature is solely that of the seer. In *madhyamā*, however, because those two are both distinct and indistinct...
The sequential emergence [of speech] occurs as follows:

in *vaikharī*, however, the apprehension of the sequence of specific phonemes—which are manifested by relying on the points of articulation (*sthāna*), the vocal organs (*karaṇa*), and the effort (*prayatna*)—is clearly evident; thus, in every respect, it brings about the wonder of the reflective awareness of the Great Mantra.

Kulasundarī, whose nature is the devouring of the manifold expansion of the appearance of all differentiation, even on the level of *vaikharī* speech, exists as the three-syllabled *tryakṣarī*. By means of her own non-differentiated instrument in the form of the principal mantra,
she removes the state of limited subjects manifested through the contraction of her own will, [revealing] the state of the entire universe.

With the intention that [the Lord] leads his own devotees to the ascent upon the stream of the fully inlaid universal *ahaṃbhāva* (I-consciousness), the author of the hymn, having himself attained the state of the Supreme Deity through the fulfillment of his purpose,
and being intensely filled with the essence of the great joy and exuberance arising from the manifestation of His divine power (*vibhūti*), [proceeds] himself...

Taking his stand upon the fulfillment of his purpose, and out of a natural inclination toward benefiting others, he begins with a hymn of praise to the Illustrious Supreme Deity— a hymn preceded by the expansion of blessings and grace, and which introduces the nature of the mantra and its presiding deity. Therein, [he speaks] of the Illustrious Mahātripurasundarī...
He teaches, by way of general praise, the presiding deities of the vidyās and the fruits of their worship:
"Bearing a brilliance like that of Indra’s bow between her eyebrows..."
Spreading a whiteness like that of the moon upon her head on all sides,
this very Tripurā— like the radiance of the sun always present within the heart—
is composed of light and speech; may she suddenly sever your sin with her three steps.

This very Tripurā is she who is recognized through the unity of the continuous succession of the shining manifestations; she is that whose "cities" (*puraḥ*)—meaning bodies—are the three powers, namely Will and the others, which are of the nature of the supreme, the non-supreme, and so forth.
As it is said in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*:
That power of the Creator of the universe which has been described as inherent (samavāyinī),
that goddess assumes the nature of will (icchātva) when He desires to emit [the world].
"It must be known that this is so, and not otherwise"— making this known with absolute certainty, the power of internal knowledge is called *jhagiti* in this world (*kārikā*).
Furthermore, when one thinks, "Let this object become such as it is," (7.14)
"Then that very thing, while being produced, is called 'action' (kriyā) here.
(8.15). This is because of the Śruti: "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold; knowledge, strength, and action are inherent [to Him]" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8).
Here, "strength" (bala) should be understood as "desire" (icchā). Or else, from the three...

She is called Tripurā because she is filled with, proceeds toward, and is known as the essential nature of the support for the knower, the act of knowing, and the object of knowledge; she is thus of the nature of peace (śāntātmikā). As it has been said:
"The entire universe consists of the threefold set (tripuṭī), and that too is equal within both the object of knowledge and the knower."
The digit of knowledge, though possessing a firm knot, pervades the three worlds in a single moment.

Thus, the primordial power (*śakti*), which is non-different from Brahman, consists of the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of powers such as Will (*icchā*) and culminates in the power of Peace (*śāntā*);

she is that very power designated by the term "Śrī Tripurā. Following the manifestation of her essential nature as the desire to create and so forth, she accomplishes the tasks of the universe's emanation and other functions by assuming forms characterized by the respective powers (*śaktimat*) permeated by those [individual] powers.

With the intention that she is experienced by all people in various ways— assuming designations accordingly as she extends even to the state of the limited subject whose nature is perceivable through direct perception—
it is referred to here by the word "eṣā" (this), which expresses immediate presence. Furthermore, she herself...
As the locus of rest for the emergence of the manifold universe in its various forms of the threefold city (tripuṭī),

she is recognized through her true oneness— remaining as the mass of Being-Consciousness-Bliss during states such as meditative absorption and deep sleep— as if veiled by the manifestation of space and time fashioned by her own will.
By the phrase "they are referred to by 'this' (adas) in accordance with the state denoted by that word," this praise— through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—

culminates in a real non-difference. Thus, in the first verse, the author of the hymn indicates that the supreme fruit of the reflective awareness of the nature of the Supreme Deity, who consists of one's own consciousness, is [attained].

He has indicated this through a stylistic turn: "In this way, during the states of the universe's emergence, maintenance, and dissolution, there exists a certain Fourth state (*turyā*) which is the Goddess whose nature is self-awareness and who is devoid of the condition of destruction. It is precisely with this intention that the *Śrīvāmakeśvara* states:
"O Dear One, Tripurā is the supreme primordial power, arising from knowledge and the rest."
Having begun thus: "This is that supreme power, the one and only Supreme Goddess. (p.
The goddess Tripurā is threefold, having the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa.
"O Dear One, she whose nature consists of the power of knowledge, the power of action, and the power of will creates the three worlds; she is celebrated as Tripurā.
Having practiced in the center—
"The Unmanifest herself, having attained the name Tripurā, rejoices" (4pa 4-16)— up to this point,
the Supreme Lord has explained the true nature of the meaning regarding the method of etymological derivation for the term *Tripurā*.
Also, in the *Vārāhīya*:
"In ancient times, she was worshipped by the thirty gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa;
therefore, the name 'Tripurā' was given to you by the deities.

Although, according to the Āgamas, the word *tripurā* [is derived from] being prior to (*purā*) the three—namely the qualities (*guṇa*), the seed-syllables (*bīja*), the seats (*pīṭha*), the worlds (*loka*), and so forth—...

Although it has been explained through many such modes of interpretation, if all those various explanations were presented together in one place, the treatise would become excessively voluminous from the very beginning. Therefore, for fear of causing distress to the minds of those to be trained, I desist from this; other interpretations will be provided in their respective places further on.
They will be demonstrated. In the *Tripurārṇava*, however, it is said:
"The three channels—Suṣumnā, Piṅgalā, and Iḍā—are Tripurā;
likewise, mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and consciousness (*citta*) are declared to be the three cities."

"She dwells here and there; therefore she is considered Tripurā. Thus, for you devotees who are intent upon the recitation (*japa*) and other practices of your own *vidyā*, *agha*—the sin consisting of the nature of the impurities of *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika*—is, because it is the cause of the bondage of worldly existence, always and at all times [destroyed].

One should suddenly, without delay, and unexpectedly, by the force of the most intense descent of power (*śaktipāta*), sever and withdraw [the bondage] in such a way that the constraints and mechanical fetters of the multitude of unpracticed means are destroyed.
The optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of an aspiration: "May he become inclined toward bestowing grace by cutting away the mass of evil deeds."

By this, the binding of the steps on the ladder of the sequence known as "non-means" (anupāya), which manifests the aspiration for the ultimate goal—the pinnacle of the Nīla [Tantra]—is revealed. In that context, knowledge (*jñāna*) is bondage.
(1.2) (3.2) "The class of wombs (*yonivarga*) is the body of the *kalā*s. (1.3) Thus.

According to the principle stated in the *Śrīśivasūtra*, [the object] is a particular portion of the reality of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*), whose essential nature is a mass of perfect light and bliss.

Therefore, it is characterized in the scriptures as threefold: the manifestation of diverse objects of cognition known as *māyīya* (the illusory), and that which consists of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of auspicious and inauspicious karma known as *kārmam* (the karmic).
This has been stated by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva:
The loss of freedom in consciousness, and the lack of consciousness in freedom—
this twofold atomic impurity arises from the forfeiture of one's own true nature.
"Right here, the manifestation of differentiated objects of cognition is called *māyā*, which bestows birth and experience;
when there is non-awareness in the agent, it is *kārma* [karma]; yet all three of these arise solely through the power of *māyā*. (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 3.2.20).
Thus, the very nature of the removal of impurity (*mala*) is the well-known traditional teaching regarding the ultimate reality.

The essential meaning to be understood here is that it makes resound its own stainless, consciousness-natured essence. As the Śruti declares: "Just as the tuft of a reed-stalk thrown into a fire is consumed, even so are his evils consumed.
Likewise—
Sin does not attach itself even to a Brāhmaṇa who is constantly engaged in recitation, provided he is endowed with knowledge and austerity, even if he is a performer of evil deeds.

Sins do not dwell with those who recite prayers, those who perform fire-sacrifices, those who practice meditation, those who reside at sacred fords, and those who have bathed while observing the head-vow.
Thus says the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti. Likewise, in the Puṣkara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa: "Even a heap of sinful karma as large as Mount Meru perishes in a mere instant upon reaching Kātyāyanī."

"The hero who is constantly devoted to the worship of Durgā is not tainted by the defects arising from great sins (mahāpātaka), just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. Thus it is said. Also in the Devībhāgavata:
Even after cutting, piercing, and killing all beings, and having destroyed this entire world,
one who bows his head to the Goddess is not defiled by sins.
"Whether one has fallen into every possible state or is joined with all manner of sins, a man who beholds Durgā becomes purified and proceeds to the supreme abode. (p. 8) and so forth.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Even for those most sinful men who are devoid of caste (varṇa) and stage of life (āśrama),
by the mere meditation upon His form, their evil deeds turn into meritorious ones."

Here, having set aside any aspiration for his own sake by means of the phrasing "for you," the illustrious author of the hymn, the teacher of Dharma, reveals within himself an inclination toward a purpose centered solely on the benefit of others— an inclination that takes the form of a "remainder" (*śeṣavṛtti*).

This indicates that, although all desires have been attained, because one has accomplished what was to be done, all stains and delusions of worldly and transcendental conceptualization have dissolved away.
As it was said by the venerable Abhinavagupta:
For one whose nature is to shatter the entire web of constraints and mechanisms,
there is no purpose whatsoever in maintaining a residual mode of existence other than [bestowing] grace.

This world, perceiving its own duty as something to be accomplished, strives with effort, yet it does not direct any of its own activity toward the welfare of others. But he who has destroyed all the impurities of worldly existence and is filled with the state of Bhairava—
"His duty is clearly this much alone: the performance of what is required for the world.
And it is remembered in the Smṛti:
"But that man who should find delight only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self,"
"And for one who is satisfied in the Self alone, there is no duty to be performed" (Bhagavad Gītā 3.17).
"O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that must be done by Me;
there is nothing unattained to be attained, yet I continue to engage in action" (Bhagavad Gītā 3.22).

And by the phrase "thus one should cut off evil," it is indicated that the very absence of sin is the increase of dharma; thus, the fourfold aims beginning with dharma are also characterized by the cutting off of evil.
The nature of the Śrī Tripurā-vidyā as a means of accomplishment (sādhana) is indicated [here]. As it is stated in the *Prapañcasāra*:
"The seed-syllable Vāgbhava is said to bestow the excellence of sovereignty over speech;
furthermore, it effects the agitation of the three worlds, subjugation, and attraction."
The King of Desire (*kāmarāja*), which effects agitation, subjugation, attraction, and the granting [of boons] (as accomplished by Ārtharaeva-lāna), p. 9.
This seed-syllable of Śakti is said to remove poison, bestow poetic talent,
and grant the wealth of Dharma, worldly pleasure, and liberation to practitioners. (9.4)
Thus [it is said].
Of what nature is she? She is characterized by the three places, such as the forehead and so forth, which are indicated by the three feet just mentioned, and which are perceived within them.

The meaning is that she is being perceived in those locations, which serve as indicators (upalakṣaṇa) for the true upāsaka practitioners. The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of a qualifying characteristic (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, she is also [described] as "she whose indicators are the three cities—the heart and so forth—which are the very nature of the mass of self-luminous consciousness."
He explained the method for etymologically interpreting the word *Tripurā*:
"By this—'With the senses dissolved in the space of the heart, situated in the midst of the lotus-calyx, with a mind focused on nothing else, O Fortunate One! one shall attain supreme good fortune.'"

It should be understood that [the Lord] also favored this group of means described in such passages as: "The manifestation of the dream-object occurs in the heart through the impact of the mind. Furthermore, he is characterized by the three words which, through the composition of the treatise, suggest the essence of the syllables of the *vidyā*.

"Śrī" means the form of knowledge (*vidyā*). Consequently, because she existed prior to the three—the seeds of speech, desire, and power (*vāk-kāma-śakti-bīja*), which consist of the powers of knowledge and so forth presided over by Brahmā and the others—she is "Tripurā. Thus, he introduces another etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) that presents his own intended wonderful view as her collective essence (*tatsamaṣṭisvarūpa*).

Now, in response to the inquiry, "What is the essential nature of this supreme deity named Śrī Tripurā?", he states her unique defining characteristic, beginning with the words "consisting of light" (*jyotirmayī*).
Because she is the very life-force of limited lights such as those of the sun and so forth, she illuminates everything without exception.
With its own radiant form, it has surpassed all other light; everything shines only after it shines, and by its light all this universe is illumined.
"Indeed, O Gārgī, it is by this [Brahman] that the sun and the moon stand held apart," according to the Śruti (p.
10); and thus:
"Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines That."
And because of such Smṛti passages as these; and for this very purpose, the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta explained it as follows:
"Where neither the sun, nor the moon, nor even fire shines..."

"Nor is there any light belonging to the sun, moon, or fire that exists independently of its manifestation; rather, consciousness itself shines forth in this manner. By this, since it is self-luminous, there is no operation of means of valid cognition such as perception and the like therein.

It has already been demonstrated that there is no utility in establishing [the existence of] a signifier (*jñāpaka*) and so forth. Nor should it be argued that because the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed in the senses of "modification" (*vikāra*) and "part" (*avayava*), there would consequently follow here [in the case of the *tathāgatagarbha*] the occurrence of transformation (*pariṇāma*) and the like;
for by means of a formal split (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *nityaṃ vṛddha-śarāvādibhyaḥ*, the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied in the sense of identity (*tādrūpye*).

This is to be resolved by the fact that [it] has been so ordained. Since that supreme light (*paratejaḥ*) is filled with the universe, its nature is indeed inherently and non-artificially constituted precisely by the full awareness of "I" (*aham-parāmarśa*), which is its necessary correlate. Otherwise, in the absence of such reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), [it would not be consciousness].
"She is to be worshipped by means of the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, which is a mere radiance in the form of crystal. This is stated in the *Saubhāgyahṛdaya*:
"In the womb [of the triangle], she has the luster of a mass of gold; in the heart, she is like a flash of lightning."
O Maheśvarī, your great splendor in the Ājñā-cakra is like the moon.

In this way, each individual [seed-syllable] is to be known as Śrī Tripurā under the names of Fire, Sun, Moon, and Kuṇḍalinī, because she is the collective totality (samaṣṭi) of their splendors. Thus, the locations for the seed-syllables of the Vidyā are to be understood according to the sequence described above; however, they are not to be determined by a similarity to the specific locations mentioned for each individual syllable as suggested by the aforementioned quarters (pādas).
This will also be stated later in the second hymn, in the verse beginning "the moon shining upon the crest. Thus,

it is well-known in the Āgamas that these seed-syllables— Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti— which are indicated by the structure of this composition, bestow the fruits of dharma, kāma, and mokṣa, and are non-different from the venerable Tripurā.
As it has been stated in the venerable *Vāmakeśvarīmata*:
"In the *vāgbhava* [syllable], Vāgīśvarī is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), whose form is liberation;
in the *kāmarāja* [syllable], she is the digit of desire (*kāmakalā*), whose nature is action (*kriyā*) and whose form is desire."
"In the seed-syllable of Śakti, Parā-Śakti is indeed Will (icchā) in the form of Śiva.

with his mind fixed on *kumbhaka*, should cause the vital air to move upward.
By the power of the support of the wind, the fire situated in the Svādhiṣṭhāna blazes;
awakened by the impact of that blazing fire and the blow of the wind, the sovereign serpent is aroused.
Then, having pierced the Brahma-knot, one pierces the Viṣṇu-knot;
and having indeed split the Rudra-knot, one pierces the six lotuses.
In the thousand-petaled lotus, Śakti rejoices together with Śiva;
that state is to be known as the supreme (parā), and it alone is the cause of liberation from worldly existence.

Thus, by the phrase "always, at all times," it is indicated that such a state— which consists of the non-manifestation of the vital breaths and so forth in every living being— is not delimited by time within one's own self. Of the universe...

[She] is that [power] by whom effort is exerted toward the act of generating— that is, the process of production— of the entire expansion of the six paths (ṣaḍadhva), which consists of the nature of the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge, or the class of desirable entities, or the essence of the signified and the signifier, according to the sequence of the unfolding of the [powers] such as Paśyantī.

This refers to the fact that consciousness, by its very nature, possesses the inherent capacity to manifest all objects of knowledge and effects as external forms through its own self-surging, because it is the agitator [of the universe]. This is stated here as being established by its own nature, characterized by a firm exertion and a spontaneous intensity of engagement.
As it has been stated by the venerable Abhinavaguptapāda:
"The nature of consciousness is agitation; it is both agitated and it agitates.
Agitation is the state of being an attribute of the object of knowledge, while the act of agitating (kṣobhaṇā) is its externalization."
The desire to emit, which is a portion of the single seed-syllable that is non-different from the universe yet resides within it, is "agitation" (kṣobha).
They know that agitation to be the manifestation of the will toward that [emission], while the will itself is the state of being that [will].
"When that desire, having attained oneness, becomes effective, the disciples of the venerable Somānanda call this the 'substratum of arousal' (kṣobhādhāra)" (Tantrāloka 3.82).
An exposition of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) will be elaborated upon later. This [which is]...
Furthermore, that very Supreme Speech (*parāvāk*), whose nature is inseparable from Kāmeśvara— the essence of the mass of unsurpassed bliss—

is the cause of the manifestation of the universe; because it takes the form of the acceptance of the desire to manifest externally, it is known by the name *paśyantī*, which is the nature of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*).

23) Because of the predominance of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), it is determined as the "intermediate" (*madhyamā*) state, since it extends itself as a mere modification of the intellect (*dhī-vṛtti*). This is due to the predominance of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).

Furthermore, when manifested through the activity of the organs such as the palate, this play of speech known as *vaikharī-vāk*— consisting of the manifold sounds, both worldly and transcendental— is in its totality the very expansion of the powers of will (*icchā*) and the rest. As it was said by the venerable Abhinavagupta:
First is Paśyantī, then another is Madhyamā, and [the third] is Vaikharī; these are the goddesses Parā, Parāparā, and the last is of the nature of Aparā.
"This very triad of powers, beginning with Will (icchā), is thus described; it is only when animated by this that worldly activity unfolds" (Tantrāloka 1.271–272).
Likewise, in the *Uttara-catuḥśatikā*:
Thus, this very power of will (icchā-śakti) exists in the form of Paśyantī;
likewise, the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) is declared to be the speech known as Madhyamā.
"But this power of action is Raudrī, who is Vaikharī and whose form is the universe.

Thus, having known that Supreme Space— the power of consciousness of Brahman— whose essence is the manifestation of the universal "I-consciousness," because it is the nature of the life-force of all things in the manner described above;

The meaning is that those people who, having recognized [the Self] as non-different from their own nature, have been purified by the descent of the Supreme Lord’s power (pārameśvara-śaktipāta), do not again touch the state of being an embryo— the state of a child— within the womb of a mother; that is, they are not born again.
"Indeed, there is nothing further to be known" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.12).
According to the Śruti: "Having known Him alone, one transcends death" (Muṇḍaka Saṃhitā), and "Having known Him, one goes beyond death" (Haṃsa Upaniṣad 4).
And as it is said: "Upon knowing the God, there is the falling away of all bonds" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.11).
This is because they possess knowledge of the secret of such supreme, perfect worship, which is attainable by those of such superior qualification.
The meaning is that [liberation occurs] at birth. And the Śruti says:
"For him there is delay only as long as he is not released; then he shall be united" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2).
"He does not return again" (Nirāloka 33). And the Smṛti says: "That supreme abode of mine, having gone to which they do not return" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.6).
"Of one who fosters non-return.

Thus, the primary fruit of the practice of *sanādabindu* as described above has been stated to be liberation itself. We—whose hearts are confident through such contemplation and inquiry—*manmahe*, that is, we understand and realize.

The meaning is that we solemnly affirm this. By the word "touching," since even the mere touch of the mother's womb is prohibited, it is stated that contact with her clothing is all the more utterly excluded. By the word "they," [it refers to those] who [are characterized by] the function of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) animated by the continuous recollection of what has been previously experienced.
It reveals one's fitness as a recipient of grace by generating the bliss of immersion in You, which arises from the abundance of worship previously practiced. || 2 ||

Having thus described the fruit of meditating upon a single portion of the initial seed-syllable, he now extols the greatness of the complete recitation and meditation on the seed-syllable by means of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic, while proclaiming the fruit of the remaining portions of the seed-syllable, which consists in the perfection of the flow of speech:

O Giver of Boons! O Goddess! when even he who, upon suddenly seeing a startling object, involuntarily utters "ai ai" here—even though devoid of the nasal dot (bindu)—certainly attains Your grace immediately through that very act.
From the lotus of his mouth issue forth words that discharge the flowing essence of the nectar of well-spoken verses.

"O Giver of Boons!"—this has been explained in the immediately preceding verse. By the statement "by whatever person, whoever they may be," it is indicated that there is no restriction regarding the division of eligibility for the worship of Śrīvidyā.
Therefore, even by one who is unexpectedly possessed by fear and so forth in this world...
Upon seeing some object— such as a tiger or other predatory creature that has suddenly appeared, which causes agitation and generates a surge of fear— one may,
even out of curiosity or for the purpose of dispelling fear and so forth, utter the syllable "ai ai" incidentally, even without the nasal dot (bindu).

Because it was uttered with a lapse [of memory], it would be devoid of the *anusvāra*, consisting of the seed-syllable of the first letter of the *vidyā*, and spoken or recited in an incomplete manner.
O Goddess! She is called *Devī* because she plays (*dīvyati*) and sports;

this very play consists in her shining forth as the soul of the entire universe—from Śiva down to the earth—within the ether of her own self through her sovereignty, by the excellence of her nature as a mass of bliss, and entirely independent of any purpose regarding what is to be rejected or accepted. Thus:

She plays and desires victory, thus she is the Goddess (*devī*). This very desire for victory is the wish to exist with preeminence over the universe manifested by her own will; likewise, she plays and acts, thus she is the Goddess. And this "acting" (*vyavahāra*) consists of the objects of cognition and so forth, whose nature is the manifestation of non-ultimate difference.
It is the internal discourse within one's own undivided self, in the form of "I have expanded" and "I know this.

Likewise, it is *devana*, which means shining; and that is the manifestation of the entire universe consisting of subjects and objects, as well as the class of subjects beginning with the Mantramaheshvaras and their corresponding objects of knowledge.

She is called *Devī* because she is praised (*divyate*) and extolled (*stūyate*) by those who, from the moment they attain their own essential nature (*svarūpalābha*), act in dependence upon her and remain bowed before her. Likewise, she is called *Devī* because she knows (*devyati*), that is, she perceives and expands forth, due to her being the very essence of the powers of perfect knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā-śakti*), which are undifferentiated and all-pervasive through both cognition and emanation. Thus it is stated in various scriptures.

The etymological derivation of the word *Devī*. This will be elaborated upon later. O You whose nature is the play of protecting the entire universe without exception! By the maxim that "fire indeed burns even one who has been touched by it unintentionally," when Your grace—which is characterized by the descent of the supreme *śakti* and Your favor—has arisen and occurred; [then...]

Because their hearts have been purified by that [grace], there is no obstacle of temporal delay whatsoever; rather, it occurs instantly, immediately upon the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). Their words are such that they emit—that is, they flow forth—*sūktayas*, which are utterances of sweet and captivating eloquent speech, acting as streams of the essence of nectar, like a downpour of the taste of immortality.
They issue forth, they emerge from the lotus-face, the lotus-like mouth; this is indeed certain, this is surely a fact.
Alternatively, "dhruvam" (certainly) may be used for the purpose of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*); by that, the meaning is "we fancy.
[As it is said: "By such words as *manye*, *śaṅke*, *dhruvam*, *prāyaḥ*, *nūnam*, and so forth [poetic fancy is expressed]."
The poetic conceits (utprekṣās) are manifested by words; the word "iva" (as if) is also of such a nature.

From this statement by the learned, it is suggested by the word "by whom" (*yena*) that, regarding the scope of both the wise and the ignorant, there is no distinction in the grace characterized as the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). By the word "thereby" (*tarasā*), it is expressed that the means for attaining knowledge and supernatural powers (*vidyāsiddhi*) are independent of the attainment of results. By the word "also" (*api*), there is a sense of wonder because of the lack of dependence on fixed periods of recitation (*japa*) and so forth.

It is illuminated [by this]: if even when devoid of the bindu—meaning even in an incomplete pronunciation—it is sufficient for obtaining the fruit of Sarasvatī, how much more so when accompanied by the bindu? Here, the repetition (vīpsā) is used to indicate urgency. As it has been stated in the *Catuḥśatī*:
And the seed-syllable situated in the center is intended solely for the ritual application of speech;
it is designated as the supreme syllable in the Rudrayāmala Tantra.
Thus it is said; likewise, in the third book, ninth chapter of the Devībhāgavata, Dvaipāyana says to Janamejaya:
"Even a name that is indistinct, if spoken even in passing..."
It bestows all desired objects, even those that are in every way difficult to attain.
If one cries out "Ai! Ai! out of fear upon seeing a tiger or other wild beast in the forest, even if uttered without the nasal drop (bindu), it indeed grants one's desired wish.
In this regard, O best of kings, the example of Satyavrata is evident even before our eyes,
as it was witnessed by us sages of purified souls.
O King, I have heard in its entirety and in great detail that example being recounted by the wise among the assemblies of brahmins.
There was a twice-born man named Satyavrata, who was illiterate and a great fool;
having heard a syllable from Kolamukha, he then himself began to utter it.
Due to the omission of the nasal drop (bindu), he was born as that most excellent of the wise;
at the mere utterance of the vowel "ai," the Blessed Lady was then pleased.
The Supreme Goddess, moist with compassion, made him a king of poets;
and that twice-born man, Kavi Satyavrata, became renowned throughout the three worlds.
And so forth. In this way, the greatness of the seed-syllables of Vidyā and the rest is demonstrated in two ways: by the fruit of liberation and by the fruit of the flow of eloquent speech.

This is the underlying meaning here: while the attainment of results occurs upon the successful worship of other deities according to the prescribed rules, for this [Vidyā], [the result arises] even with the mere utterance of its name, though indistinctly and impurely.

Even as a secondary consequence (*prasaṅgataḥ*), the fourfold aims of human life (*puruṣārthacatuṣṭayī*), beginning with dharma, are accomplished. How is it that she is not to be propitiated by all? This will be corroborated by the illustrative narrative of Satyatapas, which is about to be told.
Thus, the fruit of the worship of the second seed-syllable, *kāmarāja*, is not merely the subjugation of kings and the like.

However, even a single part of that [mantra] possesses the power to bestow the grace of Sarasvatī, just like the previously mentioned seed-syllable *vāgbhava*; this is illustrated by the following citation:
"O Eternal One! Your other syllable of the mantra, *kāmarāja*, is partless (*niṣkala*)."

Only some rare wise man on earth understands that this is the *Sārasvata* [Purāṇa], as the twice-born recite at the beginning of every section this narrative of Satyatapas, which is devoted to the seat of the *Praṇava*. (Note: The variant reading *praṇayitām* is also acceptable, meaning "devotion" or "affection.")
Having led [them], they clearly utter [the mantra]. || 4 ||

That which is called "eternal" (nitya) is devoid of temporal succession; likewise, the supreme consciousness (parā saṃvit), although manifesting in the form of the knower, the known, and so forth, is eternal because, according to the established principle that "this Self shines forth all at once," there is no interruption in its activity of manifestation.

Because it is not delimited by time, it takes recourse in a nature that never sets. Furthermore, unlike other actions, its delimitation by time is not possible due to its sequential nature, because it is non-worldly (alaukika). As they say:
"And the sequentiality of worldly action arises from the power of time."
But it does not apply to that which is eternal; for it would follow [absurdly] that the eternal possesses a beginning, just as a lord possesses power.
Thus it is said elsewhere:
"Even as consciousness surges forth, because it is devoid of temporal succession,
it is already arisen, full, and takes on the form of the subject, the object, and so forth."

Thus [he says]. Therefore, O Eternal One! since You are not delimited by time, Your essential nature is that of the supreme consciousness which never sets; for in reality, Consciousness is beyond the categories of eternal and non-eternal—intending this very point, the venerable feet of Utpaladeva also said in his *Muktakas*:
"That which is neither 'not then,' nor 'always,' nor even 'at one time'—wherein no conception of time occurs—that is this Your own teaching; it is neither eternal, nor is it described otherwise.
(Uttara-stotra 12) Or else, [it refers to] the fifteen [energies] beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā.

Among the Nityās of the lunar days (*tithi-nityās*), whose nature is figurative eternity, the sixteenth is the Nityā named Śrī Mahātripurasundarī; she possesses the quality of non-figurative, unceasing eternity because she is the locus of their dissolution and emergence. As it has been said:
There is only one supreme Great Lord, known as Light,
whose power called Vimarśa is proclaimed by the wise to be eternal.

Thus: O Eternal One! O Thou whose nature is supreme consciousness unconditioned by time! That which is Thy *Kāmarāja*—residing in the venerable *Śrīvidyā*, the "King of Desires" (*kāmarāja*) being so called because it is sovereign over all desired objects (*kāma*), like a universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*) capable of bestowing them through its independence as it requires nothing else—that second, other syllable of the mantra; [that is, the syllable *Klīm*].

If it is argued that the Śrīvidyā is of the nature of the supreme syllable (parārṇa), which is "partless" (niṣkala) because the letters *ka* and *la* have departed from it— thus being merely the fourth vowel (*turyasvara*) and producing the Siddhi of eloquence and other gifts born of Sarasvatī’s grace— then [it follows that] such a person is rare, not every one among thousands of men.

Someone on this earth—praiseworthy due to the descent of an intense *śaktipāta* that has arrived—may understand or realize [this]. For generally, among all people, he possesses knowledge such as the power to bestow sovereignty and the ability to subjugate others. That wise man would be a poet, his fame renowned through the power of his scholarship in the fourteen branches of learning; he is rare.

From this statement, the rarity of such knowledge is indicated; or rather, he who knows is the wise one, and that alone constitutes his state of being a knower. Otherwise, even if one were to obtain knowledge beyond that, it would be pointed out as being largely devoid of essence.
By this, it is stated that even a single part of *kāmarāja* possesses a meaning identical to that of the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable. Thus...

Having demonstrated through the first half [of the verse] that Kāmakalā is also Sarasvatī, he states the second half by way of providing the reason for its further strengthening as a generator of clarity of speech, preceded by the presentation of the narrative of the sage Satyatapas, beginning with the words "ākhyānam" (the narrative). "Yad" means because of which cause, "pratiparva" means in each parvan.

On the days of festivals such as the Viṣuvat, or at the junctions of times such as the new moon (darśa), the twice-born, proclaiming— that is, causing others to hear— the narrative (ākhyāyikā) of the seer Satyatapas, whose synonym is Satyavrata; that is, a story concerning the realization of the true meaning of truth— by this [phrase].

Because they possess a second birth consisting of the emergence from the state of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), and because they have been purified by the forty sacraments beginning with conception (garbhādhāna), Brāhmaṇas are of the nature of a portion of Rudra; thus, their fitness for spiritual authority is indicated. [The term] "praṇayin" refers to one who is devoted to the Praṇava, the syllable Oṃ.
That which is the locus, the foundation, and the substratum—affection (*praṇaya*) means familiarity with that; thus, one who possesses it is "the affectionate" (*praṇayin*).
Since whatever is commenced begins with the utterance of *praṇava* (Om), there is a dependence upon it.
Therefore, at the commencement—the beginning of the narration and recitation of that [text]—there is the reality consisting of merely this much: *īm*.

Having clearly brought— that is, having reached— the state of being equivalent to the *praṇava*, because they share the same meaning and purpose with it, [the practitioners] utter and loudly chant that which has the nature of a portion of the previously mentioned secondary seed-syllable (*aparabīja*) and which results in the awakening of Sarasvatī. This is because the *praṇava* was [previously] to be uttered at the beginning.
The meaning is that, according to the prescribed rule, they recite together after having placed that seed-syllable (*bīja*) as its representative.
As it is stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"That which is not preceded by the *oṃ* slips away, and that which is not followed by it falls apart."
Thus it is said. Also in the *Dālabhya-pariśiṣṭa*:

"The sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), and the rites for the gods, sages, and ancestors—if performed without the *oṃ* [syllable], none of it will bring about success."

Śāṭyāyana says: One should commence acts such as giving, sacrifice, austerity, Vedic study, recitation, meditation, the twilight worship, breath control, oblation, the utterance of mantras for the gods and ancestors, and the commencement of Vedic study, after first pronouncing the Praṇava.
The Śruti also states:
"By the syllable Om, all speech is encompassed" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.3). "Encompassed" means enclosed or contained within.
As for the narrative:
Among the Kosalas, there was a certain twice-born man renowned as Devadatta;
being childless, he performed a sacrifice for the sake of a son according to the prescribed rites.
Regarding that [king], for whom the curse and favor of the Udgātṛ were equal,
his son first became a fool and later became wise in the course of time.
In his childhood, he was mocked by his parents and severely reviled by people.
Passing his days in the forest by subsisting on wild fare out of world-weariness,
he remained there, O Giver of Boons, speaking only the truth and never again uttering a falsehood.
People indeed gave this twice-born man the name Satyatapas;
I have been made a fool by fate, and there is no other cause for it in my own power.
"Having attained this most excellent birth, my life has now become in vain"—
thinking such things as these, he remained there detached, biding his time.
He performed no worship, nor meditation, nor even the recitation of sacred mantras;
he was renowned among all people solely as a speaker of truth.
Once, when a boar had been pierced by a hunter and fled past the sage,
he was overcome with compassion and then [uttered] that seed-syllable of Sarasvatī.
Having uttered that which had never been heard before and was unknown to him, he sank into grief;
thereupon Śivā became gracious and bestowed the knowledge of Brahman upon him.
Through the utterance of the seed-syllable, the entire Vidyā of the Goddess flashed forth;
and just as it had happened previously for Vālmīki, he indeed became a poet.
To the hunter who asked him, "Where has the boar gone?", that righteous brahmin,
desiring to speak the truth, spoke this verse:
She who sees does not speak; she who speaks does not see.
Oh, hunter seeking your own interest! Why do you ask again and again?
Thus addressed by him, the hunter, having lost hope regarding the boar and thinking, "This one is venerable and not fit for further questioning," then went home.
Having recited the Sarasvata hymn, Satyavrata became renowned in the world;
honored by his father, he was led to his own home like the Lord of Speech himself.
Indeed, the sages sing this narrative at each of the sacred festivals;
for even his fame is exceedingly vast, and it is introduced at the very beginning of this work.

Thus, according to the author’s method of composition and presentation, it is suggested that the sage likewise muttered another *sārasvata* [mantra], which is partless (*niṣkala*). As for those who say:
"O Sarasvatī, those who mutter even once your seed-syllable (*bīja*), which has arisen from the conjunction of the *Ṛg*, *Sāman*, and *Yajus*... they...

Those who say that the ancient accounts— such as those concerning Munis who knew the three Vedas and became happy after obtaining the Atharva-veda and other scriptures— are concerned solely with the primary *vāgbhava* seed-syllable,
have failed to fathom the hidden depths of that ocean of unfathomable heart. For...
The meaning of "he sees" (*paśyati*) is as follows:
the question you raised—"By which path did the boar come?"—is only tenable if seeing and speaking share a single agent; and that is not the case here.
Because these two have different agents [of action]. For it is thus:

that consciousness which is the witness of all, as propounded by the Śruti text, "While the other eats not, he looks on" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1), is what sees. "Everything shines after Him who shines; by His light... [it is said].

She does not say this, because the scripture, "All this shines" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.15), establishes that the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) alone is the illuminator of everything. Furthermore, according to the system of the Sāṃkhya and others, the agency of speaking belongs to the intellect (*buddhi*) alone, not to the power of consciousness; thus, the intellect which speaks does not [perceive] the object due to its insentience (*jaḍatva*).
[The Self] sees and reveals.

[Objection: But surely, because of the superimposition of identity between those two—the conscious power and the inert power—there is a well-known worldly convention that "whoever sees, he alone speaks. Why, then, do you not likewise employ such a convention? [Response: It is not so.

"Since even ignorance, the cause of superimposition, has been destroyed, and such a state of affairs exists, oh hunter! You seeker of your own ends, why do you ask again and again? It is not proper to ask this. Thus, there was fear both of the sin of killing the boar and, conversely, of the sin of speaking untruth.
By means of his skill in speech born from the grace of Sarasvatī, he brought the hunter to rest. Here,
by the word "niṣkala" (partless), the venerable Mahākāmakalā— consisting of divine syllables composed of red, white, and mixed drops—
is indicated as having internalized within herself the expansion of the potency of the great mantras and the infinite mass of phonemes.
The supreme secret known as Mahātripurasundarī has been introduced. As it is stated in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*:

"The pair of white and red points, representing the distinct Śiva and Śakti in their states of contraction and expansion, is the cause of the creation of word and meaning, clearly interpenetrating one another."
I am the *bindu*, whose nature is the *ahaṃkāra*; the Sun is this form of the union of the couple in equal flavor (*samarasa*).
Kāma is so called because of his desirability, and the *kalā* is the *bindu* consisting of the forms of Fire and Moon.
"Thus, this Kāmakalā-vidyā, which consists of the sequence of the Devī-cakra, by whomsoever it is known, he becomes liberated and takes on the form of Mahātripurasundarī. (6–8).
Also, in the Śruti:
"He who abandons the friend who knows the truth—for him there is no portion even in speech" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.3.1).
"If he hears this, he hears in vain; for he does not know the path of righteous action.
This will be made clear further on. However, in the reading *praṇavāspadapraṇayitām*, the word *yat* refers to the aforementioned seed-syllable (*bīja*).
The meaning is that, at the commencement of the narrative of the sage Satyatapas, [the text] establishes it as being situated within the *praṇava*.
By this, since its purpose is identical to that of the *praṇava*, one should ascertain that its primary fruit is exclusively liberation (*mokṣa*).
And the Śruti says:
"Meditate upon the Self as 'Om' alone; abandon other words. This is the bridge to immortality.
(Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.6) || 4 ||

Having thus demonstrated the fruit of the worship of the first and second seed-syllables (bījas) and their respective parts, he now shows that the third seed-syllable of the Vidyā and its parts likewise have eloquence (sārasvata) as their fruit:
"That which is seen by the wise to possess immediate power in setting speech in motion..."
I bow with my mind to that third seed-syllable (*bīja*) of yours, which shines like the moon;
may it, like the submarine fire (*aurva*) following Sarasvatī, serve to dry up the waters of dullness.
The word "gauḥ" exists on the mountain; it certainly bestows perfection even without [the knowledge of] *yoga*. || 5 ||

The vocative "O Eternal One" (*he nitye*) is to be understood as carrying over from the preceding [verse]. "That seed" (*yadbījam*) means immediately, at once, or without delay (*sadyaḥ*, *sapadi*, *acirāya*). It refers to the act of initiating the flow of words—specifically, the composition of eloquent, flavorful utterances endowed with poetic figures and qualities (*sālaṅkāra-guṇopeta-sarasasūkti-padagumphānām*).

That which possesses the power—the capacity for generating speech—observed and experienced by the wise and learned in the act of composing beautiful literary works consisting of prose and verse flowing without restraint; by this it is shown that the erudition of the wise authors of great epics (*mahākāvya*) arises solely from its grace. Therefore, therein...

It has been stated that there is an absence of the distress caused by doubts such as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Because it possesses the splendor of an extensive flow of speech, it is described by the wise as being "in agreement" (*sasaṃvāda*). The third itself—using the suffix *īkak* after *tṛtīya* according to the rule *tīyād īkak*—is your seed-syllable; situated within your Vidyā, it is the seed-syllable of Śakti, *sauḥ*, which has the luster of the moon.

"I mentally bow to and meditate upon that [Lord] who is as white as the rays of the moon"—thus, even the opportunity for mental worship (*mānasārcā*) is shown; the same should be understood for what follows hereafter. Here, by the sudden emergence of the vision of offering everything to Brahman through its phenomenal nature as the essence of consciousness (*cidātmatva*), the necessity of this practice is illuminated.

Because of the constant connection between *yat* and *tat*, there must be the supply (*adhyāhāra*) of *tat*; however, in the reading "that which belongs to the third [chapter] is that" (*tārtīyaṃ tat*), there is no need for such a supply. The meditation on the white color, described as "having the luster of the moon," is consistent with the fruit of the arising of speech. As it was said by the venerable Durvāsas:
For those who contemplate her white form, words issue effortlessly from their mouths.
Thus it has been demonstrated that even the seed-syllable of Śakti yields the fruit of eloquence: "The seed-syllable situated below the twice-born (the letter *u*), conjoined with speech (*vāc*)—
this is the seed-syllable of Sarasvatī, which instantly brings about the power of speech."
Thus:

"Then, [one should contemplate] the final seed-syllable situated in the letter A, possessing the white luster of a mass of pervasive rays, vibrating within the womb (yoni) located at the 'End of the Twelve' above the head, which is the lunar orb risen there."

Having meditated upon the Sarasvatāccha [mantra] which is bathed in the waters of nectar, the practitioner of the mantra— who composes divine poetry and other works— constantly and swiftly destroys the afflictions of poison, untimely death, planetary influences, and misfortune.
Thus [it is said]. Some say that "I" (*ahaṃ*) refers to the non-existent ego-sense (*ahakāra*). That [interpretation] depends on the intention regarding the seed-syllables *ha*, *sauḥ*.

Nor does such a result belong only to the complete seed-syllable, but even to a single part of it; this he states with the latter half [of the verse], beginning with "let it be" (*astu*). By the word *vaḥ* (you), the Goddess is grasped; by the word *sarasvatī*, the Vidyā; and by *vo*...

May that word *sauḥ*, which follows the Sarasvatī belonging to you—or which, residing within the third seed-syllable of knowledge (*vidyā*), expresses the meaning of the Goddess of Speech—also serve to cut through the water of dullness; that is, may it bring about the cessation of dullness, which is the very water of mental sluggishness. The word "not" (*na*) is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. Of what sort is it?

Thus, by repeating [the word], the term *sa* should be explained as a qualifier. The meaning is that he whose *s*—the letter *s*—is non-existent (*asat*) possesses only the essence of a portion of the seed-syllable (*bīja*). For it is stated in the Śruti (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.15): "That very fire is situated within the water. This refers also to Aurva, the submarine fire (*vāḍavāgni*).

"Following Sarasvatī"—that is, near the river named Sarasvatī which enters the ocean, he is cast into the very sea and dries up the water; thus there is a suggestion (*dhvani*) based on both simile (*upamā*) and pun (*śleṣa*).

In this way, by virtue of the similarity between the stated seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*) and its meaning, this [word] functions through the phonemes of other words whose objects are the meaning of "Sarasvatī."

Since it does not transcend the state of being the fruit of Sarasvatī, he says: "The word 'cow' (gaur). Thus, the word "cow" invariably resides in Sarasvatī; because its function consists in referring to the deity Sarasvatī, it is certainly expressive of her. Even that [word] bestows perfection without requiring the application of methods such as meditation and the like.

It becomes the producer of the perfection (*siddhi*) consisting of the grace of Sarasvatī. He who knows the syllable *aga* as *ga* is known as "he" (*sa*). Alternatively, the sound *auḥ* signifies Sarasvatī; as for the question "what is he like?", the word *aga* should be analyzed and applied through repetition as a qualifying attribute. *Aga*.

The meaning is that for which the letter *ga* does not exist, that [word] is merely its own essential form (*svarūpa*) because it is uncombined. Nor does this [word] produce only the aforementioned limited result, because its capacity for individual, specific causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-sāmarthya*) has also been traditionally taught; in that regard, some mantras...
Some [mantras] are inclined toward bestowing specific objects, while others grant all objects in general. As it was said by the Teachers:
"The four diphthong mantras are the accomplishers of all purposes.
Even when separated from the letter *sa*, this [mantra] possesses the quality of being born from the play of speech with necessity; how much more so, then, when it is conjoined with it?
The word "also" (*api*) further illuminates this point. In this way, *aiṃ*, *īṃ*, and *auḥ* are taught both as pure [syllables] and separately.
Thus, the seed-syllables situated within the Śrīvidyā possess not only the capacity to produce the aforementioned results of eloquence and the awakening to reality, but also [other powers].
By the phrase "as far as other fruits [are concerned]," he establishes in general the capacity for the production of fruit:

"O Goddess! Each and every one of Your sinless seeds—whether with or without its phonetic adjuncts (*vyañjana*), whether fixed (*kūṭastha*), or arranged in a separate sequence, or even situated out of order—"
Whatever desire one has in view, by whatever method or through whatever means it may be— whether meditated upon or recited— it swiftly brings all of that to fruition for human beings.

"O Goddess" has been explained previously. "Each one of yours"—meaning every single seed-syllable (*bīja*)—is "sinless," which is to say, being unjoined with consonantal letters (*vyañjana*), it is for the most part pure; and it is "of the nature of the unborn (*aja*)," which should be interpreted through repetition [as applying to each syllable]. He clarifies this very point by saying: "with and without consonants. Consonants (*vyañjana*)...

The [syllables] ending with the *sparśa* (stops) and designated as *ūṣman* (sibilants), when joined with any one of those [consonants] and accompanied by a *vyañjana* (consonant)—according to the manner stated as "as it stands," such as *haiṃ*, *hīṃ*, *hauḥ*, and so forth—[are the *vidyā*s]. The meaning is that [the *vidyā*s] distinct from those are the nature of the secret *vidyā*s (*saketavidyā*) as being merely vowels (*aj-mātra*). Alternatively, even though they possess *vyañjana*s, [they are so designated].

According to the sequence of the conjunction of two or more consonants, it consists of a fixed mass of syllables (*kūṭastha*) as described by the term *sahasā*, such as *hsaiṃ*, *hs klīṃ*, *hsauḥ*, and so forth; or it may be presided over by six consonants, such as *h s k l r ḍaiṃ*, *hasakalaraḍīṃ*, *hasakalaraḍauḥ*, and so forth. Likewise, it exists in its essential nature as situated within individual *kūṭas*.

Having abandoned the nature of conjunct consonants by means of the separation of the sequence of phonemes, it is arranged in rows; although existing as distinct units, it remains within the sequence, situated in the order beginning with Vāgbhava, as has been explained previously. Or else:

By the phrase "situated by way of transgression, that is, by the reversal of the sequence, according to the order of Śakti and so forth, or according to the order of Kāmarāja and so forth," he has indicated that even the sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭi), maintenance (sthiti), and withdrawal (saṃhāra) depends upon the specific mode of worship suited to one's stage of life (āśrama), such as celibacy (brahmacarya) and the rest. Accordingly, in the phase of emanation, there is recitation according to the sequence; in the phases of maintenance and withdrawal, there is recitation without sequence. In that regard:

When there is the simultaneous commencement of the practice of the three [mantras], there is an investigation into their sequence or lack thereof; however, at the beginning of the practice of individual means (*sādhana*), there is no such investigation into sequence and so forth, because in that case they do not depend upon one another due to the difference in their respective desires. As it is said in the *Rudrāyāmala*:
O Goddess! The first is Vāgbhava, the second is Kāmarāja, and the third is Śaktibīja, which should always be joined with Śiva.
This is declared to be the Bālā [vidyā], which is free from all defects;
one should place the initial seed-syllable in the middle and the middle syllable at the beginning.
Thus, whoever recites this mantra shall become a possessor of sovereignty over the three worlds;
one should employ the first at the end, the last in the middle, and the middle at the beginning.
Having done thus, one should recite the mantra and shall attain all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*).

Thus: with regard to whatever object—whether easily obtained or difficult to obtain, whether a desired object of longing, or any one of the four aims of life beginning with *dharma* (righteousness)—or even something else, having focused upon it, by means of any method or procedure whatsoever...
Whether by means of the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the limbs beginning with envy (*īrṣyā*), or by the sequence of merely recollecting the sandals of the venerable Guru,

or else by whatever method— whether according to the procedures taught in the scriptures or arrived at spontaneously— that deity who is one's own object of expression has been meditated upon and realized as being identical with oneself. As it has been said:

"Contemplating the oneness of the deity, the guru, and the mantra with oneself"—this means contemplating [them] as identical with the deity, whether in their manifest (sakala) form, their unmanifest (niṣkala) form, or as possessing both natures. As it has been said: "Contemplating the oneness of the deity, the guru, and the mantra with oneself," [referring to them] in their manifest form.

It is indicated that whether one meditates on [the deity] as being partless or as possessing both natures, and whether one recites [the mantra] according to the fixed number of hundreds of thousands prescribed in the scriptures as "prior service" (*pūrvassevā*), through the distinctions of *upāṃśu* and so forth— thus, even in the absence of a conjunction of meditation and recitation as alternatives— the desired goal is accomplished.

Because of the general statement "of men" (*nṛṇām*), which refers to human beings, there is no restriction regarding those qualified [to perform the rite]; thus it should be understood that women, Śūdras, and others are also entitled to this worship and so forth.
For indeed, Brahmins, wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*), and others are certainly qualified.

For it is observed that the entirety of scriptural activity proceeds with that very [liberation] as its goal. In this regard also, it will be stated later: "O Brahmins, [there are] kings, Vaiśyas, and others besides them. One attains each respective desired object—the entire, complete thing—swiftly and immediately in this very birth; it does not abide as a transcendental result (*apūrva*), as is the case with the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such sacrifices.
"In another world" means that it makes the fruit fruitful, i.e., it produces the result.
As it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:
"Therefore, for all worlds without exception, there is nothing other than the worship of Tripurā [that achieves this]."
But enjoyment and liberation do not exist simultaneously anywhere.

With his mind fixed on That, his vital breaths absorbed in That, performing sacrifices for That, and his efforts directed toward That, one who performs actions with the sense of identity with That shall attain liberation. This secret has been declared out of a desire for the welfare of all.

Thus, there are four basic divisions which are pure; through the accompaniment of one, two, or more *vyañjana*s as prescribed, their subdivisions become manifold. As for the ritual procedures (*vidhi*), they are well known as those demonstrated by the teachers in their manuals (*paddhati*s), following their respective traditions.
Enough, then, with this effort to demonstrate that point. Regarding the characteristics of recitation (*japa*) and so forth, it is stated in the *Kulārṇava*:
"Recitation aloud is declared the lowest; whispered recitation is remembered as middling;
mental recitation is the highest, O Goddess! Thus recitation is said to be of three kinds."
Excessively short is a cause of disease, and excessively long is the destruction of ascetic merit;
that mantra which is joined with both the imperishable and the perishable does not succeed.

kha) One should recite [the mantra] joined with syllable after syllable, like a string of pearls. ga) By means of joining syllable after syllable, one should recite it like a row of pearls. [From the *Mūlasaṃvara*:
The cause of disease is the excessive haste [in recitation], which leads to the depletion of ascetic merit (*tapas*).
One should recite it by joining the syllables together, like a string of pearls.
O Goddess, he who merely remembers the hymn in his mind or mutters the mantra with his speech—
both are fruitless, like water in a broken vessel.
Birth-impurity occurs at the beginning, and death-impurity at its end;
a mantra (or yantra) that is joined with both types of impurity does not attain success.
He who does not know the meaning of the mantra, the consciousness of the mantra, and the yonimudrā—
no accomplishment arises for him, even through a hundred million recitations.
O Dear One, those mantras whose seed-syllables are hidden or asleep will not yield fruit; however,
mantras endowed with consciousness are said to grant all accomplishments.
"Mantras are said to be devoid of consciousness; they are merely phonemes.

They do not bestow fruit at all, even from a hundred thousand or ten million recitations. (Uttarakhaṇḍa, verses 54–61). And the procedure for the recitation of each individual seed-syllable (*bīja*) is as follows:

One who, radiant and adorned with pure ornaments, recites the Vāgbhava mantra one hundred thousand times within a house made of earth, performs the prescribed oblations ten times that number, and applies collyrium consecrated by the mantra,
shall fill the entire world with his own poetry composed in various meters and themes.
Furthermore, he is incessantly served by beautiful women who are overwhelmed by the pangs of love.
Clad in red ornaments and a deep-red silk garment, pleasing with the application of menstrual blood,

observing silence, and comfortably seated in an earthen hut, the practitioner of mantra should recite one hundred thousand times the seed-syllable consisting of the Lord of Rati (Kāmadeva), at the conclusion of which the prescribed fire-oblation is performed.
He who is served and honored in the world by gods, asuras, and humans.
Likewise, in a cellar, one who is self-controlled— adorned with white flowers, garments, ornaments, and unguents— should mutter the final mantra a hundred thousand times;
then, from his mouth, Sarasvatī shall flow forth incessantly.
And the world, with its manifold paths of words, comes under his control. || 6 ||

Regarding the nature of the illustrious Supreme Deity, which is described in the Āgamas as threefold— namely, by way of the divisions beginning with the *niṣkala* (partless)— the author of this work has taught therein that the *niṣkala* nature consists of light and speech;
and the indication that it is "like that of Indra," who possesses the nature of both the *sakala* (manifest) and the *niṣkala*, serves as its designation.
Now, with five verses, he teaches the nature of the remaining meditation as the object of focus common to all three previously mentioned pure seed-syllables:
Holding a book in her left hand and bestowing fearlessness, with her right hand gracefully granting boons to her devotees while holding a rosary, she is as radiant as camphor and the *kunda* flower;
she gazes with a gentle luster from eyes as beautiful as the petals of a blooming lotus.
O Mother! for those who do not cultivate you with their minds, whence can there be poetic genius? || 7 ||
She is Ambā because she perceives the universe through her own self-manifestation in its state of fullness;
as it has been said:
"When one beholds the vibration of the Self, that is the supreme *kalā*."
Having assumed the form of Ambikā, she became the supreme speech uttered from the ocean.

Thus: O Mother! O Mother of the Universe! those people who, desiring poetic inspiration (*kavitva*), do not cultivate you with a mind turned inward through non-conceptual mental activity—that is, they do not concentrate upon you or meditate on you with one-pointed attention;
this also implies that they do not even chant your mantra. This is what is meant by "contemplated."
Or rather, because they have previously departed [from this world], they do not even recite your mantra preceded by meditation;

how then could their capacity for poetry—the possession of the creative intuition for composing poetic works—possibly arise from any cause other than that [mantra]? And yet, poetry is indeed the vision of what transcends [the ordinary].

The state of knowing the three times. Alternatively, the word "not" (*na*) connects with the phrase "how [could it not be]? (*kutaḥ*); the meaning is this: for those who cultivate you, how could their poetic power (*kavitva*) not exist? Since there is no cause for its non-arising, it would certainly exist. In reality, this is because one observes that the attainment of the aforementioned results occurs precisely through the primacy of fixed recitation (*japa*) and other practices preceded by meditation (*dhyāna*).

Thus, the construction of the sentence should be made through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Of what kind [is she]? She holds a book in her two left hands in the sequence of upper and lower, and she displays the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*), because she is the foundational support for the entirety of mundane and supramundane literature.

She holds a book consisting of the script of the fifty-letter alphabet and displays the gesture of fearlessness (abhayamudrā); likewise, in her two right hands, she holds a rosary of beads in an upward and downward position respectively; and she is described in the Āgamas as being of two kinds, according to whether she is conceptualized (kalpita) or non-conceptualized (akalpita).
Thus it is said in the Kulārṇava:
"The rosary (akṣamālā) is declared to be of two kinds: the constructed (kalpitā) and the unconstructed (akalpitā).
The constructed is fashioned from beads, while the unconstructed is the Mātṛkā."
"Because her essence consists of the letters from 'A' to 'KṢa', she is celebrated as Akṣamālā" (Uttarakhaṇḍa 48–49). Likewise,

she is one who bears the *vara-mudrā* (the boon-granting gesture), for her hand— meaning her palm— is beautiful, skillful, and ready to bestow boons, that is, to grant the desired objects to those devotees who are worthy of receiving them and who worship her.

Regarding the meditation on the weapons due to having four arms: here, the state of bestowing boons and granting fearlessness is intended to manifest the awakening of the nature of the Supreme Deity, who consists of knowledge and action, and who grants accomplishments and eradicates all fears. Likewise:

*Karpūra* is camphor (*ghanasāra*), and *kunda* is a specific flower of the spring season; thus, she is "radiant" (*ujjvalā*), meaning shining and white in color. By this, her possession of qualities such as whiteness, fragrance, and delicacy is expressed. She is clad in white unguents, garlands, and garments.

And it should also be understood that he has the moon as a crescent upon his crest. Likewise, "ujjṛmbha" refers to that which has arisen, namely yawning or blossoming; thus, the lotus (*ambuja*) is "ujjṛmbha," meaning fully bloomed.
The eyes (*nayana*), which are as beautiful and captivating as the inner petals of such a lotus within a lake—their [beauty]... [is described].

"Endowed with that luster which is glossy and smooth radiance, she possesses an illumination—that is, the act of seeing—[with eyes] whose beauty is like the petals of a blossoming lotus. Thus it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*, beginning the practice of the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable: [The text continues: "She who gazes with a glossy luster from eyes as beautiful as the petals of a blossoming lotus..."
The wise man, recollecting Vāgīśī, should mutter the Vidyā known as Vāgbhava,
who is white as camphor and adorned with bright flowers and ornaments.
She is clothed in exceedingly pure garments, adorned with ornaments of diamonds and pearls,
and her hands are radiant with a rosary made of pure pearls and stainless gems.
One should meditate thus, O Maheśānī, on her who holds a book and a boon-granting gesture, and bestows fearlessness; by doing so, one shall become a sovereign of all vidyās.
