Thus [it is said]. The contemplation of this meditation has its locus in the *mūlādhāra* of the practitioner. Regarding this, it is stated in the *Śrīvidyārṇava*, concerning the *Pañcadaśī*:
"The wise one should contemplate the syllabic peak (*kūṭa*) known as *vāgbhava* in the *mūlādhāra*."
The seer (ṛṣi) of the peak-syllable known as Vāgbhava is declared to be Brahmā.
The meter is declared to be Gāyatrī, and the deity is Vāgadhīśvarī;
the first syllable is the seed (bīja), while the last is said to be the power (śakti).
The triad of the middle [syllables] should be the *kīlaka*; this is the application for the attainment of speech (*vāksiddhi*).
Thus, meditation (*dhyāna*) is also described as follows:
"White, with clear unguents, garlands, and garments, radiant with a crescent moon,
holding a book, a rosary, and a jar full of nectar," and so forth.
Furthermore, because of the similarity in the description of her weapons alone, it should be understood that Bhairavī, the bestower of prosperity, is also included here;
her worship and so forth are like those of Bālā, but her visualization (dhyāna) is as follows in the Jñānārṇava:
"She has the luster of a thousand rising suns, and her matted hair is adorned with a throbbing crescent moon."
She was adorned with a crown variegated by shimmering jewels and pearls,
resplendent with a garland of severed heads dripping with the mud of blood;
she was enriched by the beauty of three eyes and possessed a face like the full moon.
She has breasts like high jars belonging to a queen adorned with strings of pearls,
wears red garments, and possesses a form intoxicated by youth;
she holds a book and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, and a rosary in her right.
One should meditate upon her who is ever intent on granting boons, eternal, and the bestower of great prosperity.
The extraction of the mantra for this [goddess] has already been explained in detail previously.

Now, having first demonstrated the worship of the specific locations of the very nature of the object of meditation just described, he reiterates the fruit that is the playful manifestation of the power of speech:
"Those who [meditate on] you, whose beautiful luster is as clear as a cluster of white lotuses..."

O Bhāratī! As they meditate on you stationed upon their heads, as if drenching those heads with the liquid of nectar, your speech issues incessantly from their lotus-like mouths in verses of grand and distinct syllables.
Like the restless, trembling waves of the celestial river.

O Bhārati! O Goddess presiding over speech, O Sarasvatī! Those who, desiring the perfection of speech through their righteousness, meditate upon you—contemplate you as abiding at the crown of the head, established as the object of meditation in the station of the *dvādaśānta*. Of what nature are you?
Like a cluster— a multitude— of white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*), which are pale and stainless, it is clearly beautiful due to its distinct and extreme brilliance.

And she whose radiance—the beauty of her body—is "pleasing to the mind" because it captivates the hearts of those who behold her; here, although white lotuses possess the quality of whiteness, there is no pointlessness in the qualifier, as it expresses an excellence of brightness. Likewise, the "head"—meaning the crown of the head—belongs to the meditator.

Because she is situated upon the crown of the head, she is as if sprinkling or raining down showers of the essence of nectar (*pīyūṣa-rasa*) that has flowed from her own body in the form of liquid ambrosia. The word "as if" (*iva*) is used for poetic embellishment (*vākyālaṅkāra*). As it is said:
"She whose radiant form bestows boons with a book and a rosary [resting] upon her head."
One should meditate upon her whose essence is Śiva and Śakti, possessing a radiance as white as a kunda flower or the moon.

Thus: from the interior of the lotus-like mouths of those who had attained meditative absorption and obtained the grace of Sarasvatī through the ripening of that cultivation, there issued forth words consisting of distinct syllables and phrases—words that were *vikaṭa* (grand), being endowed with the quality of *ojas* due to their abundance of compounds, and *vistīrṇa* (extensive). [In the reading *vikaca*, it means "blooming"].

That speech—consisting of prose, verse, and so forth—is such that its words, both nominal and verbal, are endowed with the ornaments of sound and sense; they are radiant with qualities such as clarity (*prasāda*) and profundity (*gāmbhīrya*); they are composed of distinct syllables; they are capable of manifesting their respective meanings; and they are free from defects such as harshness to the ear (*śrutikaṭutva*). Such speech flows without ceasing.
It flows forth and issues out without weariness and without ceasing. How? Like the restless waves of the celestial river;
that is to say, like the restless and flickering ripples of the great surges of the Bhāgīrathī, so too does it issue forth as an uninterrupted stream of well-spoken verses.
According to Hemacandra’s *Abhidhānacintāmaṇi*, the word *ūrmi* refers to pain born of longing, the breaking of a wave, manifestation, a fold in a garment, and a line.
And this practice of the Vāgbhava-sādhana has been described in the Vāmakeśvara[tantra]:
"One who knows the essence of sound, grammar, logic, and poetic ornaments, as well as the meaning of words and sentences— [one who knows the six systems of philosophy (Ṣaṭtarka)—
] should present [the arguments], which are like the rows of waves on an ocean lashed by the wind."
O Goddess! A composer of mahākāvya arises through word-compositions preceded by extremely delicate, expansive meters and poetic ornaments. (4.27–28)
Having thus described the nature of the object of meditation for those who seek the power of speech and other such dharmas,
he now states the fruit of the second seed-syllable— namely, the subjugation of passionate women— preceded by a demonstration of its meditation:
"Those who [behold] this heaven and this earth covered with masses of vermilion powder by Your splendor..."

With minds focused on nothing else, those women— exhausted by the fever of love and possessing eyes like those of frightened young deer— behold her for even a moment as if she were submerged in a spreading expanse of molten lac.
They clearly become submissive. || 9 ||

Here, the vocative "O Bhāratī" is to be supplied. O Bhāratī! O Goddess of Speech! those practitioners (*sādhakas*) who, out of desire for their aims—desiring to bring women and others under their control—by means of your splendor—that is, by the splendor of you whose color is visualized as red in accordance with their desires, [and] by the splendor of your form described as being red like lac—[attain their goals].

The earth, or the ground, was as if colored by masses of vermilion powder, and as if submerged in a spreading expanse of liquefied lac; "liquefied" means melted, and this liquefied lac—the juice of *alaktaka*—possesses an exceedingly deep red hue due to its being purified through melting; she was as if sunk in the flow or current of that substance.

As if submerged; for one who is immersed in a red color, there is the perception of the arising of redness. By this, it is understood that the two worlds—heaven and earth—possess the nature of being distinct from your mass of splendor, which is your collection of rays.
This should be understood similarly in what follows. As it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:
"The circle of the universe is submerged in the flood of her own ruddy radiance.
And: "The multitude of her powers is the universe" (Śivasūtra 3.30). And: "Her powers are the entire world.
The word *iva* ("as if") should be applied to both instances by way of *tantra* (elliptical extension). With a mind focused on nothing else for even a moment...

"Those whose mind and consciousness do not exist elsewhere, having no other object, are 'single-minded' (*ananyamanasaḥ*); having become such, with their mental fluctuations focused on a single point—thus *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal of the senses) is shown.

The meaning is that, having first removed their defects through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and other means, they withdrew their senses, together with the mind, from their respective objects such as sound.
By the expression "even for a moment," the intention is this: [this applies] only to those who have attained perfection through mantras.

The attainment of the prescribed fruit occurs through the mere activity of meditating for a single moment. For others, however, its accomplishment depends upon prior service consisting of *puraścaryā*; this should be understood in the same way for what follows as well.
Now, [it may be objected]: "But it has been said: 'Now, he who worships another deity, thinking, "He is one and I am another," does not know, like a beast.'"*
Those who, having abandoned the meditative absorption on the Self according to the Śruti (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10), meditate upon other deities,
beg for abundant wealth; yet even after begging, they remain hungry.

Furthermore, since loathing (*jugupsā*) is heard of in such Smṛti passages, how could the meditator himself attain the wonder and delight of that [deity’s] majesty by reflecting upon the majesty and so forth residing in an object of meditation distinct from himself— by means of which the subject matter of this context,
such as subjugation (*vaśyatva*), might occur? For one person cannot experience satisfaction or nourishment through the eating and so forth of another.

And because it would be illogical for [the two] to exist [as separate], there might be the apprehension that the worship of those who perceive duality would be fruitless; therefore, it should be explained otherwise: "with undistracted mind" means possessing a self-reflection non-different from [the Lord], [identifying] their own self as being identical with the nature of Him who possesses such qualities.
The meaning is that they worship You, whose nature is as described above, by apprehending You as being identical with their own self.

As it has been said: "Having become the Goddess, one should worship the Goddess. Thus, the sense is that they behold the two horizons (*rodhasī*) by means of the state of oneness with the object of meditation, contemplating them until the very end. Now, what is the fruit?
To show that they were to be attained by them once again, he says "of them" (teṣām). Of those who were observing the contemplation of meditation in the manner described,

their slender bodies had become exhausted and rendered helpless by the fever of love— the torment born of passion arising from the sight [of him] and so forth— and likewise, there was a young deer fawn who was terrified and afraid.

Even passionate women—who possess the playful charm of beauty in every limb and whose eyes are like those of a young deer—certainly become submissive and dependent upon him. The particle *api* (even) is to be construed with a different word order; thus, it is not only women who fall under his sway, but even kings.

"They shall become submissive. Thus it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*: "O Supreme Goddess! One should contemplate the three worlds filled with the sindūra of her radiance; she will delude the three worlds in an instant."
O Goddess of the Gods! Just as Kandarpa is the destroyer of the pride of women, so do kings, serpents, rākṣasas, and gods come under his control.
"One who should contemplate [thee] with the mind shall become submissive like a female slave.

Here too, as before, the attainment of the fruit should be understood to occur through the fixed number of recitations (*japa*) and so forth prescribed in the scriptures. Since a specific location was mentioned in the immediately preceding verse, [it applies] also to the subsequent one beginning with "those who [place thee] in the heart."
Since it will be explained later, the specific location is not indicated here;
however, by the authority of the Teacher’s statement, it is understood that this is called the "support" (*ādhāra*) and pertains to the aforementioned object of meditation.
As it has been said:

Upon the foundational lotus, one should meditate on her who resembles the bandhūka flower, who possesses the form of Kāmarāja, and who is marked by a bow, arrows, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Likewise,

having visualized the seed-syllable of Madana situated in the secret place— reddish like a hibiscus flower and flowing with red nectar— the adept, being skillful, places the person to be acted upon within it and surely brings them under control.
Thus it was said. And by Durvāsas as well:
"O Mother, whose luster is like fresh vermilion! Those who meditate upon you in their hearts—upon them fall the surging waves of the side-glances of the lotus-eyed one. (9)

Thus, having taught the meditation and its fruit as the second seed for the attainment of desires by those seeking desire, he now states the fruit— the accomplishment of the fulfillment of that [meditation]— preceded by the instruction on the nature of the object of meditation for those seeking wealth:
Those who, having fixed their minds upon you, meditate for even a moment on you wearing shimmering golden earrings and armlets, with a girdle and garland fastened,
find that in their houses, [the splendors] expand daily through your grace for a long time.
Fortunes, as unsteady as the flapping ears of elephants in rut, attain stability [only through such means]. || 10 ||
Here too, the word "Bhāratī" should be supplied [from the previous verse]. O Bhāratī! O Sovereign of Speech!

those practitioners who, out of a desire for wealth, seek the abundance of cattle, horses, animals, gold, jewels, land, and so forth—by the word "that," the meditation upon that [state] residing in their minds is to be understood; thus, it refers to that which resides in the meditation.
Having established stability in the mind which is one-pointed through meditation,
and having resorted to *dhāraṇā*— which consists of binding [the mind] to a specific place— in accordance with the reading "sthirām" (stable).

Having made [the deity] steady in the heart-lotus, having rendered it motionless for even a moment— meaning for a mere instant— this refers, as before, to the practitioner of the perfected mantra (*siddhamantra*). They meditate upon you, that is, they worship you through the contemplation of identity with one's own self, and not otherwise.

For it has been stated that there is a delay in the attainment of the fruit when one perceives a distinction between the mantra and the deity through the relationship of the worshipper and the worshipped. Thus it is said in the *Śrīśrīkaṇṭhasaṃhitā*:
"The mantra is separate and the practitioner is separate; [if so], one never attains success."
All this has its root in knowledge; otherwise, it is not accomplished at all.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Śrīspanda*:

"This very emergence of the object of meditation occurs in the mind of the meditator—that attainment of identity with that [object] which belongs to the practitioner who so desires" (*Spandakārikā*, Chapter 2, Verse 6).
Thus: "In what manner do I behold you?"—you who wear shimmering golden earrings and armlets.
"Earrings and armlets" (*kuṇḍalāṅgadāni*) refers to the ornaments for the ears and arms; "shimmering" (*cañcanti*) means brilliantly radiant;
"golden" (*kāñcanāni*) means made of gold; these "earrings and armlets" are the decorations of the ears and the upper arms. You are the "bearer" (*dharām*), meaning she who wears them.

The root *dhṛ* (to hold) takes the suffix *ac* according to the rule *pacādyac*, thus forming *dhṛt*. The meaning is that she is wearing golden earrings on her ears and golden armlets (*aṅgada*) upon her creeper-like arms.
Likewise, she has "bound a girdle-wreath" (*ābaddhakāñcīsraj*); that is, she by whom a girdle (*kāñcī*), a wreath (*sraj*), a waist-band (*raśanā*), or a cord (*dāma*) is bound or fastened.
A specific ornament for a woman’s waist, or a cloth-tie, is called a *kāñcī*.

This is an illustration of the crown-jewel, the necklace, the anklets, and so forth. As it has been said: "She whose forehead is adorned by the pair of earrings that have become the orbs of the sun and the moon, and who possesses arms made beautiful by golden armlets and bracelets."
Adorned with girdles of tinkling jewel-bells,

and so forth. In their dwellings and palaces, there were [women] as tremulous as the flapping ears of intoxicated elephants— those intoxicated elephants whose temples are bursting open, causing the flow of rut-fluid to stream forth.

Even fortunes— consisting of the abundance of elephants, horses, vehicles, wealth, jewels, and so forth— which are as flickering and unstable as the flapping of the ears of scent-elephants (*gandhagaja*), and which by their very nature are transient, attain long-lasting stability and remain constant;
this refers to how that which is inherently unstable [attains permanence].
By means of establishing stability,
it is characterized by the performance of an extremely difficult task, consisting in the alteration of one's own nature.
Or, by resorting to the manifestation of various forms such as elephants and horses through sport (*līlayā*), they expand day after day, every single day;
the sense is that they undergo increase, reaching fullness and growing, rather than diminishing.
As it has been said:
One should meditate upon the seed-syllable of King Manmatha, which arises from within the womb of the radiant solar orb situated in the heart-lotus,
possessing a splendor equal to the midday sun, surrounded by the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*,
and which agitates the entire universe.
Even by giving away Ramā, who increases one's sovereignty and royal power, one would delight the world.
And by the venerable Durvāsas it was said:
"Those who meditate upon you—fair as a golden needle, with a pair of earrings swaying at your ears and a smiling face—they alone are the givers of land and wealth. (10)

Thus [ends the previous section]. Now, he teaches the meditation on its presiding deity— which is to be cultivated by those seeking liberation and is fruitful— as an internal means for the direct realization of the essence of Sarasvatī through the partless syllable (*niṣkalākṣara*) residing within the second seed-syllable.

With playful grace, they meditate upon you— four-armed and three-eyed, with a mass of matted hair adorned by the crescent moon, wearing a garland of human heads and garments as red as the Bandhūka flower, seated upon a corpse-throne, and possessing full, lofty breasts.
With a body marked by three folds in the middle, for the sake of perceiving your true form. || 11 ||
Here too, as before, the vocative phrase is to be supplied; and the word "some" (kecit) is to be understood as an ellipsis. O Bhāratī!

some who desire liberation characterized by conformity with your own nature, for the sake of realizing your form—that is, for the realization (*saṃvitti*) of your form, which is the specific object of meditation being contemplated—in order to fully attain it, [meditate upon] your form.
The meaning is "in order to attain. The status of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is established by the rule *tumarthācca bhāvavacanāt*.

They meditate, that is, they contemplate with the cognition of non-difference. Of what kind? "With *ārbhaṭī*," which means with great reverence; or alternatively, *ārbhaṭī* refers to a specific type of posture. As it has been said:
(47) Placing both thighs upon the thighs, this posture is called *ārbhaṭikāsana*.
Thus, with the *ārbhaṭikāsana* characterized as described above, she sits upon the *pretāsana*; [the practitioner] has come together with her in an eminent manner.
Having entered into that state where the "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) is submerged and the "this-ness" (idantā) is manifest,

and having attained a state of intense connection with the entire universe— from the level of the Lord (Īśvara) down to the earth— by this etymological derivation, he is called *preta* here; through the lower pervasion (*aparā vyāpti*), he is Sadāśiva in his gross form, and through the higher pervasion (*parā*), he is Śiva in his unconditioned (*anāśrita*) form.
However, it should be understood that she exists in the form of *nāda* through the sequence of higher and lower [levels].

Since the entire network of lower principles (*tattva*) up to that point constitutes her seat, this Goddess abides by relying upon all the *tattvas*; thus, according to the *Devībhāgavata*, she occupies that seat as her defining characteristic.

"By way of habit" (*tācchīlyena*) means "one who has ascended upon that. Furthermore, when the five *pretas*—namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others—are deprived of their respective powers (*vāmādi-śakti*), they become incapable of performing tasks such as creation due to the portion of *dharma*; she is therefore seated (*adhyāsinīm*) upon a throne fashioned by them, sitting above it. As it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
O Great Lord! Speak of those five *pretas* and the cause of their state;
tell me, how is it that they are soulless, indestructible, and eternal in form?
With these words and others, the Lord spoke in response to the Goddess’s question: "Well asked by you, O blessed one! How is the seat of the five *pretas*?
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva."

O lady of excellent hips! O Supreme Goddess! those five pretas are always motionless. O Parameśānī! the agency consisting of the form of creation is to be known as the Vāmā-śakti; Brahmā is a preta, without a doubt.
"Śiva has no instrument (karaṇa), because the instrument belongs to Śakti. Beginning from this point,
O Dear One, Sadāśiva is the great preta, solitary and motionless.
O Goddess! Deprived of power, one is not capable of anything whatsoever.

Thus far. Likewise, she is one whose mass of matted hair (*jaṭājūṭa*)—the collection of locks—is adorned or decorated with a crescent moon (*śaśikhaṇḍa*). Alternatively, by the word *jaṭājūṭa*, the crown (*mukuṭa*) is indicated.

She is the one whose crown is adorned—that is, inlaid—with *candrakānta* gems shaped like crescent moons; she is the one who wears a garland of human skulls—a necklace consisting of a string of pearls as large and brilliant as human skulls. Some, however, say she is "possessing a garland of jasmine" or "wearing a wreath of *campaka* flowers."

She wears garments as red as the bandhūka flower; that is, she wears clothes that are as crimson as the bandhūka blossom or the bandhujīvaka flower— she who is clad in smooth, red silk garments— and likewise possesses four arms.

She has four arms due to the excellence of the expansion of the powers of Śāntā and the others from the goddess Bhinnā who has transcended quiescence (śāntyatītā); she has three eyes—that is, she possesses three eyes—due to her union with the triad of powers beginning with Icchā, which are illuminated by her own majesty; likewise, [her breasts] are full, fleshy, prominent, and elevated.

She whose breasts were full and high— possessing such plump and lofty breasts— and therefore whose slender body was marked by three folds (the contraction of the skin) that had arisen in the middle region of the waist, appearing deep and sunken as if from being weighed down by their burden; or rather, whose body was low and bent.
The meaning is that her body was marked by the three-fold bend (tribhaṅgī) and was beautiful in every limb. As it is said in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"With three folds on her waist-band, which presses against the middle due to the weight of her breasts. (11)

Now, he introduces the point that for those who worship the Goddess through one of the types of meditation just described, the supernatural powers (siddhis) such as universal sovereignty and omniscience are easily attained, by means of an illustrative historical account:

Although born into a family that was merely ordinary among kings and possessed of few attendants, Śrīvatsarāja— exalted by his majesty and with his feet worshipped by hosts of Vidyādharas— attained the status of a universal sovereign over the entire earth.
O Goddess! This is that very manifestation of grace arising from prostration at your lotus feet.

O Goddess! O You whose nature is sport such as the creation of the world! There was indeed a king named Śrīvatsarāja—also known by the name Udayana—in the city of Kauśāmbī; he belonged to a lineage that was merely common among kings, that is, a family of rulers that was ordinary and not particularly exalted, but certainly not low. (Note: The word *mātra* is used here in the sense of limitation or exclusion.)

Because he was a regional ruler (*māṇḍalika*), he was among the consecrated (*mūrdhābhiṣikta*) Kṣatriyas. In what kind of family was he born? He was born into one with few attendants (*alpaparicchada*); that is, a family in which there were few—only a small number—of attendants such as elephants, horses, cattle, wealth, grain, fields, and so forth.
49) Although he has attained birth, he is a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of the entire earth bounded by the four oceans;
his nature is to rule over the circle of the land (*bhūmaṇḍala*) or the circle of kings (*rājamaṇḍala*), or else his *cakra* is his army.

One whose nature (*śīla*) is to turn the wheel (*vartayituṃ*) and move [the wheel] upon all lands (*sarvabhūmau*) is a "wheel-turner" (*cakravartī*). Because he is the lord of the entire earth, he is a universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*); having attained and reached his station (*padavīm*), that high position, he is "exalted by majesty" (*pratāponnataḥ*).
"Majesty" (*pratāpaḥ*) refers to the splendor (*tejaḥ*) born from the treasury, the army, and so forth; "exalted" (*unnataḥ*) means tall, lofty, or increased.
One should know that those whose feet are worshipped by hosts of *vidyādharas*— where *vidyādharas* refers to the learned who uphold and practice the sixty-four arts (*kalās*),
the Vedas with their six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), the Mīmāṃsā, and so forth, numbering eighteen through study, teaching, and the performance of their meanings— are the *vidyādharas*.
As it has been said:
"The four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the extensive Nyāya, the Purāṇa, and the Dharmaśāstra— these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge" (Nāradīya Purāṇa 5.9).
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda— these three,
along with Arthaśāstra as the fourth, are indeed recorded as the eighteen branches of knowledge (vidyās).

Thus: he whose feet were saluted and worshipped by the multitude and assembly of those *vidyādharas*; and who, being thus, was both an omniscient universal emperor (*sarvajña-samrāṭ*)—by virtue of his expertise in various sciences, his worshipfulness by the community of the learned, and his status as a ruler by the command of kings; he is this very one.

"Born from prostration at your lotus-feet" means that it arises— having that as its cause or nature— from the prostration characterized by devotion, such as worship and service, directed toward those two lotus-feet; for they possess qualities such as tenderness and ruddiness, and thus are like actual lotuses.

The "arising of grace" (*prasādodayaḥ*) is the manifestation of favor; the meaning is that this is the fruit of service to You alone. Regarding this, some claim that the word *vidyādhara* refers to those who are conversant with the *Śrī Tripurā-vidyā*; however, that is untenable.
For if that were the case, by virtue of [the Lord] being worshipped by them, it would imply that he himself lacks devotion toward the Supreme Deity.

But others, belonging to the divine classes of beings, such as certain celestial denizens (vaimānika) skilled in song, dance, and so forth— since it is impossible for those sporting in such a divine station of the Vidyādharas to be servants of earthly kings, this [claim] is not logical.
"If this entire earth were filled with wealth for him, he would be but one..."
"Joy belongs to humans and gandharvas," so it is heard in the scripture. || 12 ||

Now, he explains by way of a statement of contrast (*vyatireka*) that for those who are devoid of the propitiation of the Goddess’s feet and so forth, the aforementioned fruit of universal sovereignty and the like is difficult to attain:
O Caṇḍī! Those whose hands have never acquired familiarity with the tips of thorns broken by the crushing of *bilva* leaves during the rite of worshipping Your lotus feet,
become lords of the earth, marked with the staff, goad, discus, bow, thunderbolt, śrīvatsa, and fish.
How indeed [could it be compared] to hands possessing the luster of lotuses? || 13 ||

O Caṇḍī! O you who are prone to anger toward those averse to your own worship! From the fear of doing what is displeasing to you, it is said in the Śruti: "From fear of him the wind blows; from fear of him the sun rises;
from fear of him fire and the wind, and death as the fifth, run forth" (Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa).

Indeed, precisely because it possesses the characteristic of instilling fear, it was stated in the *Kampana* section that in the scriptural passage, "Great is the fear, the raised thunderbolt," the word *vajra* refers to Brahman. [This applies to] those living beings whose hands— their very palms— are engaged in the rite of worshiping Your lotus feet, which are like two lotuses.

Because those two lotus-feet possess qualities such as redness and tenderness, the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*) for the purpose of performing their worship— namely, the ritual of the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*). However, in the reading *arcanakṛte*, the meaning is "for the sake of worship" (*arcanārtham*).

"By the tips of thorns breaking from the plucking of *bilvī* leaves": [the compound] *alpo bilvavṛkṣo bilvī* means "a small *bilva* tree is a *bilvī*"; [it refers to] the daily plucking (*ulluṇṭhana*), that is, the cutting away, of those leaves—the *bilva* leaves.

It should be understood that the verb *truṭ* (to break) is established as transitive here by virtue of having the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied within it; otherwise, it would not be so.
They did not undergo, nor did they attain, familiarity— that is, repeated contact— with the tips, the sharp points, of those thorny trees whose branches rend hands while gathering leaves;
for bilva trees are by nature beset with thorns, and thus those who gather bilva leaves have their hands scratched by those prickles.

The meaning is that they did not exist. Regarding this, some explain [the term] as "of those being broken or cut," but that is not tenable; for there is no intention to refer to the cutting of thorns, and because of their inherently very hard nature, it is impossible for them to break on their own. Alternatively, [it refers to] by the crushing of the *bilva* fruit with the palm of the hand.
The compound should be analyzed as "of the thorns which are breaking and being cut along with [the leaves]," because of their contact with them;
or alternatively, "by the tips of the thorns which are breaking," since in the Āgamas the bilva leaves are prescribed by counting the flowers. Thus it has been said:
Among leaves, the *bilva* leaf is used; no other leaf is superior.
The lotuses of the *hayamāra* should be slightly blossomed.
Thus it is said. They [are distinguished] by marks such as the staff, the goad, the discus, the bow, the thunderbolt, the *śrīvatsa*, and the fish.

The staff (*daṇḍa*) is a club; the goad (*aṅkuśa*) is a hook; the discus (*cakra*) is circular or triangular in shape and so forth; the bow (*cāpa*) is a bow; the thunderbolt (*kuliśa*) is a *vajra*; the *śrīvatsa* is a particular emblem; and the fish (*matsya*) is a fish.

How indeed could kings—those lords of the earth—be born who are not distinguished by hands marked with the figures of crocodiles (*makara*), resembling lotuses in their form, possessing the quality of redness like the *lohitya* gem, and having the luster of a lotus? The word "indeed" (*iva*) is used as a poetic ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*). Those very [kings]... [who are such].

The sense is that those very hands, which have been wounded by thorns and the like, and which bear marks such as the discus and the goad in place of those wounds, obtain birth in royal families to enjoy the earth. As it is said in the *Sāmudrika*:
"A spear, a javelin, and arrows are clearly visible in the middle of the hand."
A man whose [mark] has the shape of a chariot wheel and a banner attains a kingdom.
He upon whose palm there appears an elephant goad, an earring, or a wheel shall possess a most excellent kingdom, according to the words of the *Sāmudrika*.

And so forth. The mention of "hands" is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), because the characteristics of kingship have been stated due to the presence of the aforementioned marks even on the soles of the feet. || 13 ||

Now, as the ritual for the worship of the Goddess’s feet has been introduced, he says that through the propitiation of the King of Mandalas (*cakrarāja*) by means of the prescribed substances and instruments according to one's qualification, the attainment of the fruit will be free from obstacles for the devotees: He says: [the following].
O Goddess Tripura, composed of the supreme and the non-supreme! Having gratified You in the ritual of worship with milk, clarified butter, honey, and fermented liquors, the Brahmins,
Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and others— whatever their minds desire, that very thing shall surely be theirs who possess steady intellect.
They swiftly attain their respective accomplishments, having been rendered free from obstacles by those who have struck down the impediments. (14)
Brāhmaṇas, or *vipras*, are those endowed with the knowledge of the Vedas (*śruti*), the law-books (*smṛti*), and so forth. As it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"One is known as a Brāhmaṇa by birth; he is called a twice-born (*dvija*) through the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). (p. 52)
Through knowledge one attains the status of a Brahmin; by means of these three, one is called a Śrotriya.

Thus, because they alone possess knowledge of the Vedas and so forth, and because they are the primary refuge for all deities, the Brāhmaṇas alone have the authority to worship the Goddess and perform similar rites. This is according to the Śruti: "Whatever deities there may be, they all dwell in the Brāhmaṇa who knows the Veda" (Sahavaiśvānara Upaniṣad 19). Through honor and other such means, the Brāhmaṇas [are to be revered].

Their spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) becomes diminished, and it is with the intention that their restoration may be achieved through the recitation of mantras and other means directed toward the Supreme Deity— that the satiation of the entire *bindu-cakra* consisting of bliss must necessarily be performed.
As it has been stated in the Āpastamba-smṛti:
"From insult there is an increase in austerity; from honor there is a depletion of austerity.
A Brahmin who is honored and worshipped perishes like a cow that has been milked dry."
Just as a fire is nourished by blades of grass produced from nectar during the days,
so too is the twice-born nourished again by means of recitations and burnt offerings.
Thus: "kṣoṇibhujaḥ" refers to the protectors of the earth (kings); "viśaḥ" refers to the Vaiśyas; and "taditare" refers to others than those, such as women, Śūdras, and so forth.

By this, the distinction of eligibility is implied: that the Vedas are to be studied by the three higher castes, whereas the Āgamas are to be studied by all four castes. And so it is stated in the Rudrayāmala:
The state that is reached by means of the Vedas is also reached by means of the Tantras;
therefore, all—Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—are qualified [for them].
Thus [it is said]. Likewise, "O Goddess Tripurā, those who are the four castes," as before.

All the meanings of the root *div*—namely, play (*krīḍā*), desire for victory (*vijigīṣā*), worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), brilliance (*dyuti*), praise (*stuti*), joy (*moda*), intoxication (*mada*), splendor (*kānti*), and movement (*gati*)—are present here.
Except for dreaming, because the deities do not dream; therefore, she plays (*dīvyati*), sports (*krīḍate*), desires victory (*vijigīṣate*), and transacts (*vyavaharati*).
The etymological derivation of the name "Devī"—meaning she who "shines" (dyotate) or "is praised" (stūyate), and so forth—has been determined previously and will be determined hereafter.

You, who consist of both the supreme and the non-supreme, whose essential nature comprises both the manifest (*sakala*) and the unmanifest (*niṣkala*), and who are the embodiment of the equilibrium of Śiva and Śakti; you, who are to be satisfied and gratified by the offering of the *bindu*—or rather, of what nature are you?

The Supreme (Para) is the primordial, consisting of both the higher and the lower; the Non-Supreme (Apara) is the final, consisting of emission (visarga). Because it possesses the nature of both, it is the essence of the potency of mantra, which consists of the supreme reflective awareness of "I" (ahaṃparāmarśa), by virtue of which mantras [attain their power].

Upon the infusion of power (*śaktyādhāna*), those [mantras] that have attained capacity develop the skill to accomplish their respective, specific functions; otherwise, due to being lifeless, they would be fruitless, as it is said in the *Tantrasadbhāva*:
"That imperishable Power (*śakti*) which is remembered as the very life-force of mantras..."
O lady of excellent hips! Deprived of her, [the world] is as fruitless as an autumn cloud.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Spanda*:
"Having seized that power, mantras, endowed with the power of the Omniscient One, proceed toward their respective functions, like the sense organs of embodied beings. (Spandakārikā 2.10)
And so forth. Also, in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*: "This unartificial and untainted awareness of this very form is what they call 'I'; this alone is the luminosity of the Light."
For this vigor is the very heart-essence of all mantras;
without it, they would be inert, like living beings without a heart.
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, the supreme and the non-supreme are the powers of will (*icchā-śakti*) and action (*kriyā-śakti*); from the union of these two, this is known as "thus is this" (*evam etad idam*). (This reading, *evam etad iti jñeyam*, is found in the manuscript of Mu.)
"Since it is well-ascertained that the reality is not otherwise, that which makes this known in this world is called the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). (Kārikā 6–7).
According to the principle stated in the *Mālinīvijaya*, [the Goddess] consists of the internal threads of will (*icchā*) and action (*kriyā*).
The meaning is that she is of the nature of the power of knowledge, designated by the terms *parā* and *aparā*. As was observed by Abhinavaguptapāda:
"The three bonds of duality, scorched by the mass of blazing light, are flashing forth."
May this spear of knowledge arise, capable of cutting through both the true faction and its adversaries.

Thus, generality (*sāmānya*) is twofold—transcendent (*para*) and immanent (*apara*)—and that which consists of both is the third, called the "transcendent-immanent" (*parāpara*). Brahman also is twofold, being called transcendent and immanent through the distinction between the pure (*kevala*) and the variegated (*śabala*), according to the Śruti:
"O Satyakāma, this indeed is the transcendent and the immanent."

(From the *Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad* 6.5: "Two Brahmans are to be known: the higher and the lower," according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*). And the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* states that knowledge is twofold: the higher and the lower. Also, in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*:
Two Brahmans are to be known: the higher and likewise the lower. Among them, O best of the twice-born, the lower consists of the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda.
Likewise, the Sāmaveda and the Atharvaveda, which accomplish all aims;
as well as Śikṣā, Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, and Chandas.
It is established that the science of astrology (*jyotiṣa*) is an inferior knowledge (*aparā-vidyā*), whereas the Supreme is the Imperishable (*akṣara*).
That is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage, and without color.
And so forth. The *praṇava* is twofold: supreme (*para*) and non-supreme (*apara*). As it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"The *praṇava* is considered to be of two kinds through the division of supreme and non-supreme. The supreme is the further-supreme Brahman, characterized by consciousness, bliss, and so on."
Since the supreme Brahman is by its very nature eternally new,
the other Praṇava is the manifest, perfectly pure form of sound.
It is remembered as *praṇava* because it is the cause of excellence (*prakarṣeṇa navatva*);
or alternatively, it is *praṇava* because it is the cause for attaining the supreme *praṇava*.
Thus [it is said]. The meaning of the Vedas is also twofold: the supreme (*para*) and the non-supreme (*apara*). As it has been stated in that very same work:
"The meaning of the Vedas is traditionally held to be twofold through the division of supreme and non-supreme;
the supreme meaning of the Vedas is directly the Supreme, which is higher than the highest."

"Another may possess the notion of dharma, which is the means for attaining that [higher state]. Thus, knowledge is threefold—superior, inferior, and both superior and inferior—as it is stated in the Yogaśāstra:
"That knowledge should be known as threefold, according to the distinction between the superior and the inferior."
Among these, the first is the supreme knowledge, which consists in the vision of the Self as distinct from the fetters of the bound soul (paśu).
The second is the lower knowledge (*aparajñāna*), which consists solely of the vision of bonds (*pāśa*);
it is like the difference in sight between a man’s eyes and a cat’s eyes at night.
Likewise, knowledge characterized by such distinctions is declared to be both supreme (parā) and inferior (aparā).
Thus [it is said]. A specific mantra included within the *mantrapārāyaṇa* is also called *parāparā*, as will be explained further on.
The Goddess herself is also named *parāparā*. As it is stated in the *Varāha Purāṇa*:
"Therein, the creation (*sṛṣṭi*) is declared to be *parā*, having the nature of the color white."
She who belongs to Viṣṇu, the large-eyed one, whose essential form is red in color.
That other [form] is declared to be Raudrī, who is both supreme (parā) and non-supreme (aparā).

Thus, worship characterized as supreme, non-supreme, and so forth, as well as other matters such as the states of speech, fire-offerings (homa), and the like, should be applied according to availability. In this manner, within the ritual procedure of worship, there is "worship consisting of the supreme and non-supreme" (parāparamayārcanā), as described by these characteristics.

Having gratified [the deity] with milk, clarified butter, honey, and fermented liquor—these substances prescribed according to the sequence of the castes, beginning with milk—and having fully pleased [him] by offering drops of the special *arghya* water accompanied by perfumes, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and flowers consecrated by that [offering], [one should proceed]. (In this regard, the sequence is: for a Brāhmaṇa with milk, for a Kṣatriya with clarified butter, and for a Vaiśya with honey.)

"One should satisfy the Śūdra with Āsava. For those of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes whose intellect (*dhī*)— that is, their mind (*manaḥ*, *cetaḥ*)— is steady and unwavering in devotion to You, whatever accomplishment (*siddhi*),
meaning the attainment of results consisting of enjoyment, liberation, or both, whether pertaining to this world or the next, [they shall obtain].

One who prays and earnestly entreats for various attainments surely obtains and reaches them with speed, force, and without delay; the word "eva" (surely) is placed out of its logical order. As it is said in the Pādma Purāṇa:
"He who bathes Caṇḍikā with sugarcane juice..."
He rejoices together with Viṣṇu, who possesses the wings of Garuḍa and who is ever-moving.
Because of this statement, even such things as wandering through other worlds are accomplished through this worship and other practices. Also elsewhere:
"Where there is worldly enjoyment, there is no liberation; where there is liberation, there is no enjoyment.
But for those intent on the libation to the venerable Śaṅkarī, both enjoyment and liberation are held in the very palm of their hand."
Thus, because the worship of the Goddess is prescribed even for the attainment of the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*), her adoration bestows the fruits of those four aims.
As it is stated in the *Puṣkarakhaṇḍa* of the *Pādmapurāṇa*, in the section on daily rites (*āhnika-prakaraṇa*): [p. 56]
Beyond this, the wise person should cause the worship of the gods to be performed;
he who worships Gaṇeśa is not obstructed by obstacles.
One should worship the Sun for the sake of health; Mādhava for the sake of dharma and liberation;
Śiva for the sake of dharma, wealth, and liberation; and Caṇḍikā for the sake of the four aims of life.
Thus [it is said]. Or else, "attainment" (*siddhi*) refers to the state of being the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśvaratva*) and so forth. As it is stated in the *Śivasūtras*:
"From the arising of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), there is the attainment of the status of Lord of the Wheel" (1.21).
And in the *Vārttika* as well:
When, no longer desiring limited accomplishment, he again desires the supreme accomplishment whose form is the manifestation of the universal self, then indeed for him—
Through the arising of pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā), one attains the state of being the sovereign of the wheel (cakrarāja) and achieves perfection;
desiring the manifestation of universal selfhood, one unites with one's own power.
When one is a yogi who touches the state of Sadāśiva,
then Īśvara is his external unfolding (unmeṣa), and Sadāśiva is his internal withdrawal (nimeṣa).
And according to the principle that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the cognition of "Being" (*sad-vidyā*) and the cognition of "I-this" (*aham-idam-dhī*),
the realization that "the entire world is indeed I" [is established].
That pure and stainless Vidyā, through its manifest arising, causes the power of the Self to emerge;
one should perpetually contemplate that power of one's own Self.
When the yogi [attains this], then his unsurpassed status as the Lord of the Wheel is accomplished for the yogi through the excellence of the absorption into Māheśvarī.

Thus, how are they—unperturbed by obstacles (*vighna*)—able to obstruct the accomplishment of their task? Obstacles are of three kinds, such as those internal (*ādhyātmika*) and so forth, as well as specific deities presiding over them;
"unperturbed" means not being agitated by these. And yet...

By the six lords of the army of Heramba, numbering seventy million, such as Āmoda, Pramoda, and others, who are the masters of obstacles—precisely with this intention it was stated in the *Jāyaṃtīya-Nimi-saṃvāda*:
For those who serve you, many obstacles created by the gods arise as they cross over their own abodes to reach your supreme station;
yet for no one else do the powerful offer up their own portions upon the sacrificial grass.
"You set your foot upon the head of obstacles if you are its protector. (11.4.10) [The source from which this was extracted is not known.
Likewise, elsewhere—
Likewise, O Mādhava! those who are yours and have bound their affection to you never fall from the path;
protected by you, they wander about fearless.
"O Lord, upon the heads of the hosts of Vināyakas! (10 Pū0 2-33). [It is not found where this was extracted from.
Herein is the description, in the order of their colors, of the substances such as milk and others mentioned for the worship of the venerable Supreme Deity.

It should be understood that the Teacher has prescribed only those practices appropriate for the sequence of the Kṛtayuga, because it is stated in scriptures such as the Rudrayāmala that the rules for the secondary rites (anukalpa) in other ages are common to all castes. As it is said there:

In the Satya Yuga, one should worship the Goddess with milk, ghee, honey, and flour-cakes by means of the four castes; in the Tretā Yuga, one should worship the Goddess with ghee by all social classes.
In the Dvāpara age, one should worship with honey and all varieties of colors;
in the Kali age, the Goddess is to be worshipped with those very spirituous liquors alone.

Thus, although the primary ritual procedure (*kalpa*) prescribed for the fourth caste (*varṇa*) has been stated according to the sequence of truth, even so, all castes must resort exclusively to the inclusion within the alternative procedure (*anukalpa*). Furthermore, regarding the Brāhmaṇas,
[the primary procedure] is prohibited, as follows:
Wine made from molasses and ginger is not permitted for a Brāhmaṇa;
however, that which is made from molasses (gauḍī) may be drunk by a Kṣatriya, and that made from honey (mādhvī) by a Vaiśya.
Wine mixed with plantain and honey, rice-skin, or wine alone—
all these are declared permissible for a Śūdra, or whatever else may serve as his sacrificial oblation.
p. 58) Here, the specific mention of *gauḍī* and *mādhvī* is intended to refer to desire. Likewise:
"One should offer coconut water in a bronze vessel, and likewise honey in a copper one."
Likewise, curdled milk in a copper vessel, as well as curd mixed with molasses.
Or else, one should prepare jaggery and fresh ginger for the purpose of worship.

These and other such statements concern secondary alternatives (*anukalpa*). Likewise, regarding substances as well, since prohibitions are observed among Brahmins even when those substances remain in their original state through contact with various vessels and the like— on the grounds that they are equal to the primary substance—
as in "A Brahmin shall not drink liquor, nor shall he eat meat," and "Wine [is] always [forbidden],"...

"A Brahmin should avoid [these]," and so forth, according to the Śruti. The word "constantly" (nitya) indicates that this prohibition applies whether the act is committed intentionally or unintentionally. And the Smṛti states:
"By inflicting pain upon a Brāhmaṇa, by smelling what should not be smelled, or by drinking intoxicants..."
Deceit and sexual intercourse with a man are recorded as causing loss of caste.
Thus it is said in the Bhairavītantra:
"By giving wine to a Brāhmaṇa, one falls from the very state of being a Brāhmaṇa;
by giving the blood of one's own body, one incurs the sin of self-murder."
Also in the *Kramasaṃhitā*:
"O Goddess of the gods, those who offer us flesh, blood, or even liquor,
without considering the dharma appropriate to their caste and stage of life,"
They become *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, or *brahmarākṣasas*.
Furthermore:
"A Brahmin should worship Śivā with only *sāttvika* materials."
With a purely sattvic disposition, the Brahmin should satisfy Śivā.
And thus:
"In this manner, a Kṣatriya also should never offer liquor made from flour;
he may offer coconut water in a vessel of bell-metal, and likewise honey in a copper vessel."
(59) A gift may be given by a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, but never by a twice-born Brāhmaṇa;
by merely giving [in this manner], a Brāhmaṇa becomes short-lived.
Thus, even in the case of obligatory rites as well as optional ones and so forth, a Brāhmaṇa should adopt only the secondary rule (anukalpa).
As it is stated in the Bhairavītantra: "In that [rite] where the taking and offering of wine is strictly prescribed..."
The Brahmin, however, should prepare honey-wine in a copper vessel.

Thus it is said. As for the investigation of the matter as taught in the Kaula scriptures: "One should worship the Supreme Goddess according to the sequence of the Kula tradition. Since the worship of the Kula Goddess is prescribed by the inherent principle of all the Tantras to be performed using Kula substances alone, there is the application of consecrated Kula substances, just as in sacrifices such as the Sautrāmaṇī.

Because it is prescribed by scripture, it is not perceived as a means for unrighteousness (*adharma*), and furthermore, because its basis is the Veda inferred from the traditional law (*smṛti*) and the scriptures that will be cited hereafter. As for the previously mentioned scriptural passages, they must be reconciled as referring to those who have not undergone initiation; the subject there is not the mere Brahmin. For this very reason:

The scriptural passage from the section on the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice states: "One should purchase a Brāhmaṇa who will drink the remnant. Therefore, its utilization—whether enjoined or prohibited in the Āgamas according to the distinction between those qualified and unqualified—is sometimes made the subject of a counter-exception (pratiprasava). As it is said in the Kulārṇava:
In the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, Saura, and Sugata-darśana; likewise in the Bauddha, Pāśupata, Sāṃkhya, Māntra, Vrata, and Kālāmukha (or Kulamukha).
O Pārvatī, in the systems of the Dakṣiṇa, Sadakṣa, Vāma, Siddhānta, and the Vedic traditions,
worship performed without liquor and meat shall be fruitless.
O Goddess, if one performs recitation, sacrifice, austerity, vows, worship, or penance without the ritual substances of one’s family,
that becomes fruitless— just like an oblation poured into ashes.

Just as the drinking of soma is prescribed for the wise during sacrifices without being considered a fault, so too, O Goddess! the drinking of *ali* (wine)—which bestows both enjoyment and liberation when consumed at the proper time—is like the drinking of soma in granting both enjoyment and liberation. (Uttarakhaṇḍa 5, verse 67)
p. 60) Thus:
free from doubt, fearless, heroic, shameless, and devoid of curiosity.
Having ascertained the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, one may drink the Varuni wine that bestows boons.
If there were a lapse in the performance of that rite for men performing it,
how then could the seven crores of lords of sages perform it?

Because the use of substances is prescribed for qualified practitioners who have been purified by initiatory rites (*dīkṣā*) and other consecrations through such scriptural statements; likewise, in the Sāṃkhyāyana branch of the Ṛgveda, it is heard that the attainment of sovereignty occurs through the propitiation of Śrīsundarī by means of the libation of *bindu*.

"Having understood this, the wise ones rejoice with the intoxicating liquor that flows forth, satisfying their own seats"— having thus understood, they rejoice with the wine that flows forth, satisfying their own seats.
"They dwell upon the back of the great heaven and enter the supreme abode of Tripura. (Thus says the *Tripurā*).

Furthermore, hundreds of scriptural statements prohibiting those who are devoid of initiation (*dīkṣā*), purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), observances (*samaya*), and conduct (*ācāra*) are traditionally recited as being intended for their condemnation. As it is said in that very same [text]:
Having worshipped the enclosures (āvṛtis), the lineage of gurus, and Vaṭuka and the others,
a hero who drinks here in vain shall incur the curse of the deities.
Without having worshipped the god Bhairava and without having performed the satiation of the mantras,
even a hero who drinks according to the rite for drinking the *paśu* will go to hell.
He who engages in this scripture without knowing the Kaulika conduct and without having worshipped the sandals of the Guru— you certainly cause him suffering.
But in the Kaula knowledge, O Goddess, he who is unaccomplished yet desires to consume that substance should be known as a great sinner, excluded from all dharma.
For one who has fallen away from the conduct of the *samaya*, who acts according to his own whims, and who is evil-minded, there are no spiritual accomplishments;
rather, there is a fall from his lineage—all of that leads to hell. Therefore, one should not associate with such a person.
and ||
He who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, acts according to his own whims.

He who lives according to his own will, sporting about and devoid of the purificatory rites of initiation, does not attain success in this world, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal. He does not attain success, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal. He who lives according to his own will, sporting about, is one who is bereft of the consecration of initiation.
For such a person, there is no good rebirth anywhere, despite austerities, pilgrimages, vows, and the like; for they drink unrefined liquor and engage in sexual intercourse through force.
One who eats meat brought [or killed, according to alternative readings] for one's own pleasure shall go to the Raurava hell.

This is because, as stated in passages such as *Kulārṇava* (Uttara-khaṇḍa 5, verses 92–99), the use [of these substances] is prohibited for those who lack the requisite qualification (*anadhikārin*). However, in some instances, a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) is indeed heard regarding their use for specific refined (*saṃskṛta*) objects of worship. As it has been said:
Having devoutly accepted a piece of *ālī* fruit obtained by chance at some time,
and having recollected the Guru and his *pādukā* while reciting the root mantra;

"One should take [the substance] joined with the three principles while reciting the root mantra," and so forth. Alternatively, even according to the Kalikrama, because the aforementioned substitute substances are equal to wine and are prohibited for Brahmins, one should perform the libation of the *bindu-cakra* with milk even in rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya-karman*).
Having grasped the intended conclusion that [the body] is to be considered [as such], supported by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the Teacher established this sequence. As it has been said:
"For a Brāhmaṇa, [it is] always *apeya*. Here, by the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ā*, he makes known that the state of being unfit for consumption (*apeyatva*) is perpetual.
Also in the Mahākālasaṃhitā: "The Brāhmaṇas are to be gratified with milk, those born of the royal lineage with ghee,
the Vaiśyas with honey, and those of the Śūdra caste with fermented liquors (āsava)."

In this passage as well, by the mention of "by the Brāhmaṇas," it is stated that even though the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the elevation of their caste has been performed, they still maintain an attachment to their former caste. As for those who [cross] the insurmountable...

For those who have crossed the ocean of attachment to caste and who have reached the further shore of the Kaula conduct (*kaulācāra*), the arrangement of steps upon the very staircase of the supreme conduct (*anuttarācāra*)—shining forth by virtue of transcending all conventional conduct—does not overstep their own will; enough, therefore, with excessive elaboration. Thus, even here:
Since the taking of substances is most delightful precisely when it does not transgress the inclinations, intellects, and powers of practitioners,

[the author now describes] the manner of the creation of sound through the sequence of the expansion of speech— beginning with Paśyantī and so forth— of the Goddess who consists of both the supreme and the non-supreme.

By defining the arising and dissolution of even the creation of objects through their inseparable connection with Him, He declares that she is of the nature of the supreme power of speech (*parāvāk*):
"In this world, you are called Vāgvādinī, the mother of all words."
From you, Keśava, Vāsava, and the others clearly manifest;
indeed, at the end of a kalpa, even Brahmā and the rest dissolve into you.
You are that certain Supreme Śakti, whose form and majesty are inconceivable, as you are sung in the scriptures.
The address "O Goddess" (*devī*) is to be understood as continuing [from the previous context]. As for the referent of the word "Goddess," it is exactly as before.

For you are the mother of words—whether worldly or trans-worldly, divided by infinite variety—and of the denoters consisting of phonemes, words, and mantras, [arising] from the ground of the root *parāvāk* through the sequence [of *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*].

The meaning is that she is the Supreme Mātṛkā, because by the manifold variety of the differentiation in the expansion of the power known as Jyeṣṭhāraudrī, she causes the manifestation of the fifty phonemes beginning with 'A' and ending with 'Kṣa'— both those pertaining to Māyā and those not pertaining to it— and because the expansion of the entire manifold of objects, which consists of the meanings expressed by those phonemes, is thereby logically established.

For the Śruti states: "In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated; it became differentiated by name and form" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7). Thus, the manifestation of the world—consisting of names and forms, and characterized by the relationship between the signifier and the signified—is heard in scripture. And it has been said:
"Knowledge is not superior to the Mātṛkā. Also, in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*:
"O Dear One, all mantras consist of phonemes (varṇa), and they, in turn, consist of Śakti."
Power (śakti), however, should be known as Mātṛkā, and she should be known as having Śiva as her essence.
O Goddess! That Mātṛkā who is endowed with the supreme splendor—by her this entire universe, including the world of Brahmā, is pervaded.
And when, O Goddess, worshipped by the gods, that [state] is established there and pervades all,
then, O Beloved, though situated beyond all letters, it remains as the letter itself, omnipresent.
"I shall thus explain clearly to you for the sake of certainty," beginning with these words,
[he says]: "That power which is supreme and subtle is celebrated as 'beyond conduct' (nirācārā)."
Having encircled the bindu at the heart, it takes the form of a serpent in deep sleep.
There, O illustrious Umā, while you were asleep, you perceived nothing—
not even the fourteen worlds with their moon, fire, sun, and stars.
But that goddess, having been cast into the belly, became as if bewildered by the poison;
she was awakened by a supreme sound consisting of primordial wisdom.
O lady of excellent complexion, as long as she is churned by the drop residing within her belly,
so long does the churning continue within the form of the Śakti through the force of her whirling motion.
But from that division, those drops (bindus) arise first, possessing extreme luster;
and when she has risen by means of that, Kuṇḍalī becomes subtle as a digit (kalā).
The Lord, the Bindu consisting of four parts, resides within the womb of Śakti;
through the application of churning and the churner, O Dear One, straightness is produced.
That Jyeṣṭhā-Śakti is remembered as being situated between two *bindus*;
having reached a state of agitation through the *bindu*, she is indeed the line of Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
That [line] in which both dots (bindus) are at the end is to be known by the name Rekhiṇī;
it is called Tripathā and is sung of by the name Raudrī.
Or she is designated as Rodhinī because she obstructs the path to liberation;
Ambikā has the form of a crescent of the moon and is like the half-moonlight.
In this way, the one supreme power alone is born as threefold;
from these [powers], both joined and separate, the group of nine arises.
It is traditionally taught as ninefold, characterized by nine groups;
O Goddess, it consists of the five mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, in their proper sequence.
Therefore, O leader of the gods, it is said to be fivefold;
O Goddess, it is described as residing in the twelve vowels and occupying twelve places.

The fiftyfold division, beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the letter *kṣa*, resides within the heart; it is said to be the first monosyllabic [form], while the second is said to be located in the throat.
The three-syllabled [vowel] should be known as always residing at the root of the tongue;
there is no doubt that the production of phonemes occurs here at the tip of the tongue.
"Thus is the manifestation of sound; the moving and the unmoving are pervaded by sound.
Also, in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*:
"The pair of white and red points is the contraction and expansion of the distinct Śiva and Śakti."

"The cause of the creation of word and meaning, with their distinct forms mutually interpenetrating. (6) Thus, Mātṛkā, whose nature is the Supreme Power (Parā-śakti), is the mother of the universe consisting of the expansion of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) which are the essence of the signified and the signifier. Therefore, here in this world of three realms (triviṣṭapa)...

In that which is called the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), you are sung and praised as Vāgvādinī, whose form consists of Bhava and the other [deities]. She is called Vāgvādinī because it is her nature (*śīla*) to speak or to cause others to speak, appearing in the forms of speech known as *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*. Furthermore, she always exists for all her devotees in the form of speech.
Because her speech is established, she is renowned in the world as Vāgvādinī.

Thus, according to the *Tripurāsiddhānta*, the designations such as Paśyantī and so forth are established for the abode of supreme speech (*paravāgāra*) itself by virtue of its taking recourse to progressively higher locations. As it is said in the *Nityātantra*:
"Arisen from the *mūlādhāra*, it is called Parā, born of the primordial sound (*nāda*)."
That very [power], led upwards, unfolds within the Svādhiṣṭhāna.
In that same way, moving gradually upward, it attains the state called Paśyantī;
in the Anāhata [cakra], conjoined with the principle of the intellect (buddhi-tattva), it is designated as Madhyamā.
Likewise, being impelled by those two, it emerges from the region of the throat in its pure state as that which is called *vaikharī*.

Thus [it is said]. This has already been elaborated previously during the occasion of defining the nature of speech (*vāṅmaya*). In this way, because objects (*artha*) are transformations (*vivarta*) of sound, she is also the producer of objects in their threefold form as the denotable (*vācya*). As they say:
"Brahman is without beginning or end, the essence of sound, which is the imperishable syllable (*akṣara*)."
"From which the process of the world evolves in the form of objects" (Vākyapadīya 1.1).

By this, it is suggested that the Tantrikas accepted the view that the world, consisting of name and form, is an evolution (*pariṇāma*) of Brahman; according to their doctrine, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is indeed real.
Since Brahman and the phenomenal world (prapañca) are perceived as being absolutely non-different— just like vision and the jar— it follows that if Brahman is real,

the reality of the phenomenal world must necessarily also exist; therefore, the statement "here there is not even the slightest diversity" is intended solely to negate the habitual adherence to difference by accepting its falsity.
"This duality is mere illusion; from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is non-duality.
"All this indeed is myself; there is nothing else that is eternal.
"In which the threefold creation is false," and so forth.
This constitutes the reconciliation of all non-dualistic statements declared in the Śruti and Smṛti;

for if there is no contradiction by that much alone, the Vedāntins' postulation of the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca-mithyātva) is purposeless— this has been explained in detail in the *Śāmbhavānandakalpalatā*.
Furthermore, "Vāgvādinī" is a specific mantra, which will be explained later in the commentary on the *Mantrapārāyaṇa*.

Alternatively, because it is indicated by the mere mention of its opening words (*pratīka*), it refers to a specific mantra of Sarasvatī named Vāgīśvarī; she is of that form, and she too [is praised] with the speech of one who has mastered the mantra.
It produces equality with Vācaspati. The extraction (*uddhāra*) is as follows:
*Tāra*, *Hṛt*, *Lohita*, *Satya*, joined with *Vaikuṇṭha* and *Ananta*;
*Bhṛgu* for me; *Śabdarūpa*; *Vāṅ*, *Māyā*, *Kāma*; and the two *Vat*.
The mantra for Vāgīśvarī consists of the words "vāgvādinī agnikāntā" (O you who speak with eloquence, O beloved of Agni) and contains twenty-four syllables;
with this mantra, one should worship Vāgīśvarī on the eastern petal.
Clearly: Oṃ namaḥ padmāsane śabdarūpe aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ vada vada vāgvādini svāhā. (p. 66)

Thus, having stated that [the Lord] is the agent of creation whose object is the mass of non-conscious matter (*acid-rāśi*), he now states that within the mass of consciousness (*cid-rāśi*) there is the creation of objects such as Brahmā and others, who serve as the causes for the production of the lower phenomenal world (*adhara-prapañca*).
These [beings], too, are well-known through scripture (*āgama*) as the creators of the universe and so forth.

Because they are not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they are designated as being remote; thus, they are referred to by the pronoun *adas*. Among those of whom Brahmā is the first, there are Keśava, Vāsava, and so forth: Keśava is Viṣṇu; Vasu is Agni; and he who has him [Agni] on his forehead as an eye is Vāsava, namely Rudra. The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule beginning with *jyotsnā*. [Thus] Vāsava.
Indra, as well as the ten guardians of the directions indicated by him, are included, according to the Vedic scripture: "The auspicious goddess who gave birth to Indra.
By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*), Īśvara and Sadāśiva are understood;
thus, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—known as the five Brahmas—are clearly and manifestly [intended].

It is conceivable that from you—who are the root-source from which the five streams flow—just as sprouts arise from a seed, they manifest and are produced even in the great creation of Śakti; the word "api" (even) is used here in the sense of possibility. Thus it is said in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:

Those objects which are eternal and those others which perish; those objects which are gross and those which are subtle and even subtler; that which is formless and that which is formed—all this, whatever exists as even a single thing among the elements.
O Goddess! Whatever objects exist on earth, in the intermediate space, or elsewhere, their attainment comes from you alone.
Or rather, it is used in the sense of wonder. As it is said in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"Brahmā and the others, down to the stationary beings, have indeed emerged from her;
the entire world, from the Great Principle (*mahat*) up to the specific elements (*viśeṣa*), has emerged from her."

Thus, at the end of the kalpa, when the duration of their respective lifespans has expired, all things indeed dissolve into You, the Root Cause, just as jars and other objects dissolve into clay. Like seeds, all this exists even then in a subtle form; that very same [reality] is emitted again at the time of creation. As it has been said:
"Her nature consists of the entire collection of principles (tattva-grāma) swallowed [by her] without remainder.
And likewise:

"Just as a great tree exists in the form of a potentiality within the seed of a nyagrodha, so too does this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings exist within the seed of the heart" (Pañcatantra 24).
Here, by the word *kalpa*, the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) is meant, not the intermediate dissolution. In that regard, [the process occurs] gradually...

At the beginning of that day, when each respective higher cause dissolves, there occurs again the manifestation of dissolution by the thousands of causes situated below it; thus, because there is no intervening interval, there is no dissolution into Śakti.

Therefore, the meaning is: "at the end of the Kalpa," which refers to the cessation of the duration of Sadāśiva's lifespan. The particle *khalu* is used as an expletive for poetic ornamentation. By this [it is shown that...]

It is suggested that even the renown of immortality among Brahmā and the other gods is merely figurative; for, in comparison with the limited duration of human life, their own lifespan merely appears long. Furthermore, although Brahmā and the others perform the cosmic functions of creation and so forth, they lack independence regarding their own dissolution and emergence; thus, their sole refuge is the independent Śakti. Her...
Furthermore, the particle *api* illuminates the fact that [the text] proclaims the state of being replete with inconceivable sovereignty. As it is said in the *Śaktisūtras*:
"Consciousness (*citi*) is autonomous, the cause of the manifestation of the universe" (*Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya* 1).

Thus, by virtue of its very sovereignty (*svātantrya*), it possesses supremacy (*paratva*), characterized by not looking toward any other source; for that which is not sovereign lacks such supremacy, as it would be impossible for it to accomplish an effect since it would require causes such as material substrata (*upādāna*).
If it were dependent on those, its sovereignty would be undermined; and that power [of sovereignty] exists as the cause of the universe.

This is proclaimed in all the scriptures (*āgama*): because the manifold world (*prapañca*), beginning with the earth, which is considered an effect, cannot arise without a cause; for those who know the Nyāya system maintain that the fact that the earth and so forth have an agent is inferred precisely from their being effects. This is indeed the very path of the followers of the Upaniṣads as well, as they say:
His power, which is devoid of objective reality and is to be understood through its effects, is like the fire-power of a magical illusion;
for no one ever perceives a power prior to its manifestation in an effect.

Thus, with the intention of explaining this meaning, he says: "That you" (*sā tvam*). She is a certain [reality] characterized by the aforementioned attributes, who is beyond the reach of mind and speech, according to the Vedic scripture: "from which words turn back. Because she is independent of anything else, she is devoid of limitation by fixed place, time, or form; and because she brings forth the manifestation of all such variety, she is that very one.
It is indefinable by means of fixed forms and the like; likewise, because it encompasses all other powers within its embrace,
the supreme power of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvarī parā śaktiḥ*), known as Sovereignty (*svātantrya*), is primary in its fullness— so say the wise.
You are praised by Śrīkaṇṭha and others. As it has been said:
"Therefore, the direct rule is that [the Lord] is endowed with the very power of absolute freedom (svātantrya-śakti).
By this, such [attributes] as "eternal," "all-pervasive," and "having the form of the universe" are implied. Or rather, from the three...
She is called *Parā* because she transcends the [levels of] *Paśyantī* and the others;
she is *Parā* because of the grace of Parānandanātha;
and she is *Parā* because she is well-known in the tantra named *Parānanda*.
"And she who has the form of a palace—she is the supreme Śāmbhavī Parā.
Or [it may be understood] according to another etymological explanation. As it has been said:
"For the independent and sovereign [Lord], there is no sequence of place, time, or form."
That all-pervading, eternal Śiva, whose form is the universe, brings these [beings] under his control.
Owing to its omnipresence, it is all-pervading; owing to its eternal nature, it is devoid of beginning and end;
and owing to its universal form, it manifests the manifold variety of both the conscious and the unconscious.
Thus says the Śruti as well:
"For him there exists neither effect nor instrument; neither one equal to him nor one superior to him is seen."
His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold,
consisting of knowledge, strength, and action, which are inherent to Him.

Thus [it is asked]: "Of what nature is the inconceivable majesty of form? That whose majesty—the greatness—of form, which has the nature of a mass of consciousness and bliss (*cidānandaghanasvabhāva*), is inconceivable; for the Śruti states, "The majesty of the deities is greater," and because, in comparison with human bliss and the like, the bliss of Brahman is unconditioned according to the Śruti.
Because it is well-known; and elsewhere as well:
"That very power of bliss is said to be that from which the universe is emitted;
she is declared to be this Goddess, the reality higher than the high and the low."
"That is its essence, that is its heart, and that is the supreme Lord Visarga.
Thus [it is said].
Now, by this Viṣṇu, the greatness of the form named Lalitā, which possesses qualities, is to be contemplated and remembered.

Her majesty consists in the slaying of Bhaṇḍāsura and his retinue for the sake of the gods' mission, or the manifestation of a multitude of her own powers (*śakti*) for his destruction. As for the essential nature of the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), it consists in identity with Śiva. Thus it is said in the *Vāyusaṃhitā*:
By the will of Śiva, the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) attains oneness with the principle of Śiva (Śivatattva);
thereafter, at the beginning of creation, she vibrates forth like oil from a sesame seed.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Saurasaṃhitā*:
"The power that is non-different from Brahman is indeed Brahman itself and nothing else;
such being the case, it has been declared in vain as 'power' by those lacking discernment."
"O learned one, the identity-in-difference between power and the possessor of power is difficult to establish.
Thus it is said; and in the *Vāsiṣṭha* as well:
"Just as wind and its movement are one, and just as heat and fire are one..."
Pure consciousness and the power of vibration are likewise always one in essence.
Thus [it is said]. The sequence of the manifestation of the universe, however, should be observed in the Śaiva Āgamas, such as the *Śrī Tantrāloka* and its summary (*Tatsāra*), and so forth;

it is not elaborated here for fear of prolixity. The sequence of dissolution is the reverse of that. In reality, this entire range from the principle of Śiva down to the earth is the surging of a multitude of waves within the ocean of consciousness. As it has been said:

"The elements, the group of subtle essences, and the senses; the individual soul (puruṣa) joined with its coverings (kañcuka), and the pure [Self] up to the power of Vidyā—this much is the manner of the expansion of waves from the ocean of one's own consciousness. || 15 ||

Having thus established the nature of the "other" aspect, he provides the etymological derivation of the unique name *Tripurā*, which is appropriate for manifesting the non-other state of the Supreme Deity:
"The triad of the gods, the three Vedas, the three fires, the three powers, the three vowels..."
The three worlds, the three steps, the three Puṣkaras, the three Brahmans, the three castes—
whatever object in the universe is regulated in a threefold manner, consisting of the three aims of life (trivarga).
All that truly follows from your name, O Blessed One, as "Tripurā. || 16 ||
O Bhagavatī! She who knows the dissolution, emergence, and so forth of all beings—that is the address "Bhagavatī.
As it is said in the Devībhāgavata:
"The origin and dissolution, as well as the coming and going of all beings..."
She is called Bhagavatī because she knows the true nature of both ignorance and knowledge.
