Thus [it is said]. She is called Bhagavatī because the meanings denoted by the word *bhaga*—namely sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and the rest—are present in her in their entirety. As it is stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"Of complete sovereignty, dharma, fame, and fortune..."
And regarding both knowledge (jñāna) and discernment (vijñāna), there is the declaration of the six as "Bhaga."
Thus it is said. Also in the *Kośa*:
"The word *bhaga* is used for sovereignty, majesty, knowledge, dispassion, and source;
for fame, heroism, effort, desire, dharma, fortune, and liberation."

Thus: in this universe, characterized by the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) and designated as "existence," "non-existence," and so forth, whatever object or essential nature of a thing exists is regulated, constrained, or fashioned in three ways by the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*), or has attained such restriction; likewise, it consists of the three aims of life (*trivarga*).
Because it is inherently threefold in nature, that which consists of a collection characterized by the three equals— namely, all that without exception—
is your name "Tripurā" in its true essence; from that reality (*tattva*), it follows, pursues, and connects with you due to the commonality of the meaning of the triad contained within the name.
In the reading *trivargādikam*, it should be understood that by the word "etc. (*ādi*), objects not explicitly mentioned are also included.
For this very reason, various etymologies have been stated in the Āgamas, such as "because she existed prior to the three" and so forth. As it is said:
"The city (*pura*) of the three—the knower (*mātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*māna*), and the object of knowledge (*meyā*)—is her essence; thus she consists of the three cities (*tripurā*)."

She whose forms are the states of waking and so forth; she whose three cities are the bodies of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; [she who arises] from the three—namely, the splendors of the Sun and others, the three worlds beginning with Bhūr, the three vital airs beginning with Prāṇa, the three locations beginning with the heart, the three qualities beginning with Sattva, and the three Siddhas beginning with Uḍḍīśanātha.
To the three gurus beginning with Divyaugha;
to the three principles beginning with Ātman; to the three seats beginning with Kāmarāja; and to the three paths beginning with Devamārga.
From the three divisions known as Kula, Akula, and Kaula; from the three secrets known as Mantra, Mudrā, and Nirīha;

from the three wheels (cakras) known as Mūrti, Prakāśa, and Ānanda; or likewise from the three drops (bindus) which are white, red, and mixed; and from the three powers of will (icchā-śakti), such as Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and the others.

Or, because she is prior to the powers of the seats beginning with Kāmeśvarī, to the *vyāhṛtis*, to the channels beginning with Iḍā, to the gross, subtle, and supreme states, or to the processes of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal; or because she is the "filler" (*pūraka*) of that which consists of the aforementioned triad— considering her as such in relation to the entirety [of existence].
She is defined as Tripurā because she embraces within her own self-conscious nature that which is characterized by the triad.
As it was stated by the venerable Teacher in the *Prapañcasāra*:

"Because she existed prior to the creation of the three forms (the Trimūrti), because she is prior (pura) [to them], and because she consists of the three Vedas (trayī), the Goddess is [called] Tripurā."
Because she fills even the three worlds, Ambikā is generally known by the name Tripurā.
In the Tripurārṇava, however, it is said:
"The three channels are indeed Tripurā— namely Suṣumnā, Piṅgalā, and Iḍā."
The mind (manas), the intellect (buddhi), and consciousness (citta) are declared to be the three cities.
"She dwells there; therefore, she is considered Tripurā.
Also, in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*, beginning with "Her mandala is a triangle," and so forth.
"Since each of the three is itself threefold, she is therefore considered Tripurā.
Also, in the Vāmakeśvara:
"O Goddess, Tripurā is threefold, having the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa."
O Dear One, [the Goddess] consists of the power of knowledge, the power of action, and the power of will.
Because she creates the three worlds, she is celebrated as Tripurā. (Kāśikā Saṃgraha, Paṭala 4, Śloka 11–12, p.
Thus it is said. Also in the Vārāha [Purāṇa]:
"In ancient times, you were worshipped by the thirty gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa;
therefore, the name 'Tripura' was then given to you by the deities."
And so forth.

Thus, in order to demonstrate the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of the term *Tripurā*, the Teacher here states the threefold meaning as taught in the scriptures in brief, using only the indicative marks (*pratīka*), beginning with the words "of the gods" (*devānām*).
According to the etymologists (*nairuktas*), the gods are first of all Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya, as they are directly perceived.

The Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas are the lords of the worlds beginning with Bhūr; likewise, according to the Purāṇas, they are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, who perform the acts of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. They are called "Devas" because they play (divyanti) or illuminate the entire universe, both internally and externally. Furthermore, there is the triad consisting of mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), and ego (ahaṃkāra). Likewise...
The fire-eaters are the fires, namely the Dakṣiṇāgni, Gārhapatya, and Āhavanīya;
these three are known by the name *tretā*. Furthermore, by way of repetition, *trayī* refers to the three Vedas—the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus—as the lexicon states:
"The Vedas are three; [collectively] they are called *trayī*" (Amarakośa 1.6.3). It is also stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
Another supreme power of mine alone is the ancient one known as the Veda;
it proceeds at the beginning of creation in the form of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Thus it is said. Also in the Devīpurāṇa:

"Because she consists of the portions of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma [Vedas], and because she resides within the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (aṅgas), she is recited in the world as 'Trayī' (the Triple Veda), which accomplishes both visible and invisible results."
Thus it is said. Also in the *Pādma*:
"Ānvīkṣikī, Trayī, Vārtā, and Daṇḍanīti are declared. Furthermore, Trayī is the science consisting of the three Vedas. As it is stated in the *Nityātantra*:
The Sāmaveda begins with the letter *a*, the Ṛgveda begins with that [same letter], and the Yajurveda begins with the letter *i*;
through the conjunction of these, one becomes pure.
O wise one! Listen to its accomplishment as it has been explained according to the sequence of the preceding and following parts.
Having first written it down, one should apply it in accordance with the rules of grammar.
Then, by means of the *Ṛg* and *Yajus* [Vedas], he performed the twilight rite (*saṃdhyā*) of the qualities; likewise,
he joined the twilight rite of increase (*vṛddhi-saṃdhyā*), whereby the pure body was produced.
"Therefore, the knowledge consisting of the *trayī* [is established] through the connection of cause and effect.

By the etymological derivation that "that which has three parts (*traya*) in its aggregate is the *trayī*," many meanings of the word *trayī* are to be gathered according to one's intelligence. Thus, by this term *trayī*, every object characterized by a triad is included within it.
It was placed there after being embraced.
As it is said in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "The three worlds, the three Vedas, the triple division [of time], and the three fires."
There are three lights, three classes, and likewise the three beginning with Dharma.
There are three qualities, three sounds, three defects, and likewise the stages of life;
there are three times, as well as the states, the ancestors, day and night, and so forth.
"And your form consists of three measures (mātrā), O Goddess Sarasvatī, who abide in the three!";

thus, several meanings suggested by the word *tri* have been indicated. Likewise—*śaktitraya* means the three powers (*tisraḥ śaktayaḥ*), namely Bhāratī, Pṛthvī, and Rudrāṇī, which are non-different from her.

Will, knowledge, and action are either supreme (*parā*), intermediate (*aparā*), or both. They are the three accents—acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and circumflex (*svarita*)—or short, long, and protracted. The "three worlds" (*trailokya*) are the three worlds known as *bhūr*, *bhuvas*, and *svaḥ*.
It is called a "world" (*loka*) because it is perceived (*lokyate*), that by which things are perceived (*lokyate 'nena*), and that which perceives (*lokayati*).

Or it consists of the three designations: the knower (*pramātṛ*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). It is the *tripadī*, the essence of all the Vedas, being the *gāyatrī* metre, according to the traditional teaching: "I am the *gāyatrī* among metres. Or it refers to the three feet of the *sāvitrī*, or the three strides of Viṣṇu, as in: "Viṣṇu strode across this; in three ways he planted his foot" (*Ṛgveda* 1.22.17).

*Tripuṣkara* refers to the three sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*), such as the Bhāgīrathī and others. It is called *tripuṣkara* because it provides *puṣa*, meaning nourishment, growth, or satisfaction, for the three—namely, the gods, the sages, and the ancestors. Some maintain that it is only by one who wears the sacred thread (*upavītin*) that the gods and others are offered libations (*tarpyante*), since one who does not wear the sacred thread lacks the requisite qualification (*adhikāra*). [The text continues: "three..."

The "lotuses" (*puṣkarāṇi*) are the *anāhata*, *ājñā*, and *sahasrāra* [cakras], or else they are the three Brahmans—the three principles known as the Self (*ātman*), the Inner Self (*antarātman*), and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—or the three-fold Brahman which is the *praṇava*. However, if one does not adopt the previously mentioned alternative regarding the repetition (*āvṛtti*), then the meaning is different: the "three Vedas," where the Veda is the principle (*tattva*).

From the *Kośa*, it is stated that "tapas is Brahman. Alternatively, primordial nature (*prakṛti*), having attained a threefold state through the differentiation of its qualities, is designated by the term "triple Brahman" (*tribrahma*). Likewise, there are three castes (*varṇa*) contained within the *Kulasundarī-vidyā* (p.
Or they are those residing in the *praṇava*, whose nature consists of the supreme will (*icchā*) and unfolding (*unmeṣa*). As it is said in the *Siddhātantra*:

"In this context, she is Kuṇḍalinī, whose essence is consciousness and who constitutes the life-force of the seed-syllables; from her arises the triad known as the Steadfast (*dhruva*), Will (*icchā*), and Unfolding (*unmeṣa*); and from that, again, the phonemes."

Thus: the phonemes (*varṇas*)—whose nature pervades both vowels and consonants—or [the castes] white, red, and black, or the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya; all this much, consisting of the universe in the form of the signified and the signifier, belongs to the Supreme Deity Tripurasundarī as her lower aspect (*apara*), while that which transcends both is her cause.
The supreme essential nature transcends the universe; it is the essence of the potency of the Great Mantra, which is pure, autonomous, and eternally manifest.

Now, having established the fruits of the service to the seed-syllables and deities of the Śrīvidyā through the aforementioned preceding text, [the author proceeds] to state the names corresponding to the specific fruits of the Goddess’s various manifestations for those seeking their respective goals.
He indicates the times for worship that produce the desired accomplishments:
one should meditate on Lakṣmī in the royal court, Jayā on the battlefield, Kṣemaṅkarī on the road,
Śabarī in a wilderness infested with carnivorous beasts, elephants, and serpents, and [Gaurī] on a mountain in a difficult pass.
By remembering Mahābhairavī in fear of ghosts, spirits, demons, and sorcerers;
Tripurā in delusion; and Tārā when overwhelmed by water, one overcomes all calamities.

The vocative "O Blessed One" (*bhagavati*) is to be supplied here. Although there are many forms of prosperity (*vibhūti*), such as Siddhalakṣmī and others, in this context the word *lakṣmī* refers specifically to Rājalakṣmī (the Goddess of Royal Fortune), because of the context of "in the royal family. Therefore, [the meaning is]: "In the royal family, at the time of entering the royal palace, and so forth, [I worship] you, Rājalakṣmī."

By recollecting [the deity] through its name and so forth, and by meditating upon it, one overcomes calamities; in the attainment of wealth and other prosperities granted by royal favor, one is liberated from poverty. Furthermore, those who are being oppressed there become freed from that suffering.
Since meditation has been described as being preceded by the accompaniment of mantra-recitation (*vidyājapa*), the extraction of that mantra is as follows, according to the *Kādimata*:
(Chapter 34) The second [mantra] of Mātaṅginī, and immediately after that, the third.
The fluids, the channels, and the water [are the first]; immediately after that, the wind and the fire.
*Rājyade*, *rājyalakṣmī*, and *hṛt*—these three arise from the transposition of *māyā*.
This *vidyā* of Rājyalakṣmī is said to consist of sixteen syllables. (Verses 66–67; clear).

"Hrīṃ śrīṃ bleṃ a i rājyade rājyalakṣmi saḥ bleṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ. Having meditated upon that Vijayā-vidyā, one should recite it daily and worship it. When pleased, she bestows a kingdom upon the practitioner without delay.
Thus [it is said]. Here, "that Vijayā" means one whose essential nature is equal to that of Vijayā. That meditation is described in that very same [text], in the fifteenth chapter:
"Five-faced and ten-armed, with three eyes in each face..."
She was resplendent with a crescent moon placed upon her shining crown.
Adorned with all ornaments, radiant in her yellow garments,
the luster of her body is like the orb of the rising sun, and she possesses a pure smile.
With his left arms, he holds a conch, a noose, a shield, a bow, and a white water-lily;
likewise, with his right arms, he holds a discus, a goad, a sword, an arrow, and a citron.
"Holding [the earth] with her right hands"—

thus, having remembered you, the goddess named Jayā or Jayadurgā, by that name and so forth, while being afflicted by enemies' armies as they set out upon the battlefield, the field of combat, and engage in battle, one is freed from calamities.

The meaning is that they cross over [difficulties] such as the defeat and destruction of their own side, and thus conquer their enemies. "Oṃ Durge Durge Rakṣiṇi Svāhā"—this is the *vidyā* of Jayadurgā.
The visualization (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
I bow to her who possesses nectar-like beauty through her side-long glances, who strikes fear into the hosts of enemies,
who bears a crescent moon upon her crest, and who holds a conch, a discus, a sword, and even a trident in her hands— she who has three eyes.

One should meditate upon Durgā, known as Jayā, who is mounted upon the shoulders of a lion, filling the entire three worlds with her splendor, surrounded by the thirty gods, and served by those desiring spiritual perfection.

Thus it is said. Alternatively, this goddess named Jayā is indeed distinct. Her mantra consists of her name situated within the seven-syllable *māyā* mantra. As for her visualization (*dhyāna*), it is similar to the previously described visualization of Vijayā, because she is stationed in the midst of her retinue of powers (*āvaraṇa-śakti*).
It is also traditionally taught that even the powers of the obstructions (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) possess forms identical to those of the Root Goddess. As it is said in that very same source:
"And the powers, too, in the worship, are provided with comfortable seats."
All the goddesses likewise have identical forms, faces, hands, and weapons.

Thus [it is said]. In a path frequented by carnivorous beasts, elephants, and serpents—where "carnivorous beasts" refers to those that eat raw flesh such as wolves and tigers; "elephants" (dvipa) refers to tuskers; and "serpents" (sarpa) refers to snakes—in such a path inhabited by these, namely one beset by tigers and the like, one should remember the Goddess named Kṣemaṅkarī.

They cross over calamities and are liberated from various impending afflictions. In this case as well, the mantra and meditation should be understood as victorious. Regarding "in a wilderness-fortress":
a wilderness (*kāntāra*) is a path beset by dangers such as thieves; a fortress (*durga*) therein refers to an inaccessible mountain such as the Himalayas or Kailāsa.

Those setting out on a journey who remember Śavarī—who appears in the form of a Śavarī—cross over calamities because she wards off that fear; they are liberated from the disturbances caused by the wicked beasts of the mountains. The Ācārya himself will describe her meditation and so forth later in the fourth hymn, beginning with the words "O you whose crest is a peacock feather."
Regarding the fear of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and *jambhakas*:
*bhūtas* are specific classes of divine beings (*devayoni*) who dwell in places such as empty wells, solitary trees, and crossroads, and serve as attendants to Rudra;

*pretas* are specific types of deceased spirits; *piśācas* are those who dwell in cremation grounds and similar places, having firebrands for mouths; and *jambha* is a name [for a specific class of spirit].

That very *dānava* is like a *jambhaka* (a bewilderer) in the sense of "counteracting" (*apratikṛtau*). Therefore, when fear and terror arise on account of *jambhakas*— such as *rākṣasas* who draw away the blood of sacrificial animals and the like, as well as the hosts of *śākinīs* and others— one should remember you, the Great Bhairavī, who possess that very form, for the sake of [overcoming] those calamities.

They cross over the great fears beginning with the fear of [the elements] *bhūta*. For the Śruti states: "The knower of Brahman as bliss fears nothing from anywhere" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4). This has been stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"Whether in a forest, in a wilderness, in water, or even on land..."
Especially in places where there is danger from tigers, crocodiles, and thieves.
"And in all the *ādhis* as well, one should proclaim the names of the goddesses.
Thus [it is said]. The extraction of the mantra for this [deity] is in the seventh *ucchvāsa* of the *Vidyārṇava*:
The letter Śiva (Ś) and Candra (C) situated in Vahni (R), conjoined with Vāgbhava (A),
and perfectly joined with Nāda and Bindu— this is extracted as the first seed-syllable (bīja).
From Lopāmudrā, the second seed-syllable, the Vāgbhava-kūṭa, has been extracted;
it consists of Śiva (H) and Candra (I) situated in Fire (R), conjoined with the vowel of Manu (U).
The third seed-syllable is declared to be endowed with the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*. (1.2.3) This is clear:
*hasraiṃ*, *hasakalahrīṃ*, *hasrauṃ*.
Thus: Meditation—[He is] possessing the luster of a thousand suns of copper-red hue, with a shimmering crescent moon and matted locks;
adorned with a crown resplendent with jewels and variegated pearls.
She is adorned with a garland of skulls rich with glistening blood,
enriched by the beauty of three eyes, and endowed with a face like the full moon.
Her full and elevated breasts were like silver jars adorned with strings of pearls;
she was clothed in red garments, her form intoxicated with the vigor of youth.
She holds a book and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, and a rosary in her right;
she is eternally intent on bestowing boons, seated upon a great corpse.

Thus: "vyāmoha" means that by which one is deluded; it is the power of *māyā*, because its inherent nature is to cause delusion. By that [power], there occurs the subduing of the obscuration—which consists in the non-manifestation (*akhyāti*) of the nature of the full consciousness—within its effect, namely, that which is of the nature of *avidyā*. Alternatively, "vyāmoha" is the act of deluding; it is the delusion (*moha*) consisting of non-manifestation residing in the limited subject (*pramātṛ*). It is not [the case that...].

Indeed, this [universe] cannot be some indefinable form consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*), as held by the proponents of cyclic transformation (*vivartavādins*), because it is impossible for such a thing to manifest this diversity of the universe if it were not a real entity;
or, if its reality were possible, it would possess full ontological status and could not be "indefinable. Nor can it be as the Sāṃkhyas hold.

Delusion is a state characterized by the predominance of *rajas* and *tamas*, for it is impossible for such a state to possess the variety of activity inherent in insentience (*jaḍatva*). Therefore, this is the sovereign freedom (*svātantrya*) of the Lord, which consists in the accomplishment of the most difficult feats.

In that delusion, which consists in the non-manifestation of one's own nature as the fullness of indivisible consciousness, those seeking liberation remember you— Tripura, Bālā Tripurasundarī, the illuminator of the principle of Mahāsarasvatī— and they cross over calamities,
the succession of births, old age, death, and so forth; they are liberated from them, reaching the state of non-return.

The meaning is that they go; for there is the Śruti: "He does not return again" (Nirvāṇa-tantra 33), and the Smṛti: "Having gone there, they do not return" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.6). As for those mantras and so forth, it is as stated in the Jñānārṇava:
O Goddess! Tripurā is threefold; hear first of Bālā, by the knowledge of whom, O Goddess, one becomes directly possessed of the splendor of the Preceptor of the Gods.
Having uttered the solar vowel (S), which consists of the bindu, nāda, and kalā,
one should place the final vowel (AU) upon the earth (L), conjoined with the fourth vowel (I).
Overcome by the Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā, the imperishable Bhṛgu possesses the power of creation;
joined with the vowel 'Śa' (the fifth), this is considered the three-syllabled Vidyā.
"She who bestows the arrangement of words like the surging waves of the Ganges;
she who generates great good fortune and grants great eloquence. Thus it is said. Furthermore—
O Maheśānī! One should meditate upon the Goddess as being situated in the midst of a Kadamba forest, within a jeweled pavilion in the heart of a great Kalpa forest.
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne in the shade of a released parasol,
she holds a book and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, and a rosary in her right.
"Devoted to granting boons, divine, and bestowing the great Sarasvatī," so it is said.
In the Vāmakeśvara [Tantra],
however, beginning with "Tripurā is the supreme Śakti" (4.4):

Up to the verse ending with "Tripurā has attained renown" (4-16), the subtle meditation on the Goddess named Tripurā, whose essential nature is the Supreme Consciousness-power (paracicchakti), has been described. Likewise, regarding one traveling by boat upon the ocean: *toyaplave* means in the water, in the liquid; *plavaḥ* means floating, or immersion therein.

Or rather, when [the moon] has reached the water, [the phrase] "those staying on a boat" (*plave naukāyāṃ vartamānāḥ*) should be applied everywhere as a qualifier; likewise, [the phrase applies to] you, the goddess named Tārā.

The meaning is that by remembering [the mantra], those who cross the ocean transcend calamities such as drowning in water and become those who have reached the further shore. The extraction of that mantra is as stated in the *Matsyasūkta*:
"Having extracted the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), one should join it with the letter 'ta' conjoined with fire (Ra)."
The second seed-syllable is extracted as joined with Māyā (Hrīṃ), Bindu (M), and Svara (Ā).
The third is the Kūrca seed-syllable (Hūṃ), followed by the syllable Phaṭ.
Thus is the complete perfected mantra, endowed with the five rays of light.
Thus: As for meditation—
one should meditate upon her who resembles the luster of ten million suns, whose crest is joined by the crescent moon,
whose limbs are red, who wears a girdle and very red garments, and whose face is like the orb of the full moon.
I bow to the Blessed Lady Tārā, the savior of the world, who holds a noose, a sword, and a great goad in her four arms, and who is adorned with various ornaments.

Thus, the extraordinary fruit for practitioners who worship the other goddesses, who are the forms of the sevenfold sovereign power (*saptavibhūti*), for the sake of liberation from the seven types of calamities, has been stated.
It should be understood that the method of recitation (*japa*) for these [goddesses] is to be known as being like the sequence of the recitation of the mantra to be described hereafter. Thus...

It should be understood that the Supreme Deity possesses various forms for the sake of bestowing grace, manifested through her own sovereignty due to the diversity of the practitioner’s varying dispositions. As they say:
"In whatever form the practitioner always remembers [her]," and so forth.
The Lord becomes identical with that [object of meditation], just like a wish-fulfilling gem.
Thus [ends the section]. || 17 ||
Then, offering praise to the Supreme Deity by means of specific names that encapsulate the method of reciting the mantra-pārāyaṇa, he says: Māyā, Kuṇḍalinī, Kriyā, Madhumatī, Kālī, Kalāmālinī.
Mātaṅgī, Vijayā, Jayā, the Blessed Goddess Śivā, Śāmbhavī, Śakti, the beloved of Śaṅkara, the three-eyed Vāgvādinī, and Bhairavī. (p. 80)
O Mother, you are Hrīṃkārī, Tripurā, composed of the supreme and the non-supreme, and Kumārī. || 18 ||

The term "Bhagavatī" is to be understood as an adjunct to "Sambuddhi" (O Goddess); its explanation is to be known as previously stated. That which is called *māyā* is the power (*śakti*) of the Lord, Brahman, whose nature is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*). She is twofold, consisting of both the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*ajaḍa*). Of these, the former is the transformative material cause (*pariṇāmy-upādāna*) of the universe, whereas Brahman possesses the status of being the illusory material cause (*vivarta-upādāna*). Therefore...
Because the universe, which is the effect of *māyā*, is itself *māyic*, it possesses both insentience (*jaḍatva*) and falsity (*mithyātva*). As it is stated in the *Bhaktisūtras*:

"That power is *māyā*, because it is common to all that is insentient. However, the non-dual (*advaita*) scriptures have as their purport the oneness of the ultimate reality. Thus, passages such as "All this, indeed, is Brahman" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.6.1) [and others]...

This is because [the first definition] refers to co-occurrence with sublation (*bādhasāmānādhikaraṇya*). The second, however, is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) eternally inherent in the Supreme Brahman; because its nature is unlimited, it is called *māyā*. As it is said: "His supreme power is heard of as indeed manifold, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action, and being innate" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8). And: "Both *māyā* and *avidyā*..."
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "He becomes himself" (Nṛsiṃhapūrvatāpanīya Upaniṣad 9.3).
Thus it is said in the Śrī Tantrāloka:
"And that which is called Māyā is the power of the Lord, non-different from Him."
For in that way, he has been made by her to possess the sovereignty of the manifestation of differentiation.
That first manifestation of differentiation which has not yet reached division—
that is the Supreme Night, in which all future divisions are held within its womb.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"This is that supreme power, consisting of me, whose form is Brahman;
she is my beloved, infinite Māyā, by whom this world is deluded."
By means of this, O best of the twice-born, I delude this entire world— including gods, asuras, and humans— and I create and dissolve it.

Thus, according to the teaching of Śiva, the fact that the universe is a manifestation of consciousness culminates in its reality. This is because the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in such Vedic texts as "All is Brahman" (Mahopaniṣad 5.113) finds its natural significance only in absolute non-difference (*atyantābheda*). Even a spatial location belongs to Brahman.
It is conceptualizable and does not transcend the appearance of all forms; likewise, "Brahman is one only, without a second" (Trika-mata-tantra 3.3)— it is not [so] here.
Because [the Upaniṣadic passage] beginning with "There is no diversity whatsoever" (Kaṭha 4.11) results in the rejection of the suitability of being the locus for the manifestation of difference;
and because of the transformation [of the Self], its distinctness [from the effect] is established by the word "originating" (ārambhaṇa) and other such terms.
Since even the aphorisms of Vyāsa (the *Vaiyāsika-sūtras*) come to rest in this very same sense, this is the position accepted by the Tantrikas.

The Sāṃkhyas declare that what is called *māyā* is *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and that it is independent; the Vedāntins, however, maintain that it is simply the power (*śakti*) of Śiva. By the term "power," however, dependence is expressed.

Thus, you are Māyā as described above; likewise, you are Kuṇḍalinī, the power known as the life-force (jīvana) residing within the microcosmic egg (piṇḍāṇḍa), because she is the one who vitalizes the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka). As it is said in the Cūḍālā episode of the Vāsiṣṭha:
"The life-sustaining [power] of the mind, which is otherwise called the puryaṣṭaka..."
Know that Kuṇḍalinī is like a flower-cluster within the fragrance.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:
"The Great Power, Kuṇḍalinī, is subtler than a lotus fiber.
As for the detailed exposition of her essential nature and other attributes, it is found in the *Śrītantrarāja*:

Situated in the midst of the fiery splendor of the fire-principle residing in the *mūlādhāra*, the power of the individual soul (*jīva-śakti*) known as Kuṇḍalinī is of the nature of vital breath (*prāṇa*); indeed, by virtue of that form of breath, she is luminous.
Having the form of a sleeping serpent, with three coils and great luster,
she whose head is Māyā roars incessantly as she rises up in the sky (or "in her own abode," according to an alternative reading).

"When that [sound] in the middle of the *suṣumnā* is not heard by one who has covered both ears, then his death occurs" (Pañcāśikā 30, verse 64), and so forth. This has been explained at length previously. *Kuṇḍale* refers to ear-ornaments.
Or, she is called Kuṇḍalinī because the solar and lunar orbs (arka-indu-maṇḍala) exist within her.
As it is said in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: [p. 82]
"Her orb of the sun and moon has become a pair of earrings.
Likewise, elsewhere it is said:
"The sun and moon are the breasts of the Goddess; they alone are considered her eyes."
"Both [ears] are a pair of earrings"—this is the Vedic revelation.

Thus, for the Supreme Lord whose nature is consciousness, action (*kriyā*) is none other than His power known as the Supreme Goddess (*Parābhaṭṭārikā*), whose essence is the principle of vibration (*spandatattva*). Because it brings about the manifestation of the manifold variety of the universe, it is called the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). For the Teachers have stated that the power of action is the capacity to assume all forms.
It bestows bondage and liberation upon limited subjects through recognition and non-recognition of that very state. As it is said in the *Spanda*:
"This power, whose nature is action, belonging to Śiva, resides within the bound soul (*paśu*)."
"Binding [the senses], abiding in its own path, and known, it brings about success. (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra, Chapter 4, Verse 28).
Also, in the Mālinī-vārtika:
"For what we call 'action' is not something other than this; rather, it is power itself."
And power, being differentiated, is the very nature of existence, distinguished by its capacity to produce results through its own conceptualization.
That power belongs only to the All-pervasive One, and He is the embodiment of the soul of the universe;
in ultimate reality, He is not divided by the distinction between the fruit and the causal agent.

"Because the All-pervasive One thus manifests differentiation even within His own undivided Self, He is called the Power of Action (*kriyā-śakti*), by which the Great Lord is the Agent. (Prakaraṇa-kārikā 3.5–3.7).
And furthermore: "He raises and lowers His hand."
Action is characterized by moments of successive operation occurring in a prior-to-posterior sequence;
some, like the followers of Kaṇāda, maintain that it is perceptible by the senses,
as they say:

Whether it be accomplished or unaccomplished, that which is designated as something to be accomplished (sādhya) is called "action" (kriyā), because it possesses a nature that depends upon a temporal sequence.
p. 83) Thus:
"A collection of parts that arise in succession [is perceived] by means of those parts which have become subordinate qualities."
That which is conceived as non-different from consciousness is designated as "action."

Thus [it is said]. Others, however, maintain that action (*kriyā*)—which is understood as an imperceptible power (*śakti*) consisting of the production of conjunctions and disjunctions for the purpose of effecting a change in form—is designated as "lifting up" when it occurs in the hand; they thus assert its inferability. This refers to action of the aforementioned kind, which is worldly (*laukikī*).

In the objective sphere (*vedyabhāga*), there is succession because it is delimited by time. However, as for that power of action belonging to the Lord—which is non-different from Him, whose nature is vibration (*spanda*), and which constitutes worldly activity—succession is not possible, since it is impossible for it to have even the appearance of a temporal division. Thus it has been said:

The sequential nature of worldly action is possible due to the power of time, but it does not apply to that which is eternal; rather, it belongs to the sovereign power of the Lord, like that of a master.

Thus it is said. In reality, however, it is the internal power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*) itself that, having manifested as far as the external, is called "action" (*kriyā*), because all external vibrations are but its offshoots. As it is stated in the *Mālinīvijaya*:
"Furthermore, when [one thinks], 'Let this object become such-and-such'..."
"Having known [the object], at that very moment performing that [action]—this is what is called 'action' here" (Mukhya-pāṭha).
Thus, action is twofold, characterized by either succession or simultaneity; you are of that nature. Likewise, *madhu* means wine.
It is called *madhumatī* because honey (or flower-nectar) or honeycomb is offered to it at the time of sacrifice and worship;

for there is a Vedic revelation stating, "Honey is indeed the form of this great deity," and another Vedic revelation stating, "In that one offers with honey, one thereby gratifies that great deity"—the meaning being that she is pleased by this. By this...
It is thus stated that Kākinī, delighted by the drinking of honey, is of the nature of Ambā. As it has been said:

"In the lotus called Svādhiṣṭhāna, which shines with six petals, she who has four faces and three eyes holds in her two hands a trident, a rosary, a skull-bowl, and the gesture of fearlessness, possessing a sense of pride."

(p. 84) We meditate upon Kākinī, who is established in the marrow-element, intoxicated with pride, joyful, joined with Bandhinī as her chief consort, yellow in color, fond of curd-rice offerings, and the bestower of desired fruits.
Thus [it is said]. Also in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:

"With marrow as her foundation, delighted by honey," and so forth, ending with "she who assumes the form of Kākinī. Alternatively, she is called *Madhumatī* because she possesses *madhu*—that is, the essence of the nectar of bliss consisting of the state of perfect equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) which characterizes all specific flavors of bliss.

"He is indeed the essence (*rasa*), whose nature is the ground of the world's bliss," according to the Śruti (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.7), and "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss," according to another Śruti (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32). Or else, "The Sun is indeed the honey of the gods."

In such scriptural passages as these, the specific knowledge known as Madhumatī is enjoined; furthermore, among the four stages of yoga well-known in the Yogaśāstra for practitioners, there are seven levels to be transcended, the seventh of which is called Madhumatī. As they say regarding that: "The stage named Madhumatī..."

Through the power of practice (*abhyāsa*) and detachment (*vairāgya*), the slightest trace of darkness (*tamas*) is cast off, and there is the attainment of *samādhi* consisting of the light of happiness and the quality of goodness (*sattva*). As it has been said:
"In that state, wisdom (*prajñā*) bears the truth. For it is precisely that knowledge which arises in that stage [of meditation].
*Tārakam* means that which delivers one from *saṃsāra*; or it refers to the *madhumatī-vidyā* well-known in the Tantras.
Its extraction is as follows, according to the *Śrīvidyārṇava*:
"The *mādana*, the seed-syllable of Śiva, and thereafter the seed-syllable of Vāyu."
Thereafter, one should extract the seed-syllable of Indra (HŪṂ) and then Mahāmāyā (HRĪṂ).

This "Madhumatī" refers to the knowledge that is honey-sweet (*madhumatī*); it may signify the specific river Madhumatī famous in Kashmir at the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) of Śāradā, or it may mean the mountain Tapati. It is the Goddess of Consciousness herself in the form of Kālī, the supreme power of absolute freedom (*parāsvātantryaśakti*), because she manifests as the countless powers of the universe through their respective forms.
Alternatively, she who performs the fivefold manifestation (*kalana*) of the goddesses beginning with Sṛṣṭi is designated by the term *Kālī*.
As it was stated by the venerable Abhinavaguptapāda, who possesses the sovereignty of the Krama system:
"Emission (*kṣepa*), cognition (*jñāna*), enumeration (*saṃkhyāna*), movement (*gati*), and sound (*nāda*)—in this sequence."
Beginning with "The casting [of the self] is the differentiation of one's own self" (p.
the Supreme [Power], performing this fivefold *kalana*, is [the agent].
The Goddess Kālī is likewise called Kālakarṣiṇī.
Thus it was said. And so too by his own gurus, the venerable Bhūtirājas:

"Because of her casting [down] and because of her knowledge, Kālī is so called by virtue of her power of limitation. Furthermore, she is Kālī because she measures even death itself, according to the Vedic revelation: "Death is the condiment for whom."
As Kālidāsa said: "O Mother, that which consists of doubt in our hearts— 'This is so,' 'But this is not so'—
is indeed Yama himself, skilled in the sport of binding living beings, who is driven away by you."
Thus it is said; and in the Āgama as well:
"She alone, the Great Goddess Kālī, is celebrated in the worlds and the Vedas, in the Itihāsas, the Tantras, the Siddhāntas, and the Kulas."

Thus: Kālī was created by Śiva for the purpose of slaying the demon Dāruka, or she who, having taken that form, slew Dāruka and agitated the three worlds with her pacified fire of wrath. To dispel that wrath, Śiva became a child and wept; she suckled that child from her own breasts, and through her milk, he [drank] even the fire of her anger.
It is well known in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa* that she drank [it] and thereby became peaceful.

Likewise, regarding "Kalā"— which is the seventeenth digit (*kalā*) whose form consists of half of half of the letter *ha*, as stated in such passages as "They call that sixteenth digit in the Person the immortal digit" and so forth— it refers to the end of the sixteen [principles], beginning with the internal organ (*karaṇa*).
She is the nourisher of the *kalās* and possesses a form that never sets. As it has been said:
"Therefore, the seventeenth *kalā* has the nature of the form of nectar;
she has spread forth through the movement of the *bindu*, which is the essential nature of both the transcendent (*parā*) and the immanent (*apara*)."
Thus it is said. And now, as for the *baindavī* digit (*kalā*), it has been stated: "Established above, bestowing supreme bliss, raining down a shower of nectar, is the supreme *baindavī* digit."
In the Bṛhatpārāśarasmṛti, however, it is stated:
"That which extends fifteen finger-breadths outside the nose..."
That wherein the individual soul becomes purified is known as the sixteenth digit.

And because of the statement in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*: "The self alone is its sixteenth digit. This will also be explained in detail further on. Or, the digit called Śāntyatītā, which resides in the ether (*vyoman*), is so called because it generates the experience of the bliss of liberation;
as it is said in the Śaiva Āgama:
[They] bestow the bliss of awakening and the nirvāṇa of non-duality beyond the kalā of Śāntyatītā.

Likewise, Mālinī is the deity who presides over the specific mantras beginning with *na* and ending with *pha*, which consist of the union of seeds (*bīja*) and matrices (*yoni*). Furthermore, she is called Mālinī because she possesses a garland (*mālā*) of Rudra’s powers; this is her primary Śākta nature.
Mālinī, who is beautiful through the emergence of emission from the union of seed-syllables and matrices,
is indeed determined to be the Supreme Power, whose form is the universe.

Thus, according to the statement, "That which is the essence of this world is the supreme power Mālinī," the meaning is that she is the form of the power of supreme reflective awareness (*paravimarśa*). Furthermore, she is capable of bestowing all supernatural accomplishments (*siddhi*). As it is said in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
Through the agitation of those whose origins are mutual seeds and from the arising of emission,
what accomplishment would it not bestow, or what deficiency would it not fulfill?

Thus [it is said]. Or else, she is Mālinī, a friend of the Goddess, or she takes that form. As it is stated in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*, in the section on Pārvatī’s marriage, concerning the taking of the seven steps: "Then the foot of Hara was grasped by Mālinī for the purpose of bestowing [the bride]."
"What do you ask for? I shall give it; release [him]," Hara said.
Mālinī said to Śaṅkara: "O Śaṅkara, grant to my friend the good fortune belonging to her own lineage; through that, you shall thereafter attain liberation."

Then Mahādeva said: "O Mālinī, I have given [you my word]; release me. (p. 87) Thus. *Mālinī* is either one whose form is the Mandākinī; for the *Viśva* lexicon states: "In the context of the Mandākinī, she is called Mālinī. Or else:

Mālinī is the deity presiding over the inner ten-spoked wheel (daśāracakra), meaning Tripuramālinī; likewise, Mātaṅgī is the form of the power (śakti) of Mātaṅga, who became the offspring of the omniscient sage Mataṅga,
and whose essential nature is an incarnation of the Great Goddess (Mahādevī)— she whom [the Lord], desiring to conquer the beloved Tripurā, [approached].
It is indeed heard that the Blessed Lord Śambhu chose [Mataṅga] for the sake of sacrifice. As it is stated in the *Brahmayāmala*:
"O child, in this world, that Mataṅga, the bull among sages, who was nearly omniscient, performed fierce penance for ten thousand years."
Delighted by that, the Great Goddess, who acts for the welfare of the gods, said:
"Choose a boon, O Blessed One; I shall grant you whatever you desire."
Having heard that, the best of the twice-born requested her for a means to attain dharma:
"O Goddess! O Mother of the worlds! If you are pleased at this moment,"
"Having attained the state of being my offspring, become the support of my lineage";
having thus entreated her, the best of sages begot that daughter.
Dark-complexioned and with a beautiful face, she is accompanied by a lute and a parrot; endowed with wisdom, she holds a śārikā bird and a rosary in her lotus-like hands.
Bearing [these ornaments], the large-eyed lady, adorned with conch-shell earrings,
that great goddess became the delight of the Matanga lineage.

"The goddess Mātaṅgī is eternally renowned as the bestower of boons," and so forth. By the practice of reciting her mantra and other rites, proficiency in the arts of poetry, music, and the like arises.
As it has been said:
One may possess great scholarship in all the scriptures, yet [this work] is distinguished by its soft composition of profound words worthy of the most refined masters.
He shall become exceedingly bold in graceful poetry,
and he shall be extremely proficient in music and in all branches of knowledge.
Thus it is said. Likewise, as for the Great Goddess Vijayā, when she conquered the Daitya king named Padma, she became renowned by the name Vijayā. As it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa (p.
Having conquered the exceedingly powerful Daitya king named Padma,
she became renowned throughout the three worlds as Vijayā and Aparājitā.

Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, she is "Victorious" (*vijayā*) because her victory is distinguished in comparison to the lineage of causes beginning with Brahmā; or else, she is "Victorious" because she possesses a distinguished victory known as the cessation of the fluctuations of the senses, and she is of the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpā*). Or again, she is of the nature of the time-period called the *muhūrta* named Vijaya, because she bestows distinguished victory. As it is stated in the *Cintāmaṇi*:
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, at the rising of the stars, that time is known as Vijaya; it bestows success upon all undertakings and goals.
Thus it is said. However, in the *Ratnakośa*:
"When the twilight has slightly passed and the stars have just begun to appear, this time is called 'Victorious' (*vijaya*); it accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings."
The eleventh muhūrta, which is proclaimed as Vijaya,
is the time during which a journey should be undertaken by all who desire victory.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, regarding the thirteenth *nityā-vidyā*, *Vijayā*, whether she is the very nature of the *nityā-vidyās* or [their manifestation], her meditations, worship, the application of yantras, and so forth, are to be seen in the eighteenth chapter of the *Śrītantrarāja*.

Likewise, *Jayā* is derived from the sense that "victory (*jaya*) exists in her" with respect to action, non-action, their transformation, and so on; this is formed by adding the suffix *ac* (as in the *arśa-ādi* group) and then the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.

The meaning is "liberated from that. This is because of the Kaṭhaka Śruti: "This is the eternal greatness of a brāhmaṇa; he does not increase by action, nor does he become less"; and also because of the Vājasaneyi Śruti (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22): "He does not become greater by good action, nor indeed smaller by evil action. [The text continues: "Not me..."
And because of the Smṛti statement, "Actions do not smear [the soul]" (Bhagavad Gītā 4.14).

Other meanings have been explained previously. The term "the divine Goddess" (bhagavatī devī) has also already been explained. Likewise, she is "Śivā" because she possesses "śiva"—that is, bliss consisting of perfect bliss; for it is said, "Of this very bliss, other beings... [are but small portions].

According to the Śruti, "They subsist upon the measure" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32). Alternatively, she is of the nature of the fourth consciousness (*turīya-saṃvid-rūpā*), because she brings about wonder through the contemplation of the expansion of power (*śākta-sphāra*) within the triad beginning with the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
According to the Śruti, "They consider the non-dual fourth to be Śiva; He is the Self," [she is] the enjoyer of the triad, the Lord of Heroes (*vīreśa*).
And because it is stated in the Śivasūtras (1.11): "As for that which is proclaimed as the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer within the three abodes... (p. 89).
But he who understands both of these, while enjoying them, is not defiled.

And thus it is said: Or rather, through the metaphorical treatment of the identity between the means and the goal, that which is called Kāmeśvara is attained by means of vibration (*spanda*); just as wind is perceived through its heat and fire is perceived through its warmth.
That which is pure consciousness, stainless and tranquil, is indeed declared to be Śiva.
"It is indeed perceived only through the power consisting of vibration, and not otherwise. Thus it is said.
Also in the *Vijñānabhairava*: "The face of Śiva is said here [to be] like the light of a lamp or the rays of the sun. (Verse 20)
"O Dear One, just as the divisions of the directions and so forth are known [through their respective powers], so too is Śiva [known] through His power.
(Verse 21) Or, Śivā is that whose essential nature is non-different from Śiva. As it has been said:
"O best of the twice-born, within the form of the power belonging to Māyā, which rests upon pure consciousness..."
That consciousness which has entered [into all things], which is free from conceptual construction, and which is self-luminous.
She who possesses the six aspects, who is supreme bliss, and who brings about the destruction of saṃsāra—
she is the auspicious Supreme Goddess, non-different from Śiva, the bestower of auspiciousness.

This will be explained in detail further on. Likewise, this is the Śāmbhavī state of Śambhu; for it is the state of Khecarī, consisting of the surging forth of supreme bliss of the nature of consciousness, through the pacification of the expansion of the agitation of Māyā which consists of all forms of duality. As it is said in the Śivasūtras:
"When knowledge arises spontaneously, the state of Śiva is the Khecarī [state]. (2-5). Also, in the *Tantrasadbhāva*:
"One attains the supreme goal through the nature of the object, by means of the path of Kula, eternally."
It moves among all living beings; that is known by the name Khecarī.
Thus it is said elsewhere:
"By the power of its emergent state, through the function of expansion, the yogi remains established in his own essential nature;
having approached the objects of the senses by himself, he experiences them while dwelling on the plane of bliss."
This [mudrā],
which is unrestrained in form and most expansive, belongs to those whose intellects are fully awakened;
for the perfected ones (siddhas) always abide within it, delighting in bliss— this is the supreme mudrā.
Thus [it is said]. But another [form] is accessible to yogis of immeasurable power who experience it by following the specific configurations of Vyāpinī and the others.
As it has been stated:
The yogi, having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), should place the Lord of the Eye in the navel;
he should lead that [breath], which is rod-like in form, as far as the three cavities (kakhatraya).
Having restrained [the breath] there, one should quickly impel it through the three voids;
by binding this, the great yogi attains movement in the sky.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, this Śāmbhavī power, known as the Śrīpādukā, is the means for the thorough realization of Śambhu, whose nature is the light of supreme consciousness non-different from his own self.
As it has been stated by the learned: "The [power] consisting of supreme bliss belongs to the self which is both supreme and non-supreme."

The Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), intent upon devouring [all things] through its own differentiation (*svavyatireka*), is celebrated as *pādukā*. Alternatively, it is that state of the powers of knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth—which, by the analogy of the two pans of a scale (*tulāpuṭanyāya*), is characterized by an absolute absence of imbalance—known as the principle of *prakṛti*; this Śāmbhavī power is inaccessible to the proponents of systems such as Sāṃkhya. As it has been said: [Quotation follows]
In the state of non-differentiation of the qualities of knowledge, action, and illusion—which have the nature of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—the reality is *prakṛti*; this is the power of Śambhu.
This is the Mother of the Śāmbhavas, or the specific form of the Śāmbhavī Mudrā. Its definition is as follows:
"The internal object of focus with the gaze directed outward, free from the opening and closing of the eyes—this is that Śāmbhavī Mudrā, hidden in all Tantras."

Thus [it is said]. Or, it is of the nature of a specific initiation (*dīkṣā*). Its other meanings will be elaborated upon later. Likewise, Śakti—known by the name Kāmeśvarī or called Sovereignty (*svātantrya*)—is for her own activity because she possesses the state of Śiva, which consists in the expression of the fivefold cosmic functions (*pañcakṛtya*) free from dependence on external instruments such as material cause (*upādāna*).
For one who has already set out, where is the search for other causal signs?
(As stated on p. 91:

Or, she is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the five powers beginning with *cit*. Alternatively, she is indeed the venerable *Parā* herself, who devours [all things] by means of an internal contemplation that embraces the three powers beginning with *parā* within her own interior.
There is a certain power (śakti) designated by various other terms such as Śrī Mātṛsadbhāva and Kālakarṣiṇī. These three are as follows, as the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta has said:
"That [power] by which this universe, from Śiva down to the earth, is both sustained and perceived as being of the nature of non-conceptual consciousness alone."
And that by which the Supreme Lord illumines is His Śrī Parā-śakti;
and that by which He [illumines] through both difference and non-difference, like a hand and so forth reflected in a mirror, is His Śrī Parāpara-śakti;
and that by which [He illumines] through mutual distinctness is His Śrīmad Aparā-śakti.

Moreover, the power of the Goddess is established as the power of majesty (*mahimāśakti*), by which this wheel of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) is caused to revolve incessantly in the forms of creation, maintenance, and so forth. For thus says the Śruti:
"Some poets speak of inherent nature (*svabhāva*); others, being utterly deluded, speak of time (*kāla*)."
"This is the majesty of the God by whom this wheel of Brahman is made to revolve in the world" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad).
And the Smṛti says:
"Causing all beings, mounted on a machine, to revolve by means of Māyā" (Bhagavad Gītā 18.61).

Thus, [the term] *śaṅkaravallabha* [is explained as follows]: *kara* means "one who acts," derived from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *ac* (as in the *pacādyac* class), or with the suffix *ṭa* according to the rule *kṛño hetuḥ*. Thus, it is "the maker of *śam* (bliss). Alternatively, it is "one in whose hand (*kare*) resides *śam*, which consists of bliss and fearlessness. Or, as stated in the Śaiva tradition: "Bliss (*śam*) is proclaimed to be the hand, which is power (*śakti*). Therefore, it refers to the power of bliss within the hand, which is of the nature of the desire to emanate.
Or [it refers to] "of whom" (yasya). As it has been said:
"She is called the power of bliss (ānanda-śakti), from whom the universe is emitted.
Śaṃkara is Kāmeśvara; his beloved (vallabhā) is his most dear one (preyasī). By this, [the nature of] the one whose essence is pure light is [described].

Since Paramaśiva’s very existence is animated by *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) and thus his attainment of selfhood is dependent upon Śakti, it should be understood that it is the substratum (*dharmin*) itself that is dependent upon its attribute (*dharma*),
and not that the attribute is subordinate. Therefore, within her,

only the status of being an attribute is conceptually constructed as her unique characteristic— namely, the nature of supreme subjectivity (*parāhaṃtā*)— but she herself is not a conceptual construction.
Therefore, she is celebrated as the pinnacle of Brahman (*brahmakoṭi*). As it has been said:
"There he dwells eternally, performing playful dalliances together with Pārvatī. (p. 92)
In the center is the temple of the Goddess; there, Śaṅkara is subject to her authority.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, she whose beloved husband is Śaṅkara is his queen (*mahiṣī*), because she has been consecrated in the *Svārājyasiddhi*. As it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:
"She is the great Mahātripurasundarī, the queen of Mahākāmeśa."
Thus, even by this twofold functioning, their state of mutual dependence culminates in their essential identity (*aikātmya*); this is the meaning. As it has been said in that very same place:
"On the mountain Īśānya-nāṭaka, there is the eternal abode of Śaṅkara."
The Lord dwells there eternally, and Pārvatī is dependent upon him.

Alternatively, those for whom Śaṅkara exists as their Lord are "possessors of Śaṅkara" (śaṃkaravantaḥ), namely the Māheśvaras; [the word] is derived with the suffix *gha* in the sense of the object (*karman*) in the root *labh* (to obtain). Thus, it means that this [reality] is to be attained by them—that is, it is to be known only by those who possess devotion to Śaṅkara. For instance, there is a Smṛti:
"But by undivided devotion alone, O Arjuna, I— who am of such a nature—
can be known in truth, seen, and entered, O scorcher of foes" (Bhagavad Gītā 11.54). And the Śruti says:
"One established in Brahman attains immortality" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.1).
Likewise, she is "three-eyed," meaning she whose eyes are the three wheels—the Mūrti, Prakāśa, and Ānanda—which are the means for the method of supreme worship. As it has been said:
O disciples of Mahāprakāśa, remember the Śrīpīṭha, the Pañcavāha, the three eyes, the multitude, and the wheels;
and remember the lineage of the gurus and the five powers beginning with Sṛṣṭi.
Thus, this threefold sequence of worship is attainable only through the service of a true guru by those whose hearts are permeated by the supreme descent of power (*śaktipāta*);
because it is a secret, we shall not reveal it here. [The three] are the forms of fire, sun, and moon.
Or, it is she whose eyes are [three];
or rather, she who leads (nayati) those to be graced—through the variety of the descent of power (śaktipāta)—to the three means of immersion (samāveśopāya), beginning with the Śāmbhava.
As it was said by Abhinavaguptapāda:
Thus, for those who wish to enter into this manifold nature of reality,
a threefold division has been described regarding the modes of immersion (samāveśa) according to the variety of means.
This Śāmbhava means is the means of consciousness (cid-upāya);
beyond that is the Āṇava means, which is the means of the insentient (jaḍa-upāya), and that too is considered to be manifold.

Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, since the word *nayana* (leading) has the sense of "instrument of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) based on its etymology—"that which leads (*nayati*) or brings about valid cognition (*pramā*)"—[the compound means] that in which there are three instruments of valid cognition consisting of verbal testimony (*śabda*), inference (*liṅga*), and perception (*adhyakṣa*).

This is because the application of the threefold instruments of valid cognition is possible in the production of valid cognition regarding that object. Among these, that which is produced by scripture (*āgama*)...

Verbal knowledge (*śābdajñāna*) consists of hearing (*śravaṇa*); inferential knowledge (*ānumānikajñāna*), produced by logical marks (*liṅga*), consists of reflection (*manana*); and direct perception (*pratyakṣajñāna*), produced by one's own experience, consists of meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*). It is taught in the sacred tradition that these three are the means for the vision of one's own Self.
"For indeed, my dear, the Self must be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5).
Likewise, the Yoga Sūtra states: "Perception, inference, and scripture are the means of valid knowledge."

The Sāṃkhya-sūtra also states: "The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is threefold. Alternatively, it may mean that she is the one whose means of valid cognition—serving as the instruments for accomplishing all worldly transactions—are the three powers such as will (icchā) and so forth; or the powers such as the supreme and non-supreme (parāparā); or Vāmā and the others; or Bhāratī and the others. [She is the one] who possesses these three...
It leads, or causes the qualified practitioners to reach, the paths known as the Southern, the Northern, and the Supreme Brahma-path. As it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa:
"The Southern world, the Northern world, and likewise the supreme Brahma-path."
The Three-Eyed One is considered the guide for this method and the class of the true path.

Thus [it is said]. These paths will also be defined further on. The mantra *vauṣaṭ* has the name *trinayana* (the Three-eyed One), or it takes that form. This will be demonstrated right here in the commentary on the meaning of the *mantraparāyaṇa*. Likewise, he speaks—that is, he fashions and creates—*Vāc*, Sarasvatī, who represents the power of poetic inspiration (*kavitva-śakti*).
She is called Vāgvādinī because she impels [all beings] by way of being the inner controller (antaryāmin),
or because she speaks; or because she speaks— that is, she shines forth— in the Veda (*vāk*) which consists of the secret scriptures (*rahasyāgama*), namely the Upaniṣads.

The meaning is: "that which is to be known through the knowledge of the inner self (adhyātma-jñāna) concerning that [object]. Here, it should be understood that the compound sentence ending in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*)—formed with the verb *vadati* in the sense of "manifesting" (*abhāsanārtha-vṛtti*)—conveys this very meaning. And thus says the *Brahmasūtra*:
"Because He has the scriptures as His source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*). This is because of the Vedic revelation: "The foot upon which all the Vedas meditate" (*Kaṭhopaniṣad* 2.15);

or alternatively, because He speaks the Vedas and so forth, which consist of speech. This is supported by such scriptural passages as: "That from which the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda are the breath," and "Whose breath is the Vedas."
Thus it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "With the breaths of his vital air, he created the Vedas— the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus— as well as the great mantras of the Atharva, through his creative will."
She created the ornaments of poetry, drama, and so forth through her sweet utterances; such is the beginning [of the passage].

Other meanings have been explained previously. Likewise, *bhairavāḥ* refers to the *vaṭukas* and others, or a multitude of those who are fearful (*bhīru*). She is their object of worship; thus, by the suffix *aṇ* denoting a mere general relationship, she is called *Bhairavī*.

"She sustains all, she causes all to resound, she is the giver of all, and she pervades the entire universe"—thus, by the constant utterance of the word *Bhairavī*, Śiva [is so called]. According to the principle stated in the *Vijñānabhairava*, because he performs the acts of sustaining (*bharaṇa*), causing resonance (*ravaṇa*), and emitting (*vamana*)—that is, performing the cosmic functions such as emission and so forth—he is Paramaśiva; and she belongs to him.

Or she is the woman associated with *vibhūti* (manifest power). Or she is the one whose nature is that *vidyā* known as Bhairavī, which arises when the letter *ra* is extracted from the middle peak (*kūṭa*) of the *Tripurāmbā-cakreśvarī-vidyā*. Or she takes the form of a twelve-year-old girl, according to the statement of Dhaumya: "Bhairavī is twelve years old. Furthermore, *udyama* (exertion) is Bhairava.
(1–5) | "The power of will is Umā, the Maiden" (1–13).
According to the principle stated in these *Śivasūtras*,

because [the subject] possesses the nature of emergent agency (*udyantṛtā*)— which consists in the surfacing of supreme intuition (*parapratibhā*)— and because of the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of all powers, [he is the Lord].
In that *Vārttika*:

"This [consciousness], which consists of the emergence of a reflection in the form of a sudden surging forth from one's own self-awareness as it flows out in the form of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)."
Exertion is the internal vibration consisting of the full sense of "I-ness" (pūrṇāhaṃbhāvanā);
it is that very state which arises from the complete equilibrium of all powers.
Because he completely devours even the diverse conceptual constructions by virtue of being full on all sides,
he is Bhairava, for his name is truly significant.
This exertion of self-awareness which has been described is of the nature of Bhairava;
it possesses a great power that transcends both sequence and non-sequence.
And so forth. Likewise:
"For one whose mind has ascended to the stages of yoga characterized by such wonder, and who practices through method the state of Supreme Bhairava, [that state] becomes eternal."
The very power of will belonging to that yogin becomes Umā;
she is indeed the Supreme Bhaṭṭārikā.
And so forth. Likewise:
"In each and every reality (tattva), the God of gods, taking hold of every stage according to his own will," and so on.
He whose singular self is full and whose nature is perfect consciousness is declared in the scripture to be the illustrious Bhairava.

And so forth. Other definitions of the term *arthāntara* will be explained later as the occasion arises; for their collection in this single place would result in an unwieldy expansion of the text that would lead to a lack of aesthetic flavor. Thus, let the discerning understand that by the word *bhairavī*, the great ground of Śakti is indicated here. Regarding the term *hrīṃkārī*:

Because *svarādi* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, the word *hrīm* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Its meaning, however, has been revealed by the Lord in the *Kādimata* through a verse of scrambled syllables (*vyākulākṣaraśloka*), because it is an extreme secret. For example: *tvaṃ kāmāmnā na praśavyo nānamasagnimātvagraroma īyo* (Note: This is a traditional example of a *vyākulākṣara* verse used to conceal the meaning of the seed-syllable *hrīm*. The intended reading is typically reconstructed as: *tvaṃ kāme nāpraśasyo 'nāmayasannimātva gṛhāṇa īyaḥ*, meaning "O Kāma, you who are not unpraiseworthy, being free from affliction, take me; come!")
"Kārvir śatanaṃtaphānmulanānnivi.

Here, by the first [syllable], *vyoma* (the letter *ha*), the nature of Paraśiva—who is the self of supreme light—is shown to be one that flashes forth spontaneously, independent of any other means of illumination. By the second [syllable], *agni* (the letter *ra*)...

By means of the fourth vowel (*turyasvara*), there is the act of assimilating to one's own self the universe that is manifested within oneself, due to one's own sovereignty, like a reflection in a mirror.

The reflective awareness of the state of *saṃghaṭṭa* (union), which consists of the merging of Śiva and Śakti, is brought about by the *bindu*—which is the nature of undivided light—as the perception of their unity and the definitive determination of that ultimate reality.
It is through this purpose that sovereignty over creation, maintenance, and withdrawal is established. Thus, [the text] says: "He brings them about."

*Hrīṃkārī*: [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied by virtue of the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*; from that which ends in *aṇ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. Alternatively, it means "she who produces shame (*hrīṃ*)," or else, since *hrīm* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) *hṛllekhā*, the suffix *kāra* is added to the phoneme; because the *gaura*-group is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied.
The meaning is: "she whose essential nature is the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī. Regarding *Tripurā*: of the three...
The city (*pura*) is that which consists of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge—or the *ātman* and the other principles (*tattvas*).
Alternatively, it is the "three-peaked" (*trikūṭa*) science, meaning she has the three peaks of knowledge as her city; that is to say, she is the locus of the science consisting of the three peaks.
Or else, she goes before (*purati*) the three authorities designated as perception, inference, and scripture, because she is not within their objective domain.
Or it is a form of the root *pur* belonging to the *tudādi* class; the suffix *ka* is applied because [the root] belongs to the *mūlavibhujādi* group, which is an *ākṛtigaṇa*.
As it has been said:
"Just as one strives to leap over the shadow of one's own head with one's own feet..."
Just as the head should not be placed at the region of the feet, so too it is with this Bindu-kalā.

Thus [says] the Śruti: "O Maitreyī, by what means could one know the Knower? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14). This has been explained in the verse beginning with "The wise [speak of Her] as consisting of the supreme and the non-supreme, and so do the lords of the earth. Furthermore, the supreme-non-supreme is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), which consists in not looking toward another for its source. For that [freedom] exists on the levels beginning with Sadāśiva.

In the state of *paśyantī*, although the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of "this-ness" (*idantā*) is merely an awakening due to its being increasingly obscured (*dhyāmalādhyāmalatvena*), the meaning is that it comes to rest in the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*) and becomes identical with that. Alternatively, [it refers to] those three powers of the Supreme Lord, beginning with Parā.

In the state where the manifestation of the sevenfold subjects, beginning with Sakala, occurs, they assume the threefold relationship of knower, means of knowledge, and object of knowledge; therein, the status of being the object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) has been established for the supreme aspect (*parāṃśa*). Among those [seven], that which is designated as the "supreme-non-supreme" (*parāpara*) means of knowledge exists within the sevenfold [subjects].

Among cognizers, that which is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) for knowledge and action according to its own suitability is called *śakti* (power). Through that very power, all cognizers attain sovereignty (*svātantrya*) such as being a knower, an agent, and the capacity for conjunction, disjunction, and synthetic reflection (*anusaṃdhāna*). You are of that very nature.
As it has been stated in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
"For thus, three powers of the Lord were described previously;
those very same [powers] are established in a threefold form as the measurer, the means of measurement, and the object of measurement."
In this context, the supreme aspect (*parāṃśa*) is the form of the Mother (*mātṛ*), while the intermediate aspect (*parāpara*) is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The inferior aspect (*apara*) is the object of knowledge (*meya*); thus, the possessor of power (*śaktimān*) and his power (*śakti*) constitute one's own true nature (*svarūpa*). (Tantrāloka 10.7–9, p.
Thus it is said. Its explanation is as follows in that very same work:
"Of the entire [perceiver], those two portions which constitute the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consist of *vidyā* and *kalā*;
they are reckoned as being of the nature of power (*śakti*) in their aspect as universals (*sāmānya*), but not in their specific divisions."
For the *layākala*, that very portion of the means of knowledge (*māna*) is supremely manifest;
however, for the *jñānākala*, manifestation occurs with the veil of the *kalā* of *vidyā* dissolving away.
Accompanied by the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of the destruction of the limited state of impure knowledge (*aśuddhavidyā*),
pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), desiring to awaken, becomes the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the mantras.

But when pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā) is awakened and conjoined with that residual impression (saṃskāra), it becomes the means of valid cognition for the Mantreśvaras; when devoid of that residual impression, it is not so.
The instrument of the Mantramaheśvaras is said to be Śakti;
she is the divine power of will, whose very existence consists solely in absolute freedom.
"That alone is the instrument of Śiva; by means of it, he knows and acts" (Tantrāloka 10.12.17).
Thus, in the Mālinīvijayavārttika:
"This ultimate consciousness, which is self-luminous in nature..."
That is declared to be self-awareness, from which the entire cosmic order arises.
And this very [power] does not transcend the essential nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
Reflective awareness is its supreme aspect; it is called *Paśyantī*, being full.

That very goddess is both the supreme and the non-supreme; let it be understood as "measure" (māna), wherein the object of cognition (meya) belonging to the non-supreme aspect abides through identity.
For there can be no determination of the object of knowledge by means of a separate instrument of knowledge;
indeed, the crow cannot possess the whiteness that belongs to the swan.
And thus the Guru Śaṅkaranandana has said this very thing:
"There is no persistence [of the object] because of its being an object of cognition, nor because it is other than that, nor because of sublation, nor because of non-persistence."
An entity does not attain proof as an external existence through its properties— which are inseparable from manifestation and whose nature is restricted to existence— unless it exists externally.
Therefore, consciousness itself consists of the threefold nature [of subject, means, and object], comprising the states of the knower,
the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.
While grasping [the object], it shines forth precisely because its very nature is self-luminosity.

"And that [consciousness], beautiful with the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the sound of the mantra which resides within it as its very self, is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by itself alone, because it does not depend on anything else due to the absence of [any] other [cause]. (Pratyabhijñākārikā 4.27–4.34).
In that same work, elsewhere also:
Thus, that reality which was indeed described as partaking in the nature of valid cognition is this very Goddess Parāparā, who shines forth in such and such ways.
Thus it is said. Moreover, the subject known as *vijñānakalā* and so forth is indeed both supreme (*parā*) and non-supreme (*aparā*), being of that very nature.
As it is stated in the *Vārttika*:
"The subject who is both supreme and non-supreme is one in whom the supreme and non-supreme are fully integrated."
He is declared to be the state of consciousness (vijñānakala), awakened and capable of transforming others.
By means of the conjunction with the intensification of *apara* [kalā], that very same [subject] is the *pralayākala*. Alternatively, the supreme and intermediate powers of Śiva known as *ghorā*,

through the emergence of the internal sense (*antaḥ*) which was previously concealed by the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*), consist of both difference and non-difference in the form of Anāśrita, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and so forth.
"Those [powers] which, as before, produce attachment to the fruits of mixed karma and obstruct the path to liberation, are the terrible Parāparā. (Verse 32).
Thus, the Parāpara emission is the Vidyā-tattva, abiding in the state of both difference and non-difference.

The determination of the meaning of such passages is frequently understood from the mouth of the Guru. Furthermore, it is well known in the world that in states of unbearable suffering and the like, people generally utter the name of their mother alone, rather than that of their father.
In that regard, for those who have experienced many mothers throughout their successive births...

Because it is impossible for [ordinary beings] to remove the threefold suffering, and because even those existing in the present lack that capacity, the status of being a Mother is established primarily in the Goddess alone.
In order to instill in her a sense of compassion toward himself, he says "Mother," intending that she is the one worthy of praise by that very word;

the meaning is that she is the destroyer of unbearable suffering and the progenitor of the fourteen classes of living beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. For it is well known that even when a child has been struck by his father, it is the mother alone who provides him with consolation.
This is well-known. As it has been said:

"A child rebuked by his father is indeed consoled by his mother. Or else, as stated in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), "There is no knowledge higher than the Mother" (*mātṛkā*); thus [it is established] within one's own heart.
She is the form of the Mātṛkā, the friction-stick for the production of all branches of knowledge, because she encompasses the entirety of the signified and the signifier.
As it has been said:
"The Supreme Goddess Mātṛkā is indeed the mother of all mantras."

Thus, its exposition has been revealed in the *Śrīparātriṃśikā* and other scriptures; it has also been commented upon by the venerable Kṣemarāja in the *Śivasūtra-vimarśinī* at the point "the awakening of the *mātṛkā*-wheel" (2.7). Furthermore, the tenth lunar day (*tithi*) is the name for the Mother of the eternal mantra (*nityā-mantra*); the meaning is that she is Kulasundarī, whose form is that [of the tenth day]. She...
And this will be demonstrated later; or rather,
even though [the Self] is colored by the manifold collection of entities characterized by succession, simultaneity, and so forth, as delimited by space and other factors,
its true form remains pure consciousness alone, filled with the bliss of non-successive, undivided Consciousness.

The meaning is that the "Mātā" (the Mother) is the nature of the independent Supreme Knower (*paramātṛ*). As it has been said: "And this intuitive flash (*pratibhā*), though colored by the succession of various objects, is the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), the Knower whose nature is non-successive and infinite consciousness."

Thus: likewise, *ku* is the earth-element (*pṛthivītattva*); that in which one dies—that is, dissolves—is the *kumāra*, the *kulakuṇḍa* known as the support (*ādhāra*). The *kumārī* is she who belongs to that, the *kulakuṇḍalinī*. She is of that nature, for the *kumārī* is she who "lowers" (or sounds deeply), according to the Vedic revelation: "She is the woman who is devoted to her husband. And furthermore:

She is one whose nature is to "kill" (mārayati)—that is, to cause the ground of *māyā*, which first emerges at the breaking of the jar (*kuṃbha*), to cease its unmanifest expansion; or rather, she "plays" (*kumārayati*) by fashioning the sport of the creation of the universe and so forth. Thus, she is the supreme power of the Lord, known as the venerable Umā, who is not to be enjoyed by others, but exists in essential identity with Kāmeśvara.
And she is throbbing; thus it is stated in the Śivasūtra:
"The power of will is Umā, the maiden" (1.13).
And its Vārttika states:
"The very will-power (*icchā-śakti*) of that same yogin becomes Umā;
she herself is Parābhaṭṭārikā, and she is proclaimed as Kumārī."
She is called Kumārī because, through the play of creating the universe from Sadāśiva down to the earth, she destroys (mārayati) "Ku," the ground of great illusion (mahāmāyā).
