And the maiden is to be enjoyed by this yogi whose self is Bhairava;
the maiden is not to be enjoyed by another, for she abides in identity with the enjoyer.

"Umā Kumārī, having abandoned all attachments, was devoted to the worship of Maheśvara; likewise, the Will-power (icchā-śakti) belongs to the Yogin. (Śiva-sūtra-vārttika 67–71). Also, in the Svacchanda-tantra:
That goddess exists through the names and forms of all goddesses;
she is the Yogamāyā, concealed as a maiden, the creator of the worlds.

Thus: you are of such a nature as being either in the form of a maiden (*kumārī*) or in the form of a young girl (*bālā*). Now follows the detailed exposition of the sequence for the complete recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) of the mantra: after the root-vidyā, [the syllables] *māyā* (hrīṃ), *kuṇḍalinī* (aiṃ), *kriyā* (klīṃ), and so forth, are applied one by one in succession.

They are joined individually: the fourfold Madhumatī consists of the pure Mātṛkā, the one joined with the Bindu, the one joined with the Visarga, and the one joined with both the Bindu and the Visarga. The names of the ten Vidyās, beginning with Kālī, are joined with these in succession immediately after Madhumatī; following that, the ten Vidyās beginning with Śakti are joined in succession.

By joining these, the *mantrapārāyaṇa* vidyās are accomplished. Among them: (1) *Śakti* is the third seed-syllable of Śrī-Bālā, namely *sauḥ*. (2) *Śaṅkaravallabhā*, the power of Rudra, is *hasrīṃ śrīṃ*. (3) Regarding *Trinayanā*, because she is characterized by her location in the eyes, it is *vauṣaṭ*. (4)
Vāgvādinī says: this is the Vidyā. (5) Bhairavī is *hasaraiṃ*, *hasaklarīṃ*, *hasrauṃ*.

(6) The syllable *hrīṃ* is the essential form, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Bhuvaneśvarī. (7) Tripurā is the Śrī-Saubhāgya-Vidyā (*ha 5 ha 6 sa 4*). (8) She consists of both the transcendent (*parā*) and the immanent (*aparā*).
The Vidyā consisting of Śiva and Śakti is *hasrauṃ* and *sahraum*. (9) The Mother is the six-peaked Vidyā:
*hasakalaraḍaiṃ*, *hasakalaraḍīṃ*, and *hasakalaraḍauṃ*. (10) The Virgin is the Bālā-vidyā; she is well-known because she was extracted in the first verse.
p.

101) Thus, the sequence for reciting (*pārāyaṇa*) these ten aforementioned mantras through their mutual intermingling, which is useful for the practitioner’s recitation (*japa*), is demonstrated as follows: having risen in the morning, [one should perform] the daily rites (*āhnika-kriyā*).
Having prepared a secluded place and sat down upon one’s own seat, one should bow to the Guru, Gaṇapati, and the Supreme Deity;

then, preceded by the recollection of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other [limbs] of the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), one should perform the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) on the hands and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). Thereafter, having worshipped one’s chosen goddess (*iṣṭadevī*) with mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*) while meditating upon her, one should become one with the deity.
One should complete the recitation (*japa*) of the *mantrapārāyaṇa* over ten daily sessions. On the first day, the root mantra is:
*hrīṃ akālī sauḥ*. In this manner—namely, by joining the root mantra *hrīṃ akālī sauḥ* with the pure *mātṛkā* in sequence—the number of recitations is fifty-one (51). Again, in the same way...
In the application of the *mātṛkā* with the nasal bindu, the number is 51. Again, likewise, in the application of the *mātṛkā* with the visarga, the number for the recitation (*japa*) is 51.
Furthermore, in the mixing of the *mātṛkā* with both the visarga and the bindu, the number is 51. Thus, by means of the *māyābīja*.

Together with this, there are two hundred and four mantras (204). By joining the seed-syllable of Māyā, or the seed-syllable known as Vāgbhava, in place of the Māyā-bīja, and combining it with the fourfold letters of the Mātṛkā as before, the number of mantras remains two hundred and four (204). Again, at the beginning [of each], one should place the Kriyā-bīja known as Kāmarāja.

Having combined them as before, the number of mantras is 204. Thus, having calculated them in this way, the mantras total 612, which is six hundred and twelve. Again, having substituted the name "Kalā" for the place of the name "Kālī," and having performed everything else remaining as before, that same number (612) results.

Thus, by substituting [the names], there are six thousand one hundred and twenty varieties of mantras. This is the procedure for a single day. In the second and subsequent procedures, at the end of the sequence shown, when the Vidyās such as Śaṅkaravallabhā are joined solely in place of Śakti, the mantras [are formed].

There would be sixty-one thousand two hundred. According to the aforementioned method, by adding the names Lakṣmī, Jayā, and so forth—though mentioned in the immediately preceding verse—to the place of Kālī and the others, forty-two mantras increased by eighty-four become additional. Thus:

And regarding the sequence of a single day (65484), if one is unable to perform it in ten days, then one should divide the recitation for a single day into five parts and perform the recitation over fifty days. Even if that is not possible, the established tradition is that it should be completed with one hundred days for each individual name. Of this—
Since the recitation [of the names] possesses the same fruit as that declared for the *nāmapārāyaṇa*, no separate fruit is mentioned. As it has been said:
"The wise person who thus performs the *nāmapārāyaṇa* daily shall enjoy all pleasures here in this world and, at the end, go to the abode of the Goddess. (18)
102) Now, indicating the sequence of the eternal ignorance of time (*kālanityāvidyā*) and the procedure for the recitation of the *Nāmapārāyaṇa*, he speaks by way of salutation:

O Tripurā! Your names, which are indeed extremely secret, arise from the consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*, joined in pairs in successive order and suffixed with the vowels starting from *a* and ending with *au*; likewise, they arise from those same consonants joined with the vowels ending in *au*.
O Consort of Bhairava! Salutations to those others beyond the twenty thousand! || 19 ||

"O Tripure! O Consort of Bhairava!"—this address is intended to signify the presiding deity of the Traipura Vidyā consisting of three syllables, which will be described hereafter; thus, "O Tripurabhairavi! As it has been stated in the *Śrītripurārṇava*:
I bow to the Goddess Tripurabhairavī, the supreme sovereign power of the universe, whose activity encompasses all names and forms within the syllable.
And so forth. The meaning of this word has already been determined part by part, and will be further determined below.
Moreover, Bhairava is the supreme light whose nature consists in swallowing the universe, which is non-dual in essence;
and that which is his very nature, being conjoined through inherence (*samavāya*), is called the Heart (*hṛdaya*).
The power of supreme sovereignty is that which fulfills the duties subject to it. As it is said in the *Bhargaśikhā*:
"Death, time, the aggregate of the digits (kalās), the web of transformations, and the habitual nature of cognition—"
Then he swallows up all that has arisen from the conceptual constructions of unity and multiplicity.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Vīrāvalī*:

"Behold that Consciousness (citi) residing within the body, whose brilliance is equal to the fire of cosmic destruction, wherein all things go to dissolution and the accumulations of the principles (tattva-saṃcaya) are consumed."
Thus, such consciousness of Bhairava is designated by the word "consort" (*patnī*), which indicates an uninterrupted state of constant union. This is also stated in the *Śivasūtras*:
"In the conjunction of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), there is the dissolution of the universe" (1.6).

Other meanings will be explained further on. Here, within the *tripurāvidyās* that are about to be demonstrated, for each syllable there are five hundred and seventy-six colors of the full mandala; among these—

In the first [set] of these Vidyās, the thirty-six phonemes of the Tattvas exist as the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable. The second set of phonemes consists of the *kāmarāja* seed-syllable, and they are joined by means of the coalescence (*sandhi*) into the form *ā ī*. The third, however, consist of the *śakti* seed-syllable. Thus, those Vidyās amount to seven hundred and thirty-six.
Twenty thousand [verses] arise. This has been stated in the *Kādimata*:
"In the first [section], there should be the syllables of the full mandala in their initial sequence;
then, in the second, there are the syllables of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) in the sequence of the winds."
"The third [set] consists entirely of fire; thus, these three-syllabled vidyās are declared in sequence to be the sources of all siddhis for those belonging to the three cities.
Their application and fruit are described in that very same place:
Having placed these [mantras] in a book and established it upon a pedestal, one should worship it;
for wherever this is done, pestilence, misfortune, planetary afflictions, famine, and enemies [shall perish].
For one who worships daily, there shall be no occurrence of elemental spirits, untimely death, or malevolent rites within his city and so forth; all his desired goals shall be accomplished.
"Thirty-six, seven hundred, and twenty thousand—that is declared to be their number; their repetition brings about the attainment thereof. (17–21).
Having thus internalized the entire purport, the determination for the accomplishment of the aforementioned Vidyā is stated as follows:

By the thirty-five letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*, which have reached the stage of patience (*kṣānti*). Of what kind? "Beginning with vowels" (*svarādi*): here, by the word "vowel" (*svara*), only the first vowel is intended; thus, it means those for which the vowel *a* is the beginning or first.

"By thirty-six consonants" means by the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) and their true natures (*satattva*). Since Mahānityā consists of both Śiva and Śakti, being of a dual nature, the first vowel—which is of the same nature as her—is also of a dual nature, consisting of both vowels and consonants; such is the secret oral tradition of the Tantras. As it has been said:
In that very place (p. 104):
Now, [the worship] of the sixteen Nityās by means of the bodies of the thirty-six principles (tattvas).
Through the phonemes, the mantras produced from them, and the yantras, one gradually attains the nature of Time.
I shall describe the ritual applications which are the causes for attaining various desired goals;
through the distinction between the knowledge and the worship of these, the mantras of the student (varṇin) achieve perfection.
The vowels are sixteen and eternal; they are joined with the consonants from *ka* to *kṣa*.
Within them reside the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), the lords of the groups (*varga-nāthas*), who consist of ninefold aspects. (25.1)
Thus: likewise, by means of the syllables *ā* and *ī* accompanied by the prefix *ā-ī*, following the sequence of two by two and joined with one another through mutual sandhi,
[they are combined] with the vowel *ā* of the second syllable known as Kāmarāja in each respective Vidyā.

The meaning is "by those joined according to the prescribed rules. Likewise, by repeating the phrase "by vowels and so forth," and taking it to mean "those which have sixteen vowels at their beginning," the sequence begins with *a-ā-ī* and *akā-ī*, and continues until *akṣā-ī*. Similarly, for *ā-ā-ī* and *ākā-ī*, and so on.
Thus, the number of names is five hundred and seventy-six (*pañcaśatāni ṣaṭsaptatyuttarāṇi*). Now, with those...
Furthermore, with the thirty-five consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*,

combined with the sixteen vowels and arranged in the sequence of *ka, kā, ki, kī*, and so forth— occupying the positions of the letters of the Vidyā-mantra as before— one should proceed with the middle conjunction (*madhyasaṃhitā*) as follows: *ka-ā-ī*, *kakā-ī*, *kakhā-ī*, and so on.
From *kakṣā-ī* up to *kā-ā-ī*, then *kākā-ī*, *kākhā-ī*, and so forth,
ending with *kākṣā-ī*; likewise from *kṣaḥ ā-ī* up to *kṣaḥ kṣā-ī*— the number of these names is twenty-one thousand one hundred and sixty (*20,160*).

Thus, those names of yours which arise from the colors of the full mandala— names that are indeed extremely secret, most secret mysteries, and the very forms of the Traipura Vidyā, exceeding twenty thousand in number— to those Vidyās, salutations; they are to be revered.
This is the meaning. Thus, that appropriate number (20,736) has been previously explained.
This procedure for the *japa* should be understood from the very mouth of the venerable teacher (*ārādhya*). However, in the *Śrīdevīrahasya*, it is said:
"Having adorned the *mātṛkā* with *ā* and *ī*, and having adorned it with the *haṃsa*..."
O Śivā, the mantra-practitioner should recite the root-vidyā, which consists of Śiva and Śakti.
Thus [it is said].

Herein, this is the sequence: first one should utter the Root-Vidyā, then the Kālavidyā ending with *haṃsa*. The thorough knowledge of the Daily Nityā-Vidyā is according to the method stated in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*).
Having calculated the sum of the auspicious days (*kalyahargaṇa*) and divided it by the number of time-cycles (*kāla-vidyā*) as previously stated, one discards the obtained completed cycles.

Dividing the remaining number of days by the number of full cycles (*pūrṇamaṇḍala*), the first syllable of the *nityā* for that day is produced by counting from the result plus one. As for the remainder:
Divide by thirty-six; having added one to the quotient, make the first syllable endowed with that many vowels.

Having fashioned the second syllable as measured by the remaining number and joined with the vowel *ā*, it becomes the daily *nityā* for that day. Thus, of the daily *nityā-vidyā* produced in this manner, the first syllable is that which is joined with the vowel.

Furthermore, the recitation (japa) should be performed according to the previously mentioned method, starting from the vowel of that [syllable] up to the vowel of that [same syllable]. It should be understood that these alone are the *tattvanityā* [mantras]. As for the sequence of the *paryāyanityā*, however, it should be understood as before, by counting the number of days starting from the day of initiation (*dīkṣā*). This being the case in the present Kali age:

Starting from the beginning, one mantra for each day occurs in sequence. In that regard, through the completion of the full recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) of the mantras, on those few days remaining at the end of that age, two mantras must be added each day to complete the cycle. As it is said in the *Śrītantrarāja*:

"In each successive day of the Yugas beginning with Kṛta, those Vidyās, whose nature is that of the Tattvas, are traditionally taught one by one; at the end, however, they are remembered as being two by two.
(Pañcārthabhāṣya 25). All of this has been demonstrated in detail by the author of the Manoramā commentary on that [text]; therefore, enough of this elaboration.
Thus, concluding the praise, the teacher points out the specific reason why it should be heeded by the virtuous:
"Having fixed the mind upon this, this praise should be understood skillfully by the wise."
In the first verse, where it is clearly stated that the mind of Bhāratī was focused on Tripurā with undivided attention,
there is a sequence of one, two, and three words.
The method for extracting the mantra, consisting of as many syllables as there are feet in your [verse], has been explained along with its specific details and endowed with the authentic tradition.

"Tripure" refers to Tripurabhāratī, the well-known Bhāratī who is associated with the preceding word. For in this Vidyā, generally in all three *kūṭas*, even during the worship of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) portions of the letters, [the following applies].

This is because it is primarily endowed with the fruit consisting of the radiance of the expansion of eloquent speech (*vāk-sūkti-prasara-sphuraṇa*). Here, the use of the word *bhāratī* (speech) is intentional. This praise just mentioned [is characterized] by the wise as being composed of strings of words and phrases of unimpeded flow, which are to be attained through the grace of *Bhāratī*. For this very reason...
Virtuous people who desire his grace should, having fixed their minds upon him— minds that are absorbed in Tripura and attached to the Goddess of Speech—
thoroughly understand and contemplate [this work] so that it may become skillful. By the word "by the wise" (budhaiḥ),
it is implied that only they possess the capacity for the immediate knowledge of extracting the mantras, and not those of dull intellect.

Anticipating the objection, "Is this not [merely] due to skill in concentration for the sake of comprehension?", he provides a qualification based on a specific cause, indicating his own poetic ingenuity (*vicchitti-vaidagdhyam*) in composing the present verse:
"ananya-manasah," meaning one whose mind does not exist elsewhere— that is, one whose mind is focused solely on that praise.

The meaning is: for the sake of that practitioner who has his mind fixed solely upon this hymn composed by me; or alternatively, it should be understood by supplying the word "my" (*asmat*)—that is, "this hymn is mine," whose mind is undistracted and whose consciousness is one with the Goddess alone. This refers to the first verse of the initial section.

The word "clearly" (*sphuṭam*) is used by virtue of its denotative power (*abhidhā-śakti*), and not through implication (*ākṣepa*) or other means; it refers to the sequence of one, two, and three feet—that is, the order of the first, second, and third quarters.

Here, it should be understood that the words "two" (*dvi*) and "three" (*tri*) have the sense of ordinal suffixes (*pūraṇapratyaya*). By the number of syllables in those respective quarters, [the meter] of that *vṛtta* [is defined].
By the number of feet being equal to the number of syllables— meaning, by virtue of the first verse consisting of the syllables *aim* and so forth,

the second foot consists of the second syllable *klīm*, and the third foot consists of the third syllable *saur*— and because of the qualifier "situated here" (*atra sthitā*), the *ha* therein refers to the *visarga*.

By performing [the procedure], the state of being with the *visarga* is obtained. The method for extracting the mantra (*mantroddhāravidhi*) has been declared; the procedure for extracting the Vidyā (*vidyoddhāravidhāna*) has been explained and specified.
Now, one might ask: since this extraction of the mantra is shown in many Āgamas, what is its distinction?
In response to this inquiry, he says "by the *viśeṣas*. This means together with the *viśeṣas*, which are the specific forms of the Tripurā-vidyā;

and those *viśeṣas* have been extracted therein. To show that this is not his own invention, he says "the authentic tradition" (*satsampradāya*). It is "authentic" (*sat*) because it is praiseworthy due to its faultlessness, and it is a "tradition" (*sampradāya*), meaning a lineage of oral instruction; [the work] is endowed with that.

The meaning is "obtained from the mouth of the Guru. Thus, by stating that the extraction of these mantras has been performed here by me only after they were received through the authentic tradition (*satsampradāya*), any suspicion regarding their lack of authority is dispelled. Therefore, [the lineage] proceeds from Paramaśiva down through one's own guru in an unbroken succession.
107) It has been indicated that the efficacy of mantras and the like depends upon being understood; otherwise, there would be the occurrence of a succession of misfortunes.
As it is said in the Vāmakeśvara:
Those who are devoid of the lineage and are arrogant merely on account of their knowledge—
for them, through the violation of their commitments, the Marīcis manifest as portents of ruin.
Thus it is said elsewhere:
"Those of small intelligence who have taken up mantras on their own own accord suffer."

Thus it is said. Furthermore, just as in the prologue (*prastāvanā*) of a literary work such as a drama composed by a great poet, the praise characterized by the indication of the dramatic subject matter to be performed is understood with undivided attention only by those who are sensitive and virtuous. In this regard:
By means of the sequence of words characterized by the assumption of one, two, or more roles directed toward the deeds of the principal hero,
the meaning— that the play is to be performed and contemplated until the conclusion of the number of acts— is also understood through this elliptical expression (samāsokti). || 20 ||

Setting aside all consideration of whether this work of mine is praiseworthy or not, may my eloquent composition attain fruitfulness solely through its utility in generating devotion to you; even in that regard,
the attribution of ownership to me is in fact produced by superimposition alone, arising from the utter helplessness of my speech in the presence of the aesthetic flavor of devotion (*bhaktirasa*).
With the intention that devotion alone is the agent because of its inherent possibility, [the author], setting aside self-importance, says:
"Whether it be faulty or faultless—what is the use of this reflection? Surely only that person who possesses devotion toward You will recite this hymn."
For even though I have firmly resolved within myself upon my own insignificance, this has certainly been composed by me as well, since I have been forcibly made vocal by devotion to you. (21)

The phrase "the wife of Bhairava" is to be supplied from the preceding verse. Let this hymn be "faulty"— meaning defective due to its lack of aesthetic flavor (*sārasatva*) and lack of poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*)— or rather, let it be "faultless," meaning free from defects based on words and sentence-meanings such as meaninglessness (*anarthakatva*), harshness of sound (*śrutikaṭutva*), and so forth.
Because it has emerged [from the context] and is endowed with aesthetic flavor (*sārasa*) and poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*), let it be faultless.
The *loṭ* suffix is used here in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*). What is the use of this reflection or deliberation? It is purposeless. Not so.
The word *kiñcit* means "something"; *vā* is used in the sense of "also. By changing the grammatical case (*kāraka-pariṇāma*), the word *stotram* (hymn) is to be construed with both sentences.

He states the reason for this: that person who possesses devotion toward You, characterized by unsurpassed love—surely, as a certainty, that person will recite this hymn; indeed, they will certainly recite it. There is no doubt in this matter.

The suspicion of error: [one might argue] that because he is afraid of the terror of birth and so forth, this is what is expressed by the word *jana* (people). If this much alone were sufficient for my labor to be fruitful, then this work must necessarily be accepted by those possessed of devotion. Indeed, unlike the compositions of a great poet, there is no need here for a preliminary examination of whether there are faults or no faults.
There is some mental construction regarding the act of abandoning and undertaking [the composition].
One might object: "Surely, by the creation of faultless poetry and so forth, there would be an exceeding weightiness of the agent's agency";
to this, he says "saṃcitya" (having intentionally). This is because, through devotion to You—devotion directed toward You—it is done impetuously and suddenly.
Reflecting that even I— who, lacking discrimination, have made myself talkative and rendered speech redundant, and who, due to my dull intellect,
have composed this hymn despite being unworthy of praise— have thereby brought about a profound sense of insignificance within myself as the instigator of such an act.
Considering that the simplicity characterized by the metaphorical attribution of agency is certain and beyond doubt,

[the phrase] "is being born" (saṃjāyamāna) means "exists" or "arises. Since devotion alone, having become the motivating cause, has rendered me helpless and impelled me to compose this work, there is no weightiness in my status as the author of the hymn.
Because [agency] has been refuted, the notion of figurative agency in me—such as "the chariot goes"—is, in short, a source of great shame.
Alternatively, one might ask: "But why is the investigation into faultlessness and so forth not possible to perform? To this he says:
because, having been forcibly made talkative by devotion to You, and having been led to impudence, even I have [spoken thus] regarding myself.

Even after reflecting upon and thoroughly considering the extreme firmness of my intellect, the lightness arising and manifesting within it, and the cleverness and fickleness involved in composing this praise— since this has been composed [in such a manner],
there is no primary intention on my part regarding the calculation of faultlessness and so forth in this treatise.

When a thorough investigation is conducted from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), it is stated in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* (1.1.3), "This indeed is the most excellent among all tastes," that the true essence of the primary taste is consciousness (*saṃvit*)—
a mass of light and bliss filled with the wonder of full-blown selfhood (*pūrṇāhantā*).

It can be experienced by connoisseurs who possess immersion in that state. Consequently, here, primarily through the excellence of the passion (*rati*) directed toward the deity, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) characterized as devotion (*bhakti-bhāva*) is manifested.

As ancillaries to that [heroic sentiment], other sentiments such as the peaceful (*śānta*), the compassionate (*karuṇa*), and the marvelous (*adbhuta*), as well as verbal and semantic ornaments (*śabdārthālaṅkāra*), should be inferred by those who know them according to their occurrence. For example:

*dṛṣṭvā sambhrama* ("Having seen, with agitation..."), *yatsadyo vacasām* ("That which immediately of words..."), *ekaikaṃ tava* ("Each one of yours..."), *ye tvāṃ pāṇḍureti* ("Those who [address] you as 'pale'...").

In the verse beginning with "devānām," there is the manifestation of the marvelous sentiment (*adbhuta-rasa*); in the verses beginning with "yannitye" and "kṣoṇī," there is the perception of the compassionate sentiment (*kāruṇya-rasa*);
in "vāme," there is the experience of the tranquil sentiment (*śānta-rasa*); and in "ye sindūra" and "cañcakāñcana," there is the erotic sentiment of separation (*vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*).

The term *ārbhaṭī* [is used] for the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the marvelous (*adbhuta*); *jāta* for the erotic of enjoyment (*sambhoga-śṛṅgāra*) and the peaceful (*śānta*); *caṇḍī* for the marvelous and the heroic (*vīra*), as in "Lakṣmī in the royal palace";
and *śabdānām* for the marvelous and the fearful (*bhayānaka*), because the essence of emotion (*bhāva-ātman*) occurs elsewhere.

It should be understood that because the beginning and the end are framed solely by the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of devotion, the intended purport (*tātparya*) regarding that very [devotion] is perceived for all the intermediate elements as well. In this same manner, the semantic ornaments (*arthālaṅkāra*) such as simile (*upamā*) and the phonetic ornaments (*śabdālaṅkāra*) such as alliteration (*anuprāsa*) are to be understood. Furthermore, the author of the hymn has [expressed] himself here...

Because its brevity is manifested, because the word "light" (*laghu*) is employed, or because it brings about swiftness, this hymn is renowned in the world as the *Laghustava* (The Light Praise). May there be auspiciousness! 21.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Laghustava* within the *Pañcastavī*, composed by the venerable teacher of Dharma,
written by the illustrious Mahāmāheśvara Paṇḍita Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrin.
In this first hymn, the root known as the *traipurakaṇḍa* mantra has been firmly established; it is a tree of the *Kulasundarī* mantra whose spreading branches and sub-branches are in full bloom,
filling those who take refuge in it with various fruits overflowing with aesthetic essence (*rasa*).
This complete commentary [is offered] out of a desire to benefit others. || 1 ||
